text:
Ruling — During the battle phase, when exactly can players play spells/interact (including battle spells and during formation setup), and does deployment happen simultaneously for both players?

You can play cards during any of the specifically marked priority windows in the turn structure. In 1v1: Planning (refresh resources, draw 2, draft, gather/activate resources, play mods from hand) is followed by Battle, split into two phases. Phase 1: the initiating team attacks into the non-initiating team's regions, priority window, non-initiating team declares blocks (and may send their own units to counter-attack), priority window, combat damage, priority window. Phase 2 mirrors this with the non-initiating team attacking into the initiating team's regions. Then Regroup (return units to your region, reset damage/buffs, erase spell tokens), then Deployment (play cards/mods from hand or bin, then end turn). If you play Magic: the Gathering, the interaction timing windows during battle are essentially the same as in that game.

(Answered by designer, designer, 2025-01-11)
title: During the battle phase, when exactly can players play spells/interact (including battle spells and during formation setup), and does deployment happen simultaneously for both players?

Ruling — For Flame Shield's "negate all effects": does "effect" include things like unit abilities and mods, does it only affect cards currently on the stack, and can Flame Shield itself be countered by something else on the stack?

An effect is a played card, or an activated/triggered ability - basically anything that goes on the stack. So "negate all effects" stops anything on the stack below it (anything above it would already resolve first). Yes, it can be countered - since it's an effect, any "negate target effect" would negate it.

Ruling — If I control Borrower of Forms copying an opponent's unit (e.g. Good Whale), and the opponent casts Recall targeting that copied unit, can Recall also target Borrower of Forms itself? And if the copied unit leaves play before Borrower of Forms resolves, does Borrower of Forms as a whole fizzle, or just its copy effect?

Recall doesn't target (you choose what to recall on resolution). Borrower of Forms can't be recalled by Recall while it's still resolving, since it isn't a unit in play yet at that point, it's an effect. If Borrower of Forms has no legal target when it resolves, it fizzles and goes to the bin. However, since Recall also recalls 'spell effects', and Borrower of Forms counts as a spell effect while resolving, Recall could actually recall Borrower of Forms in that situation.

(Answered by designer, designer, 2025-06-28)

Ruling — Does an area-of-effect ability that deals damage to each unit (like Bellowing Boulder's) count as 'targeting' those units for effects that care about being targeted? Also, when a spell is grafted onto another card, do you need to pay its activation cost (the part in brackets) at the time you graft it, or only when the host's trigger later uses the grafted ability?

Only effects that explicitly say 'target' count as targeting; Bellowing Boulder's area damage does not target. Separately, you don't need to pay the additional cost in brackets to graft a card on. That cost is only paid when the host card's ability triggers and you want to use the grafted effect. For example, you can graft Immolate onto something for just 1 mana with no sacrifice needed to graft it, and later when the host triggers, you'd pay the sacrifice cost to use Immolate's effect.

(Answered by designer, designer, 2025-06-30)

In FFA, you can only attack the two players adjacent to you (left and right), since Intent cards only cover those two directions. You still keep getting shards from all opponents though.

Ruling — Is the spell itself (e.g. Squish, Fight, Battle) the source of the damage it deals, or is the unit dealing/receiving the damage the source? Does damage dealt via Squish or Fight trigger 'whenever I am dealt damage by a spell' effects like Ember of Life? And for attribute-caring mods like the Virus Powerful, do we check the attributes of the targeted unit, or of the spell that is resolving?

The unit is the source of the damage, not the spell, so damage from Squish/Fight won't trigger 'dealt damage by a spell' effects like Ember of Life. Likewise, only the attributes of the targeted unit matter, not the spell -- so a Virus like Powerful (or Tidepool Terror) should be attached to the unit dealing the damage, not to the spell.

Can you play Fight with only 1 valid target in play, or with 0 valid targets? Can Megadeath be put on the stack if there is only 1 unit present in the region? And does the Fight portion of Megadeath's graft count as targeting 0 units in that case?

No to all of these -- you can't play Hush Mush without a target, can't play Fight with only 1 or 0 valid targets, and can't put Megadeath (with its Fight graft) on the stack if there's only 1 unit in the region. This is exactly why Caleb is considering allowing parts of grafts to fail without fizzling the entire ability -- right now it's treated the same as an additional cost you're unable to pay.

Ruling — Does 'negate' only work on things currently on the stack, meaning it can't negate an already-resolved passive/static ability in play? For example, if Arc Lightning triggers a Rune Channeler's graft abilities (putting effects on the stack), would Flame Shield negate those triggered effects but not negate a static ability already in play, such as an Augment that turns units into 3/3s?

Correct -- 'effect' is defined as something on the stack, so Flame Shield would negate Arc Lightning and Rune Channeler's triggers, but not an already-resolved static/augmented ability in play. To stop that you would need something that specifically says a unit 'loses all abilities' (like Suppression Field or Monke), or you could just kill the unit with the ability.

Ruling — Why does Hooba-Nan's 'when I attack' ability include the clause 'if I am still in formation,' while Hooba-Lin's similar ability does not need it?

Hooba-Nan's ability is unique because it creates units in the slots adjacent to it. If Hooba-Nan is killed before its ability resolves, there would be no formation slots relative to it to place the new units in -- the 'if I am still in formation' clause exists so the ability simply doesn't work if there's no Hooba-Nan in play to place bananas around. Hooba-Lin's ability instead creates a 1/1 unit in the player's formation generally, so even if Hooba-Lin dies before its ability resolves, there are still formation slots available for the new unit.

(Answered by designer, designer, 2025-11-23)

text:
Ruling — For a triggered ability whose effect includes an X value based on board state (like the number of adjacent allies), is X calculated when the trigger is put on the stack, or when it resolves?

Everything checks on resolution. There are some cards where the condition is baked into the trigger itself, like Luminary Leader, but any trigger will check its effect on resolution. Flamebreath Initiate's trigger is "When I attack or block" and the effect is the rest (create a Fireball X+1 based on adjacent allies), which is calculated based on the X value when it resolves. Luminary Leader's trigger is "When I attack in a formation of four or more units" and the effect is "Draw a card" — nothing to check on resolution there.

(Answered by designer, designer, 2025-12-18)
Related cards: Luminary Leader, Flamebreath Initiate

100.1 In Algomancy, each player's goal is to eliminate all of their opponents. A player is eliminated by bringing their life total to 0. See rule 104.

100.2 The game is played as a series of global turns. Every player goes through each turn's phases together. See rule 500.
 Example: One player finishing planning does not start the battle, and one player finishing deployment does not end the turn: both players move on together, into the same turn 2.
title: CR 100.2

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 101. Golden Rules
101.1 Printed text beats the general rules and the engine's defaults. Where a card's printed text says something different from a general rule or a default, the card is followed, unless the designer has stated a different intent for that card (rule 101.2). See rules 400.4b, 101.2.
title: CR 101.1

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 101. Golden Rules
101.2 Where the designer has stated that his intent for a card differs from its printed wording, the card works as the designer intended. See rule 802.
 Example: Crevice Lurker prints "Abilities cost [one] more to activate or trigger during battle". By Caleb's stated intent it also taxes the {Resonant} attribute's trigger.
title: CR 101.2

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 101. Golden Rules
101.3 A designer answer in the rules Q&A (RAQ) takes precedence over this project's own rulings. Where the two disagree, this document states the designer's answer. See rule 101.2.
title: CR 101.3

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 101. Golden Rules
101.4 When a card's text can be read two ways and neither reading is absurd, take the reading that lets more things happen. See rule 101.1.
title: CR 101.4

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 101. Golden Rules
101.5 An effect that cannot do everything it says does as much as it can. A part of an effect that cannot happen does not stop the other parts from happening. This does not make half of an action happen: a fight or an exchange that has lost one of its two units does not happen at all (704). See rule 704.
 Example: Recall: "Each player recalls a unit and loses 2 life." A player with no unit to recall still loses 2 life.
 Example: Amphivore carries two grafts, Flame Juggle and Ralph, and its ability runs three times. The first pass gives Amphivore to the opponent and makes three 1/1s; later passes cannot give it again, so their "If you do" makes nothing, but Flame Juggle still happens all three times.
101.5a A part of an effect that begins "If you do" happens only if the action before it was done. Parts that are not joined this way are independent. See rule 101.5.
 Example: Shoreline Specter: "After combat, you may recall target ally. If you do, each opponent loses 2 life." If its controller declines the recall, no opponent loses life.
101.5b Paying a cost is not done "as much as you can". A cost that cannot be paid in full is not paid at all, and the effect it pays for does not happen. See rule 111.
 Example: Lost Guardian with Darkblast grafted must pay [Discard a card] twice. With one card in hand nothing is discarded and nothing happens.
title: CR 101.5–101.5b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 101. Golden Rules
101.6 Every effect is specific to the region it happens in. It never affects anything in another region, and it treats the players and cards in other regions as if they do not exist. A card that says "all" or "each" means all or each in this region. See rule 601.
 Example: Cosmic Reversal, cast in one region, leaves a spell unit in another region alone.
 Example: Molten Riftbreaker dies in its controller's home region while a battle goes on elsewhere. Its "negate all allied spells" does not reach the spell on the battle region's stack.
title: CR 101.6

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 101. Golden Rules
(continues 101.6: Every effect is specific to the region it happens in. It never affects anything in another region, and it treats the players and cards in other regions as if they do not exist. A card that says "all" or "each" means all…)
101.6a Regions limit what effects can reach and count. In the digital client they do not limit what players may see: a player may read what happens in a region they are not in. See rule 601.
title: CR 101.6a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 102. Players, Ownership and Control
102.1 Each player has their own region and their own life total. See rules 601, 103.1d.
title: CR 102.1

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 102. Players, Ownership and Control
102.2 "Each opponent" means each opponent in the region where the effect happens. See rules 101.6, 601.
 Example: Bloated Manablub dies in a region where its opponent is present: that opponent loses 3 life and its controller loses none.
102.2a If no opponent is in that region, an "each opponent" effect affects nobody. This is normal during deployment, when each player is alone in their own region. See rule 601.
 Example: Bloated Manablub's "Each opponent loses 3 life" resolved in a region holding no opponent takes no life from anyone.
title: CR 102.2–102.2a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 102. Players, Ownership and Control
102.3 "Each player" means each player in the region where the effect happens. See rule 101.6.
 Example: Recall ("Each player recalls a unit and loses 2 life") cast in a battle makes both players present in that battle region lose 2 life.
title: CR 102.3

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 102. Players, Ownership and Control
102.4 A card's owner is the player whose card it is. Taking control of a card does not change its owner, and neither does moving it into or out of a player's hand, bin or cache, even another player's, nor applying it as a mod. A card that goes into a draft pack, a deck or a recycle pile leaves its ownership behind there: whoever next takes it out owns it. That holds in constructed too, where each player has a deck and a recycle pile of their own: a stolen card that goes into the thief's deck or recycle pile becomes the thief's. See rules 400.4a, 400.4c.
 Example: A unit whose control has been taken is recalled: the player it was stolen from is still the card's owner.
 Example: The same recalled unit goes to the hand of the player who controls it, not its owner's hand.
 Example: A stolen unit is recalled to the hand of the player who stole it and played again from there. Its owner is still the player it was stolen from.
 Example: A stolen card in the thief's hand is recycled. Its ownership stays behind in the recycle pile, and the player who next takes it out owns it.
 Example: Collect Remains takes a card out of the opponent's bin into its caster's hand: the opponent still owns it.
 Example: A player augments a unit with a card another player owns, out of their own hand: the mod is still that other player's card, and the player who applied it is recorded apart.
102.4a A token is owned by the player who created it. See rule 304.
 Example: Accelerated Germination makes two tokens owned by its caster; an Arcane Echo copy of an opposing token is owned by the copier; a token taken with Download stays owned by its creator.
title: CR 102.4–102.4a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 102. Players, Ownership and Control
102.5 A card's controller is the player who controls it. The controller and the owner of a card can be different players. See rules 711, 400.4.
 Example: Uglk: each player puts a unit from their own bin into play under the opponent's control. The opponent controls the unit; the card is still owned by the player whose bin it came from.
102.5a A player who plays a card, or puts it into play, out of another player's zone becomes its controller, not its owner. See rule 400.4.
 Example: Wake the Dead playing a unit out of the opponent's bin: the caster controls it, and the opponent still owns it.
 Example: The unit Wake the Dead plays out of the opponent's bin is still the opponent's card once it is in play.
title: CR 102.5–102.5a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 102. Players, Ownership and Control
102.6 "You" on a card means the controller of the effect. An instruction that names no player (such as "Gain rot") is done by the controller of the effect. See rule 102.5.
 Example: Primordial Coalescence (“Create three Wraiths and gain 2 Rot.”) gives its controller the Wraiths and the rot. Thought Extraction aimed at the opponent makes the opponent discard, and its “You gain 1 rot” still goes to its controller.
title: CR 102.6

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 102. Players, Ownership and Control
(continues 102.6: "You" on a card means the controller of the effect. An instruction that names no player (such as "Gain rot") is done by the controller of the effect.)
102.6a On a mod, "you" means the controller of the unit the mod is on. A mod applied to another player's unit is controlled by that unit's controller, with its ability. See rule 720.
 Example: Pathogenic Enclave augmented onto an enemy unit: when that unit despawns, its controller's tokens are deleted, not yours.
title: CR 102.6a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 102. Players, Ownership and Control
(continues 102.6: "You" on a card means the controller of the effect. An instruction that names no player (such as "Gain rot") is done by the controller of the effect.)
102.6b "The deck" means the deck of the effect's controller: the shared deck in live draft, and that player's own deck in constructed. See rule 401.
 Example: In constructed, Foretell glimpses the top card of its controller's own deck and leaves the opponent's deck alone. In live draft it glimpses the top card of the shared deck.
title: CR 102.6b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 102. Players, Ownership and Control
(continues 102.6: "You" on a card means the controller of the effect. An instruction that names no player (such as "Gain rot") is done by the controller of the effect.)
102.6c When an effect needs a cost paid before it can happen, the player who would control the effect pays it. If that player does not pay, the effect does not happen. See rule 111.
 Example: With an opponent's Crevice Lurker in the battle, a triggered ability asks its own controller whether to pay [one]; paying puts it on the stack.
title: CR 102.6c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 102. Players, Ownership and Control
102.7 An ally is a unit under your control in the region where the effect is happening. See rules 110, 601.
title: CR 102.7

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 102. Players, Ownership and Control
(continues 102.7: An ally is a unit under your control in the region where the effect is happening.)
102.7a A unit is its own ally. Only the word "another" leaves the source out. See rule 110.
 Example: Shoreline Specter's "recall target ally" may target the Specter itself.
 Example: Riftwalker's "another target ally in my formation" offers its column-mate and not itself.
title: CR 102.7a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 102. Players, Ownership and Control
(continues 102.7: An ally is a unit under your control in the region where the effect is happening.)
102.7b Ally and enemy follow control, not ownership. A unit you have taken control of is your ally and its owner's enemy for as long as you control it. See rule 711.
 Example: A Good Whale whose control was taken is offered to its new controller as an ally target, and not to its owner.
title: CR 102.7b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 102. Players, Ownership and Control
102.8 An enemy is a unit not under your control in the region where the effect is happening. See rule 102.7.
 Example: The same stolen Good Whale is offered to its owner as an enemy target, and not to the player who now controls it.
title: CR 102.8

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 103. Starting the Game
103.1 To set up a live draft game, follow these steps in order. See rule 902.
103.1a Choose the elements the deck is built from. A game of 2 or 3 players uses 3 elements. See rules 105, 902.
103.1b Shuffle all the cards of the chosen elements together, with the hybrid cards for each pair of chosen elements, to form the shared deck. See rules 401, 902.
103.1c Randomly choose one player to have the initiative. See rules 500, 508.
103.1d Each player's life total starts at 30. See rule 112.
103.1e Give each player two prismites. They start dormant. See rule 106.
103.1f Deal each player 16 cards from the shared deck: 4 for their starting hand, 10 for their pack, and 2 for the draw of their first turn. The 4 and the 2 together are the player's opening hand of 6 cards. See rules 409, 503.
title: CR 103.1–103.1f

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 103. Starting the Game
103.2 In live draft, the first turn's draw is dealt with the opening hand, so players do not draw in the draw step of the first turn. See rules 503, 103.3a.
title: CR 103.2

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 103. Starting the Game
103.3 In constructed there is no shared deck and there are no packs. Each player plays from their own deck. See rules 901, 503.
103.3a In constructed, the first turn has a draw phase like every later turn: each player draws 4 cards, then puts 2 cards from their hand on the bottom of their deck. Print gives the draw phase; no source says the first turn takes it, which is the client's convention. See rules 503, 103.3b, 103.2.
title: CR 103.3–103.3a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 103. Starting the Game
(continues 103.3: In constructed there is no shared deck and there are no packs. Each player plays from their own deck.)
103.3b In constructed, each player's opening hand is 4 cards. No source gives the constructed opening hand; it is the client's convention. See rules 103.3a, 103.2.
title: CR 103.3b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 104. Ending the Game
104.1 A player whose life total is 0 or less is eliminated (when that is checked: 104.1a). A life total can go below 0. See rule 112.
 Example: Haunting Memories sets a player's life total to twice the number of cards in all bins. With every bin empty that is 0, and that player loses.
 Example: A player at 3 life takes combat damage from an unblocked attacker and the game is over.
104.1a A player brought to 0 or less by an effect is not eliminated until that effect has finished: every life change one resolution of one effect makes (the unit damage is dealt in, 112.8) is applied first, and only then are the life totals checked. All the life changes of one combat damage sub-step are applied together in the same way, Lethal kills included (802.24a), and checked after all of them. Any other life change, such as rot damage, is checked the moment it happens; rot is dealt one player at a time, in initiative order, and is never simultaneous (112.13). A life cost that would by itself bring its payer to 0 cannot be paid at all (111). See rules 111, 112, 608.
 Example: Both players are at 1 life and Penance brings each of them to 0. Neither is eliminated until the effect has finished, and then both are at 0 together (104.1b).
 Example: A player at 0 is not out until the rest of the effect has happened: the effect finishes, and then the game ends.
 Example: Both players have more rot than life as deployment begins. The initiative player's rot is dealt first and that player loses before the other player's rot is dealt.
104.1b If both players are at 0 or less when the life totals are checked, the player with the higher life total wins; totals below 0 count, so a player at -1 beats a player at -3. If the totals are equal, the initiative player loses. See rule 104.1a.
 Example: An unblocked attacker and a Piercing blocker, in the same combat damage sub-step, bring both players to 0 or less. The player left on the higher total wins.
 Example: Both players are at 1 and one effect makes each lose 1. Both are at 0, the totals are equal, and the initiative player loses.
title: CR 104.1–104.1b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 104. Ending the Game
104.2 A player wins when all of their opponents have been eliminated. In a two-player game, when one player is eliminated the other player wins. See rule 104.1.
104.2a In a team game, a team wins when the entire opposing team has been eliminated. See rule 904.
title: CR 104.2–104.2a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 104. Ending the Game
104.3 In a game of more than two players, the game continues after a player is eliminated. The regions on either side of the eliminated player's region become neighbours. See rules 601, 903.
104.3a When a player is eliminated, their pack is recycled: put on the bottom of the deck. See rules 408, 409.
title: CR 104.3–104.3a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 104. Ending the Game
104.4 A player may concede. Conceding ends the game in the same way as that player being eliminated: the player who conceded loses. See rule 104.1.
 Example: A player concedes during deployment: the game is over and the other player has won.
104.4a A player may concede at any time, with no priority and in any phase, even while a decision is waiting on them. See rule 104.4.
 Example: A player who must choose a target for their own spell may concede instead; nothing else can be done until they choose.
title: CR 104.4–104.4a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 104. Ending the Game
104.5 A player who has to draw a card when their deck and their recycle pile are both empty has run out of cards. The recycle pile is shuffled into the deck before that (408.2b), and the bin never is. The player draws the cards there are, and then the game ends as 104.5a and 104.5b say. See rules 401, 408, 104.1.
 Example: A player whose deck is empty, with recycled cards behind the mark, draws: the recycled cards are shuffled in and the draw goes on. Nobody has run out of cards.
 Example: A player with 2 cards left and an empty recycle pile has to draw 4. They draw the 2, and then the draw that finds nothing ends the game.
104.5a In constructed, the player who ran out of cards loses the game, whatever the life totals. A Single Card Duel is constructed for this rule (D8.2). See rule D8.2.
 Example: A constructed player at 25 life has to draw with an empty deck and an empty recycle pile while the opponent is at 3. The player who had to draw loses.
 Example: The card step at the start of a turn is a draw too: from an empty deck and pile it ends the game.
104.5b With a shared deck (live draft), running out of cards ends the game, and the player with the higher life total wins, even if that is the player who had to draw. If the life totals are equal, the initiative player loses. See rule 104.1b.
 Example: In a live draft the shared deck runs out when a player at 12 life has to draw against an opponent at 9. The game ends, and the player at 12 wins.
 Example: If the two players are on the same life total, the initiative player loses.
104.5c Only a draw runs out of cards. Milling, revealing, glimpsing or caching from an empty deck and an empty recycle pile takes nothing, and the game goes on. See rule 401.4.
 Example: A player with an empty deck and an empty recycle pile is told to mill 2, and then to cache the top card of their deck. Nothing happens, and the game goes on.
title: CR 104.5–104.5c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 105. Elements and Affinity
105.1 The printed Manual names five elements: Fire, Water, Earth, Wood and Metal. The card pool this document describes has seven: those five, plus Light and Dark. See rule 902.
title: CR 105.1

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 105. Elements and Affinity
105.2 A hybrid card belongs to two elements. A live-draft deck is built from the cards of the selected elements together with the hybrid cards for each pair of them. See rule 902.
title: CR 105.2

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 105. Elements and Affinity
105.3 Affinity is a card's elemental requirement. A card shows it as element pips, and a player must meet it to play the card. See rules 202, 111.
 Example: With three Shards and no water, a player cannot play Curio Drifter [b]; with one water resource they can.
105.3a The 2023 Rulebook calls the affinity requirement the threshold.
title: CR 105.3–105.3a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 105. Elements and Affinity
105.4 A player's affinity for an element is the number of resources of that element the player has, other than dormant ones (see the dormant rule below). A requirement of N pips of one element is met when the player's affinity for that element is at least N. See rule 106.
 Example: With two wood resources, a player meets a [g][g] requirement however many times they play such cards.
105.4a Expended resources count toward affinity. Whether a resource has been expended this turn does not matter.
 Example: All-Consuming Blaze counts two open fire resources and one expended fire resource: 3 damage.
 Example: Sylvan Sprouting makes a 1/1 for each wood resource, expended ones included.
105.4b Meeting an affinity requirement uses nothing up. The same resources meet the affinity requirement of every card a player plays; only the mana cost is paid. See rule 111.
 Example: Two wood resources and many Shards pay for many [g][g] cards in one turn: the Shards pay the mana, the two wood meet every requirement.
105.4c A dormant resource gives no affinity until it is activated. See rule 106.
 Example: A dormant fire resource adds nothing to All-Consuming Blaze; two open and one expended fire resource deal 3.
title: CR 105.4–105.4c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 105. Elements and Affinity
105.5 Prismites and Shards give no affinity. A Prismite is not wild: it meets no element's requirement. See rule 106.
 Example: With six fire resources and two active Prismites, a player still cannot meet Dreadwave Devourer's [b][b]; two water resources meet it.
title: CR 105.5

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 105. Elements and Affinity
105.6 Card text can use a player's affinity as a number. "Your [r]" means the player's fire affinity: the number of fire resources they have, not counting dormant ones (see the dormant rule under 105's affinity count). See rule 107.
 Example: A player with two open fire resources and one expended fire resource casts All-Consuming Blaze: their [r] is 3, so it deals 3 damage. A dormant fire resource would not add to it.
title: CR 105.6

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 105. Elements and Affinity
105.7 Some effects let a player play a card ignoring affinity. Such a play does not check the card's affinity requirement. Ignoring affinity does not waive the mana cost: the cost is still paid unless the effect also makes the play free. See rules 403, 801.
 Example: A glimpsed card can be played without its pips, but a player who cannot pay its mana cannot play it.
 Example: Tides of the Cosmos plays a fire unit for a player whose only resources are water.
title: CR 105.7

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 105. Elements and Affinity
105.8 Applying a modification needs its affinity just as playing the card does. An augment from hand, a Virus applied in battle and a graft from hand or bin each require the card's affinity, and each pays its cost. See rules 720, 721, 722, 723.
title: CR 105.8

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 105. Elements and Affinity
105.9 Each game has a set of elements: in a live draft, the selected elements; in constructed, all seven. The game's elements limit nothing a player may create: by recycling or by exchanging a Prismite, a player may create an element resource of any of the seven elements. See rules 106, 901, 902.
 Example: In a fire-water-earth draft, a player may still recycle a card for a wood or a metal resource.
105.9a A player may create a resource of an element their deck has no cards of, in constructed and in a live draft alike.
 Example: In a fire-water-earth draft a Prismite is exchanged into wood.
title: CR 105.9–105.9a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 106. Resources
106.1 Resources are the source of mana: a player needs them to play cards. Resources are permanents, and they stay in play.
 Example: Two open water resources are two mana and pay for Curio Drifter; a turn later every resource is still in play.
title: CR 106.1

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 106. Resources
106.2 There are three kinds of resource: element resources, Prismites and Shards. Each element resource is of one element. See rule 105.
106.2a An element resource counts one toward its controller's affinity for its element, except while it is dormant (see 105). See rule 105.
title: CR 106.2–106.2a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 106. Resources
106.3 A resource is either dormant (face down) or active (face up). Every resource enters play dormant. Activating a resource turns it face up.
 Example: A Shard created by Swirling Shardform enters dormant.
106.3a Each player starts the game with two dormant Prismites. See rule 103.
title: CR 106.3–106.3a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 106. Resources
(continues 106.3: A resource is either dormant (face down) or active (face up). Every resource enters play dormant. Activating a resource turns it face up.)
106.3b A dormant resource cannot be expended for mana. It must be activated first. See rule 106.
 Example: Three dormant fire resources give no open mana and cannot pay Ignis Sprite.
title: CR 106.3b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 106. Resources
106.4 A player may activate at most two resources per turn. Activating a Shard counts toward that limit. See rule 502.
 Example: With a Shard and a Prismite activated, a third activation that turn is refused.
106.4a Resources are created and activated in the resource step of the planning phase. See rule 502.
title: CR 106.4–106.4a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 106. Resources
106.5 A resource can be expended (turned sideways) once per turn for 1 mana, to pay the mana cost of a card or an ability. Expended resources refresh at the beginning of each turn. See rule 111.
106.5a Mana has no element. Every resource, of whatever kind, pays generic mana.
 Example: Shards pay the mana for [g][g] cards; the two wood resources only meet the affinity.
106.5b To pay a mana cost, a player expends that many un-expended resources. See rule 111.
 Example: Rampart Guardian costs 2: of three open earth, two become expended and one stays open.
106.5c A resource is expended only to pay a cost. No action expends a resource for nothing, and mana is not kept for later use. See rule 106.5b.
 Example: Keeper of Tithes ("At the end of [Haste], if X is not 0, create an X/X unit, where X is the number of expended resources you have") is in play, its controller has six open resources and nothing to pay for: no resource can be expended, so X is 0 and no unit is made.
title: CR 106.5–106.5c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 106. Resources
106.6 In the resource step a player may create a resource by recycling a card from hand. The resource enters dormant. There is no limit to how many resources a player creates this way. See rules 408, 502.
 Example: Four cards recycled in one resource step make four fire resources, all dormant.
106.6a Recycling may create a Prismite or a Shard instead of an element resource.
title: CR 106.6–106.6a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 106. Resources
(continues 106.6: In the resource step a player may create a resource by recycling a card from hand. The resource enters dormant. There is no limit to how many resources a player creates this way.)
106.6b A Prismite made by recycling is the same as a starting Prismite: it enters dormant, takes an activation, gives no affinity, and once active may be exchanged.
title: CR 106.6b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 106. Resources
106.7 When a player activates an element resource, if they then have at least three affinity of that element, they create a Shard. The Shard enters dormant. See rule 106.
 Example: Activating a third fire resource creates a dormant Shard.
 Example: With fewer than three fire, activating a fire resource creates nothing.
106.7a The resource being activated counts toward the three.
 Example: Two active fire resources plus the one being activated make three: the Shard is created.
106.7b The bonus is paid on every such activation, not once per game.
 Example: A fourth fire resource activated later creates another Shard.
106.7c The bonus applies to every element, including those whose resource face is not among the printed cards.
106.7d Activating a Prismite or a Shard never creates a Shard, however many the player has.
title: CR 106.7–106.7d

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 106. Resources
106.8 A Prismite is a resource with no element. It gives no affinity, and like any resource it can be expended for 1 mana. See rule 105.
106.8a A player may exchange an active Prismite for another resource only in the resource step of the planning phase, never in the haste step (which resources: the element-only rule below). The new resource takes the Prismite's place and keeps its current state, so an exchange never adds mana: an expended Prismite becomes an expended resource. See rules 502, 105.
 Example: An expended active Prismite exchanged into fire becomes an expended fire resource; once the player has finished the resource step, a further exchange is refused.
106.8b A dormant Prismite cannot be exchanged.
title: CR 106.8–106.8b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 106. Resources
(continues 106.8: A Prismite is a resource with no element. It gives no affinity, and like any resource it can be expended for 1 mana.)
106.8c The exchange activates the new resource. If that gives the player three affinity of its element, the affinity bonus creates a Shard. The exchange does not use one of the player's two activations for the turn. See rule 106.
 Example: A Prismite exchanged into a third copy of an element creates a Shard.
 Example: A Prismite exchanged into a second copy creates nothing: the bar is three.
title: CR 106.8c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 106. Resources
(continues 106.8: A Prismite is a resource with no element. It gives no affinity, and like any resource it can be expended for 1 mana.)
106.8d A Prismite may be exchanged for any non-Prismite resource: an element resource of any of the seven elements, or a Shard. It cannot be exchanged for another Prismite.
 Example: In a fire-water-earth draft an active Prismite is exchanged into wood, an element outside the draft.
title: CR 106.8d

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 106. Resources
106.9 A Shard is a resource of its own kind. It enters dormant, pays one generic mana once activated, gives no affinity, and cannot be exchanged.
106.9a An effect that creates a Shard creates a Shard, never a Prismite.
 Example: Swirling Shardform creates two dormant Shards, not Prismites.
 Example: Hooba-Lan's attack creates a dormant Shard for its controller.
title: CR 106.9–106.9a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 107. Numbers, X and Symbols
107.1 X stands for a number that the card defines. An X in a mana cost is chosen by the player who plays the card. A token's X is set by the card that created it. Other cards define X with a "where X is …" clause. See rules 702, 304.
 Example: Wildfire asks its caster for X; Self-Assembly with three metal makes a Robot 3.
title: CR 107.1

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 107. Numbers, X and Symbols
107.2 An X spell's mana cost is X alone: the player chooses X, and pays X. Its pips are not part of its cost. See rules 111, 702.
107.2a X is chosen and paid when the spell is cast, before it goes on the stack. Only values the player can pay are offered. Responses see the X already chosen. See rule 702.
 Example: Wildfire: its caster chooses X from the values they can pay and pays it as the spell is cast, so the spell is on the stack with that X.
title: CR 107.2–107.2a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 107. Numbers, X and Symbols
(continues 107.2: An X spell's mana cost is X alone: the player chooses X, and pays X. Its pips are not part of its cost.)
107.2b X may be 0 unless the card says otherwise. Choosing X = 0 is legal even when it makes the effect do nothing.
 Example: No Hand Killer can be activated with an empty hand at X = 0, and its [once] is spent.
 Example: Torrential Reclamation for X = 0 recalls nothing, and nobody sacrifices.
107.2c An X spell (a card whose mana cost is X) that prints "X can't be zero" must be cast with X of at least 1. A player who cannot pay at least 1 cannot cast it.
 Example: Frosted Denial cannot be cast with no open mana.
title: CR 107.2b–107.2c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 107. Numbers, X and Symbols
107.3 An effect that refers to a spell's cost reads its printed cost, not what was actually paid after cost modifiers. For an X spell, that is the X it was cast for. See rule 111.
 Example: Squish taxed up to 4 by Stasis Sentry and Tranquility is still a 2 to Arcane Concentrator and Channeled Amalgam.
title: CR 107.3

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 107. Numbers, X and Symbols
(continues 107.3: An effect that refers to a spell's cost reads its printed cost, not what was actually paid after cost modifiers. For an X spell, that is the X it was cast for.)
107.3a An X card that is not being cast has a cost of 0. This holds for an X card in a hand, a bin, the deck or the cache, and for a unit in play.
 Example: Living Vault caches a card from hand by paying its cost: an X card in hand costs 0, so it can be cached for [0].
title: CR 107.3a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 107. Numbers, X and Symbols
107.4 When an effect lets a player play an X spell for free, the spell is played with X = 0. An X that is a bracketed additional cost is not the mana cost: it is still chosen and paid. See rules 111, 803.
 Example: A fulfilled prophecy releases an X spell for X = 0: no X is asked and no mana is paid.
 Example: Tides of the Cosmos counts an X spell as cost 0 and plays it at X = 0.
107.4a An X spell that prints "X can't be zero" therefore cannot be played for free. An effect that plays cards for free cannot play it.
 Example: Tides of the Cosmos cannot pick Frosted Denial; an X card that may be zero is still a pick.
title: CR 107.4–107.4a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 107. Numbers, X and Symbols
107.5 Stasis Sentry gives spells with a base cost of [three] or less a base cost of [three] during battle. On an X spell it raises the X instead of the price: X must be at least 3, and the spell costs exactly X. See rule 111.
 Example: Under a Stasis Sentry the X menu starts at 3, and X = 3 deals 3.
 Example: Under a Stasis Sentry, X = 3 costs [3] and X = 5 costs [5].
title: CR 107.5

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 107. Numbers, X and Symbols
107.6 A copy of a spell uses the original's X. The X is not chosen or paid again. See rule 710.
 Example: Maelstrom Charger copies Volatile Toxicity: the copy uses the original's X, and no second unit is sacrificed for it.
title: CR 107.6

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 107. Numbers, X and Symbols
107.7 A token's X is set by the card that created it. "Create a Crystal 3" creates a Crystal whose X is 3. See rule 304.
 Example: A Poison created with X = 5 reads "Put 5 -1/-1 counters on target unit."
107.7a A Robot's X is the number of +1/+1 counters on it. It spawns with X counters, and if the number of counters changes, so does its X.
title: CR 107.7–107.7a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 107. Numbers, X and Symbols
107.8 A number an effect counts, such as a "where X is …" clause or an amount "equal to" or "for each" something, is counted when the effect resolves, not when it was played or triggered. See rules 704, 706, 714.
 Example: Flamebreath Initiate removed with its trigger on the stack has no adjacent allies, so X = 0 and it still makes a Fireball 1.
107.8a An X that a paid cost defines is read as the cost is paid. Volatile Toxicity's X is the sacrificed unit's defense as it was when the unit was sacrificed.
title: CR 107.8–107.8a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 107. Numbers, X and Symbols
107.9 When a card asks a player to choose or predict a number, there is no limit the card does not print. A player may name any number in the card's range.
 Example: Prediction Prophet: a player predicts a life total nine higher than their current one. They gain 9 life during the battle, the prediction is matched at the start of deployment, and they get the 5/5.
title: CR 107.9

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 107. Numbers, X and Symbols
107.10 This document writes the game's symbols in brackets, as the card data does. The element pips are [r] Fire, [b] Water, [e] Earth, [g] Wood, [m] Metal, [l] Light and [d] Dark. See rule 202.
107.10a [x] is X generic mana. A number in brackets, as a digit or a word ([1], [three]), is that much generic mana. A number followed by pips ([3b]) is that much mana together with that affinity. See rules 202, 111.
title: CR 107.10–107.10a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 108. Cards, Tokens, Faces and Copies
108.1 A card is a physical Algomancy card: one with an Algomancy card back.
108.1a Units, spells and spell units are cards. Card text that refers to a "card" being played includes a unit being played.
 Example: Void Mandible ("When a nontoken card is played during battle, sacrifice me. If you do, negate that effect.") answers a {Battle} unit being played.
title: CR 108.1–108.1a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 108. Cards, Tokens, Faces and Copies
(continues 108.1: A card is a physical Algomancy card: one with an Algomancy card back.)
108.1b Every card has a name, and most cards have abilities. The other parts a card can have are described in section 200. See rule 200.
title: CR 108.1b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 108. Cards, Tokens, Faces and Copies
108.2 A token is a unit or a spell that an effect creates directly into play. A unit token functions as a unit, and a spell token is a spell. See rule 304.
 Example: Mycelial Mentor reads "When you create a token, target ally gains +3/+3." Its controller creates a Poison, a spell token, and the Mentor triggers just as it would for a 1/1 unit.
108.2a For card text, a token is not a card: text that refers to a "card" does not include a token, even though a unit token is a unit and a spell token is a spell. The printed rules call tokens "temporary cards" to describe them to players; that does not make a token a card. See rule 702.
 Example: A player casts a Fireball token in battle. That is playing a spell, so abilities that watch for a spell being played see it; it is not playing a card, so abilities that watch for a card being played do not.
108.2b A spell token is a token wherever it is: in play, and also on the stack after it has been cast. See rules 304, 406.
 Example: Download ("Gain control of target token") can take a Fireball token that has already been cast and is on the stack.
108.2c A unit that an effect creates is a unit token, including an X/X unit whose X the creating card sets. See rule 304.
 Example: Spawntender creates an 8/8 unit. That unit is a token, so Download ("Gain control of target token") can take it.
108.2d A token is created in the region its source is in when the effect that creates it resolves, not in its controller's home region. See rules 304, 601.
 Example: Life Plant attacking in the enemy region creates its 1/1 units in that region.
title: CR 108.2–108.2d

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 108. Cards, Tokens, Faces and Copies
(continues 108.2: A token is a unit or a spell that an effect creates directly into play. A unit token functions as a unit, and a spell token is a spell.)
108.2e A token is never trashed, because only a card can be trashed. A unit token can still die. See rules 801, 410.
 Example: A unit token dying in battle does not add to the number of cards trashed in that battle.
title: CR 108.2e

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 108. Cards, Tokens, Faces and Copies
108.3 A card in play that transforms is the same unit with its other face up. It does not leave play or enter play, and it keeps its counters and damage. See rule 710.
 Example: Scholar of the Void transforms into Beyond, Codex Incarnate: same unit, and its counters and damage survive.
108.3a A back face is not a token, and a transformed card is still a card. See rule 410.
 Example: A transformed Scholar of the Void that died can be returned from the bin as a Scholar.
108.3b A card can only transform into a back face it has. A unit that gains a transform ability from a mod transforms only if that unit's own card has that back face.
 Example: Scholar of the Void augmented onto another unit cannot transform its host.
title: CR 108.3–108.3b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 108. Cards, Tokens, Faces and Copies
108.4 A copy of a spell is a new effect on the stack. It was not played. See rules 701, 710.
 Example: Earthbound Replicator copies a spell that targets it. The copy is not played, so it does not set off the Replicator again: one copy, and no more.
108.4a A copy of a spell is not a token.
 Example: Download cannot take a spell copy made by Earthbound Replicator.
108.4b A token that an effect creates as a copy of a card is a token.
 Example: The copy Echo of Despair makes of itself is a token.
108.4c A nontoken unit that becomes a copy of a token is still a nontoken unit. See rule 710.
 Example: Borrower of Forms copying a Robot token is a nontoken unit, which Download cannot take.
title: CR 108.4–108.4c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 108. Cards, Tokens, Faces and Copies
108.5 Two copies of the same card are two different objects. Card text that says "another" or "other" compares objects, never card names. See rules 405, 110.
 Example: A host wearing two Rotbeast augments: each Rotbeast's "my other Augments" includes the other Rotbeast.
title: CR 108.5

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 108. Cards, Tokens, Faces and Copies
(continues 108.5: Two copies of the same card are two different objects. Card text that says "another" or "other" compares objects, never card names.)
108.5a An object stays the same object while it stays where it is. A unit that leaves play and comes back is a new object. See rule 410.
 Example: Engorged Caudex recalled and played again draws again from its once-per-turn graft in the same turn.
title: CR 108.5a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 109. Abilities
109.1 An ability is text on a card that describes the card's effects. Most cards have abilities.
title: CR 109.1

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 109. Abilities
109.2 An activated ability is written with a colon. Everything before the colon is a cost that must be paid to activate the ability; what follows the colon is its effect. See rules 705, 111.
 Example: Living Forge reads "[three]: Create a Robot 2." With two resources its ability cannot be activated; paying three makes a Robot.
109.2a A player may activate an activated ability any time they have priority, in battle or in deployment, as many times as they can pay its cost, unless the ability limits itself (see [once]). See rules 703, 109.9.
 Example: With six resources, Living Forge makes two Robots in one deployment, and makes another in battle when its controller holds priority and pays again.
title: CR 109.2–109.2a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 109. Abilities
(continues 109.2: An activated ability is written with a colon. Everything before the colon is a cost that must be paid to activate the ability; what follows the colon is its effect.)
109.2b An activated ability that is used from the hand can be used during battle even if its card has no {Battle} icon.
 Example: Dropslime's discard-me ability can be used in battle.
title: CR 109.2b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 109. Abilities
109.3 A triggered ability happens when something else takes place. "When" and "Whenever" mark a triggered ability; one can also happen at a stated time, such as "After combat" or "At the end of turn". See rule 706.
 Example: Skittering Blight gains its controller a rot when it spawns; Harbinger of Immolation makes a Fireball at the end of the turn; an attacking Wisp sacrifices itself after combat.
109.3a A trigger condition is checked once, when the event happens. If it was false then, nothing that happens later makes the ability trigger; once the ability has triggered, it resolves even if the condition stops being true.
 Example: A spell played at another unit and then retargeted onto Earthbound Replicator makes no copy: "a spell targeting me" is judged as the spell is played.
title: CR 109.3–109.3a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 109. Abilities
(continues 109.3: A triggered ability happens when something else takes place. "When" and "Whenever" mark a triggered ability; one can also happen at a stated time, such as "After combat" or "At the end of turn".)
109.3b An amount a triggered ability uses is measured when the ability resolves, so responses can change it.
 Example: Astral Tidewraith attacks: its trigger deals each player damage equal to the cards in their hand, counted as the trigger resolves, not when it triggered.
109.3c A triggered ability checks its condition again when it resolves only if its text says so, as "if I am still in formation" does. See rule 110.8.
 Example: Hooba-Nan says "if I am still in formation", so that is checked again on resolution: if Hooba-Nan dies with its attack trigger on the stack, no 1/1s are made.
109.3d An ability that triggers when an ally becomes the target of a spell triggers once for each targeted ally. See rule 706.
 Example: An enemy spell targeting two allies puts Earnest Defender's ability on the stack twice.
title: CR 109.3b–109.3d

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 109. Abilities
109.4 A static ability makes a continuous change to the game for as long as its card is in play. See rule 707.
 Example: While Glowhaven Elder is in play, your other units are +1/+1; when it leaves play, they lose the bonus.
title: CR 109.4

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 109. Abilities
109.5 A replacement effect, written "If … instead", changes an event as it happens. The replacement itself does not use the stack. See rules 708, 109.5a.
 Example: With Flux Resonator in play, Living Forge's Robot 2 arrives with three counters, and no extra item goes on the stack for the replacement.
title: CR 109.5

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 109. Abilities
(continues 109.5: A replacement effect, written "If … instead", changes an event as it happens. The replacement itself does not use the stack.)
109.5a If the substitute a replacement effect names includes a target, the event is still replaced at once, and the substitute is put on the stack as a triggered ability so that its target can be chosen. See rule 109.5.
 Example: Beyond, Codex Incarnate's rot replacement removes the rot damage at once, then asks its controller for the target unit that gets the -1/-1 counters.
title: CR 109.5a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 109. Abilities
109.6 An option a card offers as a spell is played, such as Maelstrom Charger's, is neither a triggered nor an activated ability. It does not go on the stack, it cannot be responded to, and effects on triggered or activated abilities do not apply to it. See rule 702.
 Example: Crevice Lurker's tax on triggered abilities does not reach Maelstrom Charger's option.
title: CR 109.6

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 109. Abilities
109.7 Text after a card's [Augment] or graft symbol is active when the card is played normally, not only when the card is a mod. See rule 720.
 Example: A Wraith token in play uses its own [Augment] text: at the start of deployment its controller puts a -1/-1 counter on an ally.
title: CR 109.7

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 109. Abilities
109.8 An effect can give units an ability. The ability goes to the units the effect names as it resolves; a unit that arrives afterwards does not gain it. An ability given this way is one of the unit's abilities while it lasts, so a unit that has the abilities of other units (Ancient One, rule 710.7) has it too.
 Example: Reforge the Dead's grant lasts until regroup and reaches only the units already there.
 Example: An Ancient One dying with Reforge the Dead's grant on it and on its two neighbours makes three Robots.
109.8a A granted ability is an ability the unit has. An effect that removes a unit's abilities removes the granted abilities the unit has when the removal applies; an ability granted to the unit afterwards is not removed. See rule 712.
 Example: A unit that loses all abilities also loses an ability Reforge the Dead gave it earlier; if Reforge the Dead resolves after the removal, the unit has the new ability.
title: CR 109.8–109.8a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 109. Abilities
109.9 An ability marked [once], and a bounded graft ([Switch1]), can be activated or triggered only once per turn. See rule 722.
 Example: Unstable Apparition ([once]: when you play a nontoken spell, create a Fireball X) makes a Fireball for the first spell its controller plays this turn, nothing for the second, and a Fireball again next turn.
title: CR 109.9

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 109. Abilities
(continues 109.9: An ability marked [once], and a bounded graft ([Switch1]), can be activated or triggered only once per turn.)
109.9a The use is spent when the ability is activated or put on the stack, whether or not it then resolves. A fizzle, a negation, or a run that finds nothing to do does not give it back. Only a declined or impossible optional choice leaves the use unspent (rule 109.9b), even when that choice comes as the ability resolves. See rule 109.9b.
109.9b A player who declines an optional ("you may") bounded ability, or who could not be offered it at all, has not spent the use. The ability can trigger again later in the turn.
 Example: Hexbane Shiitake declined on one spell is offered again on the next spell that turn.
109.9c Activating a [once] ability with X = 0 is legal, and it spends the use.
 Example: No Hand Killer can be activated with an empty hand, and the activation spends its [once].
109.9d A change of controller does not give back a spent use: the limit stays with the unit.
title: CR 109.9a–109.9d

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 109. Abilities
(continues 109.9: An ability marked [once], and a bounded graft ([Switch1]), can be activated or triggered only once per turn.)
109.9e Moving a mod onto another unit (Reconfigure) does not give back its spent use. See rule 720.
 Example: A Graxxlid augment already activated this turn and moved by Reconfigure cannot be activated again that turn.
109.9f A unit that leaves play and is played again is a new object, and its abilities have their uses again, even in the same turn. See rule 410.
 Example: Engorged Caudex recalled and played again draws from its [Switch1] graft a second time that turn.
title: CR 109.9e–109.9f

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 109. Abilities
(continues 109.9: An ability marked [once], and a bounded graft ([Switch1]), can be activated or triggered only once per turn.)
109.9g Turning a card over does not give back a spent use: a transformed card is the same unit. See rule 108.
title: CR 109.9g

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 109. Abilities
(continues 109.9: An ability marked [once], and a bounded graft ([Switch1]), can be activated or triggered only once per turn.)
109.9h If the cause of a graft composite is bounded, the whole composite can trigger only once per turn, unbounded grafts included. See rule 722.
109.9i If the cause is unbounded, the composite can trigger any number of times, but each bounded graft in it is included only the first time in a turn. See rule 722.
 Example: Omniwield Evoker activated twice in a turn creates the Robot from its bounded graft only the first time.
109.9j An effect that repeats a graft composite (Amphivore, Lost Guardian) repeats its bounded grafts too. See rule 722.
 Example: Amphivore triples a bounded "Create three" graft.
title: CR 109.9h–109.9j

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 109. Abilities
(continues 109.9: An ability marked [once], and a bounded graft ([Switch1]), can be activated or triggered only once per turn.)
109.9k Each mod has its own use. Two copies of the same bounded graft on one host each have one use.
109.9m A bounded ability that works while its card is in a bin, such as Rotling's "When I leave your bin", is limited once per turn for each player and card name: copies of one card in one player's bin share one use. See rules 405, 109.9n.
 Example: Rotling's [Switch1] works once per turn from the bin and is available again the next turn.
 Example: Two Rotling leaving one bin in the same turn share one [Switch1] use: the second copy is not offered it.
109.9n A bounded "When I am trashed" ability is limited for each trashed card, not for each player and card name: two copies of one card trashed in the same turn each trigger. See rule 109.9m.
 Example: Two Maw of Despair discarded in the same turn each trigger their [Switch1] Glimpse 2.
title: CR 109.9k–109.9n

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 110. Targets
110.1 A target is something a card or ability chooses, with the word "target", to receive its actions. The targets are selected as the card is played. See rule 702.
 Example: Fight ("Target ally and another target unit fight") takes both units as targets as it is played.
110.1a Targets are chosen as the effect is put on the stack: when a card is played, when an ability is activated, and when a triggered ability is put on the stack. Every target of the effect is chosen then. See rules 702, 703.
 Example: Plodding Pebble carries a grafted Leaping Lillik ("Delete target unit"). A Fireball damages the Pebble: as the trigger goes on the stack, the delete's target is chosen. With no enemy in the region, it must be one of your own units.
title: CR 110.1–110.1a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 110. Targets
(continues 110.1: A target is something a card or ability chooses, with the word "target", to receive its actions. The targets are selected as the card is played.)
110.1b Each "target" in an effect's text is a separate target. An effect that says "target" twice chooses two targets.
 Example: Squish chooses two targets as it is played: an ally and another unit.
title: CR 110.1b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 110. Targets
(continues 110.1: A target is something a card or ability chooses, with the word "target", to receive its actions. The targets are selected as the card is played.)
110.1c "Up to N target" lets the player choose any number of targets from none to N, and "any number of target" lets the player choose none as well. Only such words make a target optional: without them every target is required (see rule 110.7).
 Example: Twin Flame ("up to two target units") can be played with no targets.
 Example: Tilling the Graves ("Recall two target units in your bin") says no "up to": once cast, it asks for both units and offers no way to stop at one.
 Example: Penance ("Any number of target players each lose 1 life. Draw a card.") may be played with no target, and its caster still draws.
110.1d The number of targets an effect has is the number chosen as it was put on the stack. A target that is later lost still counts.
 Example: Twin Flame declared with two targets, one of them later removed, is still not "a single target" for Envoy of Lightning.
title: CR 110.1c–110.1d

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 110. Targets
110.2 A choice that an effect's text does not make with the word "target" is not a target. Nothing is declared for it as the effect goes on the stack, and an effect that answers targeting cannot answer it.
 Example: Meteor Shower's rockfall chooses rather than targets, so Boon of Protection has nothing to negate.
title: CR 110.2

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 110. Targets
(continues 110.2: A choice that an effect's text does not make with the word "target" is not a target. Nothing is declared for it as the effect goes on the stack, and an effect that answers targeting cannot answer it.)
110.2a Such a choice cannot be redirected by an effect that changes targets, and it does not trigger "when I become targeted".
 Example: The Wraith's "an ally" never fires a "becomes targeted" ability.
title: CR 110.2a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 110. Targets
(continues 110.2: A choice that an effect's text does not make with the word "target" is not a target. Nothing is declared for it as the effect goes on the stack, and an effect that answers targeting cannot answer it.)
110.2b Dividing or distributing an amount among a targeted player's units is not targeting those units. The division is made as the effect resolves. See rule 704.
 Example: Channel Through targets X allies and an opponent as it is played, and divides its damage among that opponent's units only as it resolves.
title: CR 110.2b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 110. Targets
(continues 110.2: A choice that an effect's text does not make with the word "target" is not a target. Nothing is declared for it as the effect goes on the stack, and an effect that answers targeting cannot answer it.)
110.2c The Wraith's "an ally" is not a target. The ally is chosen as the trigger resolves, from the allies in play then, so the trigger cannot lose its ally and does not fizzle while an ally is in play. With no ally in play, it fizzles. See rule 704.
 Example: Three Wraith triggers and one 1/1 ally: only the first trigger is offered the 1/1, and it kills it. The other two put their counters on Wraiths still in play, and nothing fizzles.
 Example: A 1/1 carrying two Wraith augments: the first shrink kills it, and the second finds no ally in play and fizzles.
title: CR 110.2c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 110. Targets
110.3 Only a legal target can be chosen. Whether a target is legal depends on the kind of thing the text names (a unit, an ally, a player, an effect, a card in a bin) and on any restriction written on the target itself.
 Example: Minor Kraken ("target unit with 5 or less defense") cannot target a unit with 6 defense.
title: CR 110.3

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 110. Targets
(continues 110.3: Only a legal target can be chosen. Whether a target is legal depends on the kind of thing the text names (a unit, an ally, a player, an effect, a card in a bin) and on any restriction written on the target itself.)
110.3a A clause that describes the target ("with 5 or less defense", "that targets an allied effect", "in your bin") limits which targets are legal. An "if" clause attached to the action ("delete target unit if it has a -1/-1 counter on it") does not limit the choice; it is checked as the effect resolves.
 Example: Boon of Protection is not offered against an effect that targets nothing allied.
title: CR 110.3a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 110. Targets
(continues 110.3: Only a legal target can be chosen. Whether a target is legal depends on the kind of thing the text names (a unit, an ally, a player, an effect, a card in a bin) and on any restriction written on the target itself.)
110.3b An effect on the stack can be a target. A unit in play is not an effect, so it cannot fill a target that asks for an effect. See rule 700.
 Example: Enigmatic Warder cannot become the target of a negate that wants a spell effect.
title: CR 110.3b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 110. Targets
(continues 110.3: Only a legal target can be chosen. Whether a target is legal depends on the kind of thing the text names (a unit, an ally, a player, an effect, a card in a bin) and on any restriction written on the target itself.)
110.3c "Target player" can be any player present in the region where the effect resolves, the effect's controller included. "Target opponent" is any such player other than the effect's controller. In battle both players are present. See rule 110.5b.
 Example: Soul Siphon played in battle offers its own controller as well as the opponent as "target player".
title: CR 110.3c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 110. Targets
(continues 110.3: Only a legal target can be chosen. Whether a target is legal depends on the kind of thing the text names (a unit, an ally, a player, an effect, a card in a bin) and on any restriction written on the target itself.)
110.3d "Target formation" targets one player's whole side of a battle in that region: every unit arrayed there, not a column.
 Example: Galactic Germination counts three units across two columns of the targeted formation.
title: CR 110.3d

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 110. Targets
(continues 110.3: Only a legal target can be chosen. Whether a target is legal depends on the kind of thing the text names (a unit, an ally, a player, an effect, a card in a bin) and on any restriction written on the target itself.)
110.3e A formation stays a legal target while its battle lasts, even if every unit leaves it.
 Example: Galactic Germination aimed at a formation that has emptied creates nothing, and does not fizzle.
title: CR 110.3e

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 110. Targets
110.4 An ally is a unit under your control in the region the effect is happening in. An enemy is a unit not under your control in that region. See rules 102, 601.
title: CR 110.4

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 110. Targets
(continues 110.4: An ally is a unit under your control in the region the effect is happening in. An enemy is a unit not under your control in that region.)
110.4a A unit is its own ally. An effect that targets "an ally" or "target ally" can choose its own source unless the text says "another".
 Example: Shoreline Specter's "recall target ally" may target the Specter itself.
110.4b Ally and enemy follow control, not ownership. A unit you have taken control of is your ally and its owner's enemy, in that region, for as long as you control it.
 Example: An opponent ambushes with Orblish Horroth to recall target ally. Before it resolves, you take control of that unit; it is no longer their ally, and the ambush recalls nothing.
110.4c Ally is measured from the effect's controller, never from the player making the choice.
 Example: With the opponent's Fight on the stack, an enemy unit cannot fill its ally target, while another of the Fight controller's units can.
title: CR 110.4a–110.4c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 110. Targets
(continues 110.4: An ally is a unit under your control in the region the effect is happening in. An enemy is a unit not under your control in that region.)
110.4d "Another" excludes whatever the sentence's other noun is. It excludes the source only when that other noun is the source ("I fight another target unit"); in "from target unit onto another target unit" it excludes only the first target. See rule 108.
title: CR 110.4d

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 110. Targets
110.5 An effect can target a unit only in the region where the effect is happening. See rule 601.
title: CR 110.5

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 110. Targets
(continues 110.5: An effect can target a unit only in the region where the effect is happening.)
110.5a An effect on the stack can be targeted only by an effect in its own region, since each region has its own stack (rule 601.2a). A card in a player's bin can be targeted only by an effect that resolves in a region where that player is present. See rules 405, 406.
 Example: A spell on the battle region's stack and the cards in a bin are offered as targets only where they are: the spell only to an effect in the battle region, a player's bin only where that player is present.
 Example: In deployment, an effect that targets a card in a bin can reach only the bin of the player deploying there.
title: CR 110.5a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 110. Targets
(continues 110.5: An effect can target a unit only in the region where the effect is happening.)
110.5b A player's cache, and a player as a target, can be targeted only by an effect that resolves in a region where that player is present. See rule 403.
 Example: In deployment Prismatic Observer reaches only its controller's cache; in battle it reaches both.
title: CR 110.5b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 110. Targets
110.6 Where an effect asks for two or more targets together, one object cannot be two of them, as with Twin Flame's "up to two target units". This holds when targets are changed as well as when they are chosen.
 Example: Divine Intervention cannot make Twin Flame target one unit twice.
110.6a Different effects may target the same object. See rule 704.
 Example: An opponent's Luminous Arc is aimed at one of your Good Whales; you answer with Organic Exchange targeting both your Good Whales. The Luminous Arc still resolves.
title: CR 110.6–110.6a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 110. Targets
110.7 A card or ability that needs targets can be played only if every target it requires can be chosen at the same time, each one legal and different from the others. Every target a card names is required unless the card says "up to" or "any number" (see rule 110.1c). A card that targets nothing has no such requirement. See rule 702.
 Example: Fight cannot be played unless its region holds an ally and another unit.
 Example: Rebalance, which targets nothing, can be played with no unit of its controller's.
 Example: Abduct ("Gain control of target unit with cost [x] or less …") against a lone cost-1 attacker can be played when its caster can pay an X of 1 or more. X = 0 is not offered, since at 0 there is no unit to take.
 Example: Tilling the Graves ("Recall two target units in your bin") cannot be played while its caster's bin holds fewer than two units.
 Example: Tidal Reversion ("For each player, recall target unit that player controls") played for free by Tides of the Cosmos takes one unit of each player, and Tides does not offer it while either player has no unit there.
title: CR 110.7

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 110. Targets
110.8 A target that was legal when it was chosen but is not legal when the effect begins to resolve is lost, as if it had left play. See rule 704.
 Example: A unit that grows past 5 defense before Minor Kraken resolves is not recalled.
title: CR 110.8

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 110. Targets
110.9 An effect that changes another effect's targets must choose each new target as that target was first chosen: legal for that target's own kind and restriction, and not an object already chosen for another target of the same part of the effect. Enigmatic Warder's ability ("Change a target of target effect to me") may target only an effect that Enigmatic Warder could be a legal target of. Any other effect that changes targets may target an effect with no target that can be changed, and the change then does nothing. The client asks the player to confirm before choosing a target effect whose targets the change cannot alter. See rule 110.6.
 Example: Enigmatic Warder cannot take Throw off a Cliff, which needs a unit with 4 or more defense.
 Example: Enigmatic Warder cannot move itself into a target already held by the same effect's other target.
 Example: Enigmatic Warder's ability cannot be activated with only Surly Stalker's trigger, which has no targets, on the stack.
 Example: With an opponent's Fester, Throw off a Cliff, "target ally" trigger and Invigorate on the stack, Enigmatic Warder may target only the Invigorate, whose "target unit" it could be.
 Example: Gravitational Correction may be aimed at Surly Stalker's trigger, which has no targets; the client first asks "This effect has no targets, so Gravitational Correction will do nothing. Continue?", and Continue sends the choice.
title: CR 110.9

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 110. Targets
(continues 110.9: An effect that changes another effect's targets must choose each new target as that target was first chosen: legal for that target's own kind and restriction, and not an object already chosen for another target of the…)
110.9a A target that is kept when targets are changed is not a change, and it is not judged again then.
 Example: Divine Intervention can keep one target of an effect while changing another.
title: CR 110.9a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 110. Targets
(continues 110.9: An effect that changes another effect's targets must choose each new target as that target was first chosen: legal for that target's own kind and restriction, and not an object already chosen for another target of the…)
110.9b Changing an effect's targets before it resolves can save it from fizzling. See rule 704.
 Example: A spell whose target is about to become illegal is given a legal new target by Enigmatic Warder before it resolves, and then it does not fizzle.
title: CR 110.9b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 110. Targets
110.10 Applying an augment, a graft or a Virus to a unit targets that unit. See rule 720.
 Example: Grafting onto Mohruung targets it, so its "when I become targeted" ability makes a Crystal.
title: CR 110.10

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 110. Targets
(continues 110.10: Applying an augment, a graft or a Virus to a unit targets that unit.)
110.10a A Virus being applied is an effect on the stack that targets its host. It can be redirected, an effect that answers "target effect targeting me" or an effect targeting an ally can answer it, and a unit that must be targeted if able (rule 110.12) compels it like any other targeted effect. See rule 723.
 Example: Graxxlid ("Negate target effect targeting me") can negate a Virus being applied to it.
 Example: Boon of Protection can negate a Virus being applied to an allied unit.
 Example: With a Gatekeeper of Souls in the battle, a Virus can be applied only to the Gatekeeper.
 Example: A Virus that Tides of the Cosmos plays goes onto the Gatekeeper of Souls in the battle.
title: CR 110.10a

text:
