Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 110. Targets
110.11 An ability that triggers "when I become targeted" triggers whenever its unit is targeted, by a spell, an ability, an augment, a graft or a Virus. When the effect that targeted is put on the stack, the trigger goes on the stack above it and so resolves first. When a graft targets the unit, or an augment is applied to it in deployment, the trigger resolves first, and only then is the mod attached.
 Example: Mohruung targeted by an augment makes a Crystal 2.
 Example: Grafting onto Mohruung makes a Crystal 2.
 Example: A spell aimed at Mohruung waits on the stack under Mohruung's trigger, so the Crystal 2 is made before the spell resolves.
 Example: A graft applied to Mohruung: the Crystal 2 is made first, and the graft attaches after.
 Example: An augment applied to Mohruung in deployment: the Crystal 2 is made first, then the augment attaches.
title: CR 110.11

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 110. Targets
110.12 A unit that "must be targeted if able" (Gatekeeper of Souls) must be one of the targets of an effect whose targets are selected during a battle in its region, when it can legally be one. Outside battle, or while the battle is in another region, it compels nothing. Once it is among the targets, the effect's other targets may be anything legal.
 Example: Twin Flame aims at Gatekeeper of Souls first, then at any other unit.
 Example: In deployment, a player with a Gatekeeper of Souls in play may aim an Overbloom at another unit.
 Example: During a battle in another region, a Gatekeeper of Souls at home compels nothing.
title: CR 110.12

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 110. Targets
(continues 110.12: A unit that "must be targeted if able" (Gatekeeper of Souls) must be one of the targets of an effect whose targets are selected during a battle in its region, when it can legally be one. Outside battle, or while the…)
110.12a With two such units in the region, each must be targeted if able: a two-target effect must target both.
 Example: With two Gatekeepers in the region, a two-target spell targets both.
110.12b "If able" means "if it is a legal target for this effect". An effect whose targets cannot be units, such as one that targets a formation, is not compelled.
 Example: Gatekeeper of Souls does not compel Galactic Germination, which targets a formation.
110.12c The compulsion applies only to choosing targets. It never makes a target already chosen illegal.
 Example: A Gatekeeper of Souls that arrives after an effect's targets were chosen does not make those targets illegal.
title: CR 110.12a–110.12c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 111. Costs
111.1 A cost is something a player must pay to do something: to play a card, to apply a mod, or to activate an ability. A card's mana cost, the additional costs in its brackets, and everything before the colon of an activated ability are costs. See rules 702, 705, 720.
111.1a A mana cost is paid by expending resources: each resource can be expended once per turn for 1 mana, to pay the mana cost of a card or of an ability. See rule 106.
 Example: with two open resources, paying [one] for Auric Ascendant's ability and then playing Shard Sprite expends both; a second 1-cost card is not playable that turn, and both resources are open again next turn.
111.1b Meeting a card's affinity requirement is not paying a cost. Nothing is spent to meet it, and resources that are already expended still count toward it. See rule 105.
 Example: a player with two Wood resources, both already expended, still meets a requirement of two Wood pips.
title: CR 111.1–111.1b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 111. Costs
111.2 Besides mana, a cost may require a player to pay life, gain debt, discard cards, sacrifice units, erase cards from their bin, remove counters, recall an ally or erase a mod. A cost of any kind is paid in full before the thing it pays for is put on the stack. See rule 702.4.
 Example: Slag Spewer's "[one], Erase one of my mods:" erases the mod as the ability is activated, before anyone can respond.
title: CR 111.2

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 111. Costs
111.3 A cost that sacrifices units can be paid only with units the player controls in the region where the cost is paid. They cannot sacrifice a unit they do not control, or a unit of theirs that is in another region. See rule 601.
 Example: when Volatile Toxicity is played in battle, its sacrifice menu offers the unit in the battle region and not the unit the player left at home.
title: CR 111.3

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 111. Costs
(continues 111.3: A cost that sacrifices units can be paid only with units the player controls in the region where the cost is paid. They cannot sacrifice a unit they do not control, or a unit of theirs that is in another region.)
111.3a A cost that removes counters from the player's allies, or recalls an ally, likewise uses only the player's own units in the region where the cost is paid. See rule 111.3.
 Example: Auric Ascendant’s "Recall another ally" cost offers the ally fighting beside it, never the ally at home and never itself.
title: CR 111.3a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 111. Costs
111.4 What was paid is fixed at the moment it is paid. An effect that reads a paid cost (such as "the defense of the sacrificed unit") reads it as it was when it was paid.
 Example: Volatile Toxicity is cast by sacrificing a Good Whale (7/5). Its X is fixed at 5 as the cost is paid, and it makes a Poison 5 and a Fireball 5.
title: CR 111.4

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 111. Costs
111.5 A copy of a spell does not pay the original's additional cost again. It uses what the original paid, including the original's X. See rule 710.
 Example: Maelstrom Charger copies a Volatile Toxicity; the copy makes its Poison and Fireball from the one sacrifice the original paid for.
title: CR 111.5

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 111. Costs
111.6 A cost that cannot be paid in full cannot be paid at all. A card whose cost cannot be paid cannot be played, and an ability whose cost cannot be paid cannot be activated; nothing is paid, and the play or activation is not offered. See rule 702.4a.
 Example: Auric Ascendant ("[one], Recall another ally:") is not offered while it has no other ally, so its [one] is never paid.
111.6a A cost made of several parts is paid all or nothing. If any part cannot be paid, no part is paid, including the mana.
 Example: Instrument of Reassignment ("[x], Sacrifice another nontoken unit:") with no other nontoken unit pays neither the mana nor anything else.
111.6b A player may pay N life only while they have more than N life. N is the amount the cost names; for a variable life cost it is the X chosen so far, the point being chosen included. N is not the life the payment will lose: an effect that changes how much life is lost (Arbiter of Vitality doubles it) does not change N, so the cost can still be paid, and the payment can then bring the player to 0. Without such an effect, a life cost that would bring the player to 0 cannot be paid. See rule 112.1.
 Example: at exactly 9 life, Glararr's "Pay 9 life:" cannot be activated.
 Example: A player with 4 life paying X life for Flesh Tithe can choose at most 3 points, and loses the 3 at once when X is set.
 Example: With Arbiter of Vitality in play, a player at 15 life may pay Glararr's 9 life: they lose 18 and the game is over for them.
title: CR 111.6–111.6b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 111. Costs
111.7 An activated ability's whole cost is paid when the ability is activated, before it is put on the stack. A fixed cost is paid after the ability's targets are chosen. A variable cost (one whose amount is X) is paid first, and what is paid sets X, before any target is chosen. No player may respond between the payment and the ability going on the stack, and negating the ability does not refund it. See rule 705.
 Example: Infernal Cultivator's "Sacrifice X units:" kills the units as the ability is activated, so a negation cannot give them back.
title: CR 111.7

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 111. Costs
(continues 111.7: An activated ability's whole cost is paid when the ability is activated, before it is put on the stack. A fixed cost is paid after the ability's targets are chosen. A variable cost (one whose amount is X) is paid first,…)
111.7a When an activated ability's cost sacrifices its own source, the source is in the bin while the ability waits on the stack.
 Example: Throwing Boulder ("Sacrifice me: I deal 3 damage to any target.") is in the bin as soon as the ability is on the stack.
title: CR 111.7a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 111. Costs
(continues 111.7: An activated ability's whole cost is paid when the ability is activated, before it is put on the stack. A fixed cost is paid after the ability's targets are chosen. A variable cost (one whose amount is X) is paid first,…)
111.7b A printed condition on activating an ability ("Activate this ability only if …") is checked before any cost is paid. If it is not met, the ability cannot be activated. It is not checked again when the ability resolves. See rule 705.
 Example: Throwing Boulder with no adjacent ally is not offered its ability.
title: CR 111.7b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 111. Costs
111.8 When a triggered ability's effect says "sacrifice me. If you do, …", the sacrifice is part of the effect, not a cost: the ability goes on the stack with its source still in play, players may respond, and the source is sacrificed as the ability resolves. The sacrifice is not optional. If the source is no longer in play when the ability resolves, it cannot be sacrificed, and the "If you do" part does nothing.
 Example: Eldritch Dreamtender's column deals combat damage to an opponent. Its ability goes on the stack with Dreamtender still in play; Dreamtender is sacrificed when the ability resolves, and only then is the opponent's hand looked at and a card discarded.
 Example: Dreamtender is destroyed in response to its ability. When the ability resolves, nothing is sacrificed, so no hand is looked at and nothing is discarded.
111.8a A sacrifice the text makes optional ("you may sacrifice me. If you do, …") is the player's choice. A player who declines it gets nothing from the "If you do" part.
title: CR 111.8–111.8a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 111. Costs
111.9 A payment that an effect's text asks for while it resolves ("you may pay [one] to …", "unless its controller pays [x]") is not a cost of putting it on the stack. The ability goes on the stack without it, and the player decides whether to pay when it resolves. See rules 702.5a, 704.
 Example: Xenopod Progenitor's trigger goes on the stack with no payment asked; its [1] is asked as it resolves.
title: CR 111.9

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 111. Costs
111.10 Some cards in play change what it costs to play cards or to activate or trigger abilities. Such a cost modifier works only while its source is in play, only in its source's region, and, unless it says otherwise, for every player in that region, its controller included. See rules 601, 701.2b.
 Example: an opponent's Crevice Lurker in the battle region taxes your abilities, not only its controller's.
 Example: Tranquility applied as an augment still taxes spells from its host.
title: CR 111.10

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 111. Costs
(continues 111.10: Some cards in play change what it costs to play cards or to activate or trigger abilities. Such a cost modifier works only while its source is in play, only in its source's region, and, unless it says otherwise, for…)
111.10a Cost modifiers add up. Two modifiers that each add [one] add [two].
 Example: two Crevice Lurkers make an activated [1] cost [3] in battle.
111.10b A cost reduced below zero is zero.
title: CR 111.10a–111.10b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 111. Costs
(continues 111.10: Some cards in play change what it costs to play cards or to activate or trigger abilities. Such a cost modifier works only while its source is in play, only in its source's region, and, unless it says otherwise, for…)
111.10c A cost modifier applies to what its text names. One that names "spells" applies to every spell played, spell units and spell tokens included. One that names "cards" applies to every card played, units included, and not to spell tokens, which are not cards. Neither applies to applying a mod, which is not playing a card. See rules 701.1c, 701.2b, 111.10e.
 Example: Tranquility ("Spells cost [one] more") taxes a spell token cast in battle.
 Example: Arbiter of Armistice ("Cards played during battle gain [Pay 2 life]") takes no life for a spell token.
 Example: A card played as an Ambush under Arbiter of Armistice pays the "cards played" tax.
 Example: Tranquility ("Spells cost [one] more") taxes a spell unit played in battle, and not a plain unit.
111.10d A cost modifier may give cards an additional cost ("Cards played during battle gain [Pay 2 life]"). The player who plays the card pays it, with the card's other costs, before the card is put on the stack. If it requires a sacrifice, that player chooses the unit from their own units. A card whose imposed cost cannot be paid cannot be played.
 Example: under an opponent's Vengeance, the player choosing the sacrifice is offered only their own units.
 Example: under Arbiter of Armistice, a player who cannot pay the 2 life cannot play the card.
111.10e A card played as an Ambush is a card played. During battle, an imposed cost on "cards played" applies to it: it pays the life, makes the sacrifice, and cannot be played if it cannot pay. See rule 803.
 Example: An Ambush played under Arbiter of Armistice ("Cards played during battle gain [Pay 2 life]") pays the 2 life.
 Example: An Ambush that cannot pay the imposed life is not offered.
 Example: An Ambush played under an opposing Vengeance owes the sacrifice, chosen by its player before it reaches the stack.
title: CR 111.10c–111.10e

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 111. Costs
(continues 111.10: Some cards in play change what it costs to play cards or to activate or trigger abilities. Such a cost modifier works only while its source is in play, only in its source's region, and, unless it says otherwise, for…)
111.10f A modifier that makes abilities cost more "to activate or trigger" applies to activated abilities and to triggered abilities, graft triggers and the triggers of attributes such as Alluring and Resonant included. It does not apply to static abilities, to playing or applying cards, or to an option that is neither activated nor triggered. See rules 705, 706, 707.
 Example: Crevice Lurker taxes a graft trigger.
 Example: Crevice Lurker taxes Resonant's extra damage, by the designer's stated intent.
 Example: applying an augment during battle is not taxed.
111.10g When a triggered ability would be put on the stack while such a tax applies, the player who would control it chooses whether to pay the tax. If they pay, the ability is put on the stack. If they decline, or cannot pay, it does not trigger.
 Example: with a Crevice Lurker in the battle, you decline to pay the tax on your own Origon's trigger, so Origon does not negate your first spell of the battle.
title: CR 111.10f–111.10g

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 111. Costs
(continues 111.10: Some cards in play change what it costs to play cards or to activate or trigger abilities. Such a cost modifier works only while its source is in play, only in its source's region, and, unless it says otherwise, for…)
111.10h A triggered ability that does not trigger because its tax was declined or could not be paid does not use up a "[once]" or other once-per-turn limit.
title: CR 111.10h

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 111. Costs
(continues 111.10: Some cards in play change what it costs to play cards or to activate or trigger abilities. Such a cost modifier works only while its source is in play, only in its source's region, and, unless it says otherwise, for…)
111.10i A modifier that gives spells a minimum base cost ("Spells with base cost [three] or less have a base cost of [three]") raises the cost of a spell whose printed cost is a number. For a spell whose cost is X, it instead makes the smallest X that may be chosen equal to that minimum, and the spell costs exactly the X chosen. See rules 107, 702.6.
 Example: under Stasis Sentry in battle, Wildfire's X menu starts at 3, and X = 3 deals 3.
title: CR 111.10i

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 111. Costs
(continues 111.10: Some cards in play change what it costs to play cards or to activate or trigger abilities. Such a cost modifier works only while its source is in play, only in its source's region, and, unless it says otherwise, for…)
111.10j A spell token's printed cost is 0, so such a modifier makes a spell token cost its minimum.
 Example: under Stasis Sentry, casting a Fireball token in battle costs [3].
title: CR 111.10j

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 111. Costs
(continues 111.10: Some cards in play change what it costs to play cards or to activate or trigger abilities. Such a cost modifier works only while its source is in play, only in its source's region, and, unless it says otherwise, for…)
111.10k A cost reduction a player has already paid for belongs to that player. It stays when its source leaves play, it applies in whatever region the player plays their next card, and it ends when its text says it ends: "the next card you play this phase" lasts until that card is played or the phase ends.
 Example: sacrificing Deferral Drone in response does not take away the discount already paid for.
 Example: the discount ends when the phase ends, even within the same turn.
title: CR 111.10k

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 111. Costs
111.11 When an effect refers to a card's cost, it means the card's printed cost. Cost modifiers do not change it. The cost of an X spell that is being or has just been cast is the X paid; an X card that is not being cast has a cost of 0. See rules 107, 202.
 Example: Squish, paid at [4] under Stasis Sentry and Tranquility, is read as a 2-cost spell by Arcane Concentrator.
title: CR 111.11

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 111. Costs
111.12 Some cards print another way to play or use them, with its own cost: a Prophecy or Ambush banner, or a "Discard me" line. Such a cost is paid like any other cost: its mana is spent and its affinity requirement must be met. See rules 203, 803.
111.12a Discarding a card through its "Discard me" line is not playing it. A player may do it whenever they hold priority in battle, and during their own deployment, unless the line itself is marked with a timing. See rule 701.
 Example: Dropslime's discard-me line is offered in battle.
title: CR 111.12–111.12a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 111. Costs
111.13 A card played for free (released by a fulfilled prophecy, or played by an effect such as Tides of the Cosmos) pays no mana cost and ignores its affinity requirement. Its additional bracketed costs are still paid. See rules 702.6c, 702.4e.
 Example: Tides of the Cosmos plays a fire unit for a player with only water resources.
 Example: Volatile Toxicity played by Tides still sacrifices a unit.
111.13a An X spell played for free is played with X = 0. A card that says "X can't be zero" therefore cannot be played for free. See rule 107.
 Example: Tides of the Cosmos cannot play Frosted Denial.
title: CR 111.13–111.13a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 111. Costs
111.14 When an effect is repeated by a multiplier ("trigger two copies of this graft ability"), a cost the repeated effect carries is paid once for each copy. The whole multiplied cost is paid all or nothing: if it cannot all be paid, none of it is paid and that effect does not happen. See rule 722.
 Example: under Lost Guardian, a "[Discard a card]:" graft pays twice and resolves twice.
 Example: with one card in hand, the doubled [Discard a card] is not paid at all.
title: CR 111.14

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 111. Costs
111.15 A cost a graft adds ("{graft} [cost]: effect") must be paid; it cannot be declined. If it cannot be paid, none of the composite ability goes on the stack: not the graft's effect, the host's own effect, or any other graft with it. The exception is a played spell that carries a {Modular} graft part: there an unpayable grafted cost skips only that part, and the spell is not withheld. See rule 722.
title: CR 111.15

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 112. Life, Damage, Rot and Debt
112.1 Each player begins the game with 30 life. A player whose life is reduced to 0 is eliminated. See rules 103, 104.
112.1a A life total changes only by being gained or lost. Damage dealt to a player makes that player lose that much life, and paying life is losing it. One payment, or one effect, that makes a player lose N life is one loss of N life, not N losses of 1.
 Example: Throwing Boulder's 3 damage to a player is a loss of 3 life, and the [Pay 2 life] that Arbiter of Armistice adds to a card played during battle is a loss of 2 life.
 Example: With Life Plant in play, paying X = 29 life for Flesh Tithe is one loss of 29 life, so Life Plant creates 29 units.
 Example: Torrential Reclamation, which loses 1 life for each ally it recalls, loses it as one change, so Life Plant creates that many units.
112.1b An effect that makes players gain or lose life reaches only the players in its region. "Each opponent loses 1 life" means each opponent in the current region. See rule 601.
 Example: Bloated Manablub dying in battle makes each opponent in that region lose 3 life.
title: CR 112.1–112.1b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 112. Life, Damage, Rot and Debt
112.2 The life a player has lost in a battle is the sum of all their life losses in that battle. Life gained in the battle does not reduce it.
 Example: a player loses 10, gains 8 and loses 3 in one battle; Soul Siphon makes a 13/13.
title: CR 112.2

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 112. Life, Damage, Rot and Debt
112.3 Effects that multiply life gained or lost multiply together: with n effects that each double it, the amount is multiplied by 2 to the power n. The multiplied amount is gained or lost at once, before it is checked whether the player has reached 0 life. Life paid as a cost is multiplied the same way; whether the cost can be paid is judged by the amount the cost names (see rule 111.6b). See rule 708.
 Example: three Arbiters of Vitality multiply a life loss by 8.
 Example: With Arbiter of Vitality in play, paying Glararr's 9 life loses 18.
title: CR 112.3

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 112. Life, Damage, Rot and Debt
112.4 If a player's life total "can't change", that player neither gains nor loses life while the effect lasts.
 Example: Suspend stops the target's life total moving in either direction for the battle.
title: CR 112.4

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 112. Life, Damage, Rot and Debt
112.5 Damage is dealt by a source to a unit or a player. Damage dealt to a unit is marked on it, and a unit whose total marked damage is greater than or equal to its defense dies. Damage dealt to a player makes them lose that much life. See rules 608, 713.
 Example: an attacker with 2 power blocked by a 0/2 kills it, and an unblocked 1-power attacker makes the defending player lose 1 life.
112.5a Damage marked on units is removed during the regroup phase. See rule 506.
 Example: a blocker that took 2 damage in the battle has no damage marked on it after regroup.
112.5b All the damage dealt to a unit is dealt, including any beyond what destroys it, and counts as damage dealt. See rule 608.6d.
 Example: Arc Lightning deals 6 to a Vulnerable 3/8 with nowhere for its Electric damage to jump: all 12 are dealt to that unit, not just the 8 that destroy it.
title: CR 112.5–112.5b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 112. Life, Damage, Rot and Debt
112.6 The source of damage is the thing that deals it. When a spell makes a unit deal damage (Squish, Fight, Battle), the unit is the source: its own attributes apply, and the spell's attributes do not. See rule 802.
 Example: a Powerful ally squishing deals double its defense.
 Example: a Powerful Squish does not double.
112.6a Damage a unit deals because a spell told it to is that unit's damage, not damage from a spell effect.
 Example: Squish damage does not trigger Ember of Life ("When one of your spell effects deals damage").
title: CR 112.6–112.6a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 112. Life, Damage, Rot and Debt
112.7 Combat damage is the damage columns deal to each other and to players in the combat damage step. All other damage is noncombat damage, including damage dealt by an ability that combat damage causes, such as Resonant's extra damage. See rule 608.
 Example: Resonant's extra damage is not combat damage, so Oorblak does not take it in place of the player.
title: CR 112.7

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 112. Life, Damage, Rot and Debt
112.8 All the damage one resolution of one effect deals is dealt at once. A recipient that the effect damages more than once is dealt the total once, and units destroyed by that damage are destroyed together, after all of it is dealt.
 Example: Channel Through deals damage to a unit twice; Restitution triggers once, for the total.
112.8a Each copy of an effect is a separate source and deals its damage separately.
 Example: Meteor Shower's three Rockfalls are three separate dealings of damage.
title: CR 112.8–112.8a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 112. Life, Damage, Rot and Debt
112.9 When a source would deal noncombat damage, its amount is worked out in this order: first, modifiers that add to it (such as Conduit of Pain's "plus 1") apply; then Powerful doubles the result; then a Vulnerable recipient is dealt double what reaches it. See rules 802, 708.
 Example: a Powerful Bellowing Boulder beside Conduit of Pain deals (1+1)x2 = 4 to each unit.
title: CR 112.9

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 112. Life, Damage, Rot and Debt
112.10 Damage dealt in the form of -1/-1 counters (by a Poisonous source) is still damage dealt: it triggers abilities that trigger on a unit being dealt damage. See rule 802.
 Example: Awoken Tomb hit by a Poisonous source makes its X/X.
title: CR 112.10

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 112. Life, Damage, Rot and Debt
112.11 Damage that is prevented is not dealt. It triggers nothing that triggers on damage being dealt, places no -1/-1 counters, and does not destroy a unit, even from a Deadly source. See rules 708, 608.6g.
 Example: a Deadly source cannot kill through Phytochemical Protection.
title: CR 112.11

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 112. Life, Damage, Rot and Debt
112.12 Damage that an effect replaces with something else (for example, damage dealt "as" rot) was still dealt. Abilities that care whether damage was dealt see it, even though the recipient took something else instead. See rules 708, 608.8a.
 Example: a column whose face damage Blightsea Polyp turns into rot still pays out Vroot's "that much".
title: CR 112.12

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 112. Life, Damage, Rot and Debt
112.13 Rot is a counter a player has. At the start of each deployment phase, each player is dealt damage equal to their rot, in initiative order. Rot damage is not simultaneous: the initiative player's rot is dealt and checked first, so a player it brings to 0 loses before the other player's rot is dealt (104.1a). See rule 507.
 Example: a player with 3 rot is dealt 3 damage as deployment begins.
 Example: Both players have more rot than life. The initiative player's rot is dealt first, and that player loses before the other player's rot is dealt.
112.13a Rot never decreases on its own. It deals its damage again every deployment until an effect removes it.
title: CR 112.13–112.13a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 112. Life, Damage, Rot and Debt
(continues 112.13: Rot is a counter a player has. At the start of each deployment phase, each player is dealt damage equal to their rot, in initiative order. Rot damage is not simultaneous: the initiative player's rot is dealt and checked…)
112.13b The source of rot damage is the damaged player's own rot, which is a source that player controls.
112.13c Rot damage is dealt as the deployment phase begins, before abilities that trigger "at the start of deployment". No player can respond to it. See rule 507.
title: CR 112.13b–112.13c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 112. Life, Damage, Rot and Debt
(continues 112.13: Rot is a counter a player has. At the start of each deployment phase, each player is dealt damage equal to their rot, in initiative order. Rot damage is not simultaneous: the initiative player's rot is dealt and checked…)
112.13d Rot damage can be replaced. A replacement that names no target replaces it on the spot. One that names a target ("put that many -1/-1 counters on target unit instead") puts a triggered ability on the stack to choose the target, and the damage is replaced whether or not that ability finds a target. See rule 708.
 Example: Skittering Blight takes your rot damage as +1/+1 counters.
 Example: Beyond, Codex Incarnate asks its controller for a target, and the rot damage never lands.
title: CR 112.13d

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 112. Life, Damage, Rot and Debt
(continues 112.13: Rot is a counter a player has. At the start of each deployment phase, each player is dealt damage equal to their rot, in initiative order. Rot damage is not simultaneous: the initiative player's rot is dealt and checked…)
112.13e An effect that says "gain rot" without naming a player gives the rot to the effect's controller.
 Example: Primordial Coalescence gives its caster 2 rot.
title: CR 112.13e

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 112. Life, Damage, Rot and Debt
112.14 Debt is a counter a player has. At the end of each of their resource steps, a player pays 1 mana for each debt they have, and each mana paid removes one debt. See rule 502.
112.14a Paying debt is not a choice and takes no action. It is the last thing in the resource step, so no resource can be expended after it in that step, and the mana spent on debt cannot be used for anything else that turn.
112.14b If a player cannot pay all their debt, they pay what they can. The rest stays and is charged again at their next resource step. There is no other penalty.
title: CR 112.14–112.14b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 112. Life, Damage, Rot and Debt
(continues 112.14: Debt is a counter a player has. At the end of each of their resource steps, a player pays 1 mana for each debt they have, and each mana paid removes one debt.)
112.14c Gaining debt can be a cost. Debt gained to pay a cost is gained when the cost is paid, and is kept even if the spell or ability is negated. See rule 111.2.
 Example: Hyper Beam negated by Dematerialize deals no damage, and the debt its caster gained to play it stays.
 Example: A spell with a [Gain N debt] cost that an effect plays in place still gains the debt.
 Example: Tides of the Cosmos plays Hyper Beam in a battle window: its caster gains the 4 debt.
title: CR 112.14c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 112. Life, Damage, Rot and Debt
112.15 Rot and debt are counters on players. An effect that removes counters from players removes them. An effect that changes the number of counters "put on" a player does not change how many are removed.
 Example: Burn the Blight removes rot and debt from players.
 Example: with Proliferating Slime in play, 2 rot put on its controller's opponent arrives as 3, but removing 2 rot from that player removes exactly 2.
title: CR 112.15

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 113. Timestamps
113.1 Effects that apply to the same layer apply in timestamp order. Where they conflict, the later effect takes precedence over the earlier one. See rule 709.
 Example: Monke resolves in battle, so other units lose all attributes. Afterwards a player augments Chitin Shredder, a Virus, onto their unit: that unit has Powerful, because the virus is later than Monke.
title: CR 113.1

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 113. Timestamps
113.2 An effect's timestamp is when it began to apply. A static ability's effect has the timestamp of the card that carries it, a mod's has the time it was applied, and an effect from a resolved spell or ability has the time it resolved. What a card prints is older than any effect.
 Example: an attribute granted to a unit while Suppression Field is still on the stack is lost when the spell resolves; one granted after it resolves is kept.
113.2a A change of control does not change an effect's timestamp. When a card, or the unit a mod is on, changes control, its effects keep the timestamps they already had, including when they now apply to other units. See rule 113.3.
 Example: Transmogrifant ("[Augment] Your other units gain +2/+2 and lose all attributes and abilities.") is on Player B's The Bonesculptor. Later, Pernicious Photosynthesis gives Player A's units Piercing until regroup. Then Rebalance gives Player A The Bonesculptor, so Transmogrifant now covers Player A's other units: they lose what they print and keep the Piercing, because Transmogrifant's effect is still older than it.
113.2b In a step both players take at the same time, the haste step and deployment, the initiative player's plays are timestamped before the other player's. This client stamps them so whatever order the two players made them in, and keeps each player's own plays in the order that player made them. See rules 507.3, 507.3a.
 Example: In one deployment the non-initiative player casts Pernicious Photosynthesis first and the initiative player then augments Transmogrifant onto The Bonesculptor. Transmogrifant is the older. When Rebalance later gives the non-initiative player The Bonesculptor, their units keep the Piercing.
 Example: With the same plays in the same order and the initiative the other way round, Pernicious Photosynthesis is the older, and the units lose the Piercing.
title: CR 113.2–113.2b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 113. Timestamps
113.3 An effect that removes attributes or abilities removes those the object has when the effect applies. An attribute or ability the object gains afterwards is not removed. See rule 712.
 Example: a Powerful virus attached after Suppression Field resolved makes the suppressed unit Powerful.
 Example: a Powerful virus attached after Transmogrifant is in play works.
title: CR 113.3

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 113. Timestamps
(continues 113.3: An effect that removes attributes or abilities removes those the object has when the effect applies. An attribute or ability the object gains afterwards is not removed.)
113.3a A continuous effect that removes attributes or abilities removes the printed ones of a unit that enters play after it began, because what a card prints is older than the effect. When that effect ends, the units get them back.
 Example: a unit entering play under Transmogrifant has no attributes, and gets them back when Transmogrifant leaves.
113.3b What a removal effect took stays taken until that effect ends (for a removal that lasts until regroup, at regroup). The unit does not get it back by leaving the column the effect applies to. This does not stop the unit gaining an attribute or ability from a later source (rule 113.3). See rule 113.3.
title: CR 113.3a–113.3b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 1. Game Concepts › 113. Timestamps
113.4 When two effects set a unit's base stats, the later one applies. See rule 206.
 Example: an opponent's Aberrant Statweaver ("Your units are base 3/3") makes their Wisp base 3/3. You cast Body Swap on your 1/1 and that Wisp: until regroup your unit is base 3/3 and the Wisp base 1/1, though the Statweaver is still in play.
title: CR 113.4

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 200. General
200.1 An Algomancy card can show these parts: a name, a mana cost, an affinity requirement, a timing icon, stats (power and defense), a type line of types and attributes, abilities, and a set symbol. Every card has a name; the other parts appear only on the cards that need them. Some cards also print an alternative-cost banner (203) or an augment symbol (208). See rules 201, 202, 203, 204, 205, 206, 207, 208, 209.
title: CR 200.1

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 200. General
200.2 The physical printed card is the source of truth for what a card says. Where the transcription a client reads differs from the printed card, the printed card governs and the transcription is corrected; the difference is not a ruling on the card. See rule 101.
title: CR 200.2

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 201. Name
201.1 Every card has a name.
title: CR 201.1

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 201. Name
201.2 "Other" and "another" compare objects, never names. Two cards with the same name are two different things, and each is "another" to the other. See rule 110.
 Example: A unit wearing two Rotbeast augments: each Rotbeast's trigger moves the other one.
title: CR 201.2

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 201. Name
201.3 Where a card speaks of a "unique" token, a token is identified by its name, its X and the stats the effect that created it set, together: a Robot 2 and a Robot 5 are two unique tokens, and so are a 3/3 and a 5/5 unit token. See rule 304.
 Example: Automaton of Abundance: when its controller creates a Robot 3, a Robot 2 and a Robot 1 together, those are three unique tokens, so three extra Robots are made.
 Example: Automaton of Abundance: a 3/3 and a 5/5 unit token created together are two unique tokens, so two extra tokens are made.
title: CR 201.3

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 201. Name
201.4 A card with a back face exists as its front face in every zone other than play. A transformed card that leaves play turns back over, and is binned under its front name. A back face is not a token. See rules 108, 710.
 Example: A transformed Scholar of the Void killed in play goes to the bin as Scholar of the Void.
title: CR 201.4

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 201. Name
201.5 A copy takes the name of the card it copies while it is a copy, but the physical card keeps its own name: when it leaves play it is binned, erased or returned to hand as itself. See rule 710.
 Example: A Borrower of Forms that copied a Good Whale and dies puts Borrower of Forms in the bin.
 Example: Recalled, it returns to the hand as Borrower of Forms.
title: CR 201.5

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 202. Cost Orb and Pips
202.1 The cost orb shows the card's mana cost: the number of resources a player must expend to play it. See rules 106, 111.
 Example: Good Whale (cost orb 6) cannot be played with five resources; played with seven, it expends six and leaves one open.
title: CR 202.1

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 202. Cost Orb and Pips
202.2 The pips with the cost are the card's affinity requirement. To play the card, its controller must have at least that many resources of each pip's element among their resources. The requirement is met, not paid: expended resources count toward it. See rule 105.
 Example: Two wood resources and any number of shards can pay for many [gg] cards in one turn.
title: CR 202.2

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 202. Cost Orb and Pips
202.3 The pips are not part of a card's cost. Where a card or rule refers to a card's cost, it means the mana number alone. See rule 111.
 Example: Resurrect ("cost 2 or less") can return Chitin Shredder, whose cost orb is 2 with two earth pips: its cost is 2, not 4.
title: CR 202.3

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 202. Cost Orb and Pips
202.4 An effect that reads a card's cost reads its printed cost. Effects that make a card cost more or less to play do not change the cost other effects read. See rule 111.
 Example: Squish paid at 4 under Stasis Sentry and Tranquility is still a 2-cost spell to Arcane Concentrator and Channeled Amalgam.
 Example: Tides of the Cosmos' "total cost 8 or less" is not shrunk by Tranquility.
title: CR 202.4

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 202. Cost Orb and Pips
202.5 A cost orb may show X. While a card with X in its cost is being cast, X is the amount chosen and paid, and that amount is the card's cost. See rules 107, 111.
 Example: With Unstable Apparition in play ("create a Fireball X, where X is the spell's cost"), its controller casts Wildfire for X = 0. Wildfire's cost is 0, so no Fireball is made.
title: CR 202.5

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 202. Cost Orb and Pips
202.6 A card with X in its cost has a cost of 0 wherever no X has been paid for it: in the deck, the hand, the cache, the bin, or as a unit in play. An X spell played by an effect that plays cards for free is played with X = 0. See rule 107.
 Example: Tides of the Cosmos counts an X spell as cost 0 against its budget of 8, and plays it at X = 0.
 Example: Living Vault caches a card from hand by paying its cost: an X card in hand costs 0, so it can be cached for [0].
title: CR 202.6

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 202. Cost Orb and Pips
202.7 A copy has the cost of the card it copies. See rule 710.
 Example: A Borrower of Forms that copied a Robot costs 0, so Lumengrove Lurker can recall it.
title: CR 202.7

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 203. Alternative-Cost Banner
203.1 Some cards print a banner that offers another way to play the card, for a cost of its own: Ambush and Prophecy are printed this way. A banner shows its own mana cost and affinity pips, and a Prophecy banner also shows a condition. See rule 803.
title: CR 203.1

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 203. Alternative-Cost Banner
203.2 A banner's cost is paid like any other cost, in place of the card's cost orb: its own mana is spent and its own affinity pips are required. See rules 111, 803.
 Example: Lurking Slimebeast ambushes for 3 mana with one water pip.
title: CR 203.2

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 203. Alternative-Cost Banner
203.3 A banner's cost is not the card's cost. Anything that reads the card's cost reads its cost orb, even when the card is played through its banner. See rule 202.
 Example: Lurking Slimebeast played through its Ambush banner (3 mana) still has a cost of 4, its cost orb.
title: CR 203.3

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 203. Alternative-Cost Banner
203.4 Prophesying pays a Prophecy banner's cost and puts the card into the cache with the banner's condition attached. Once the condition has been fulfilled, the card may be played from the cache for free and ignoring affinity, at its printed timing (see 803). See rules 403, 803.
 Example: A fulfilled prophecy whose card needs earth affinity its controller lacks is released from the cache with nothing paid.
title: CR 203.4

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 203. Alternative-Cost Banner
203.5 A timing icon printed in a banner governs only the play the banner offers, not the card. See rule 207.
203.5a A [Battle] icon on an Ambush banner lets the card be played as an Ambush during battle even though the card itself has no Battle timing. See rule 803.
 Example: Good Whale, a deployment unit, ambushes into the attacking column for [4bb] during battle.
title: CR 203.5–203.5a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 203. Alternative-Cost Banner
(continues 203.5: A timing icon printed in a banner governs only the play the banner offers, not the card.)
203.5b A [Haste] icon at the end of a Prophecy condition lets the card be prophesied during the haste step as well as during deployment. It does not change when the card may be played once the prophecy is fulfilled: that is always its printed timing. See rules 504, 803.
 Example: Divine Intervention ("Your life is 5 or less [Haste]") may be prophesied in the haste step.
title: CR 203.5b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 204. Type Line
204.1 The type line describes what the card is. It holds the card's attributes, its subtypes and its card type, and on some cards the augment symbol (208). See rule 300.
title: CR 204.1

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 204. Type Line
204.2 The type line of a card that can be played ends with its card type: Unit, Spell, or Spell Unit (a spell that is also a unit). A token's type line says so: Token Unit for a unit token, Spell Token for a spell token. A resource card's type line ends with Resource. See rules 301, 302, 303, 304.
title: CR 204.2

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 204. Type Line
(continues 204.2: The type line of a card that can be played ends with its card type: Unit, Spell, or Spell Unit (a spell that is also a unit). A token's type line says so: Token Unit for a unit token, Spell Token for a spell token. A…)
204.2a A Spell Unit is both a spell and a unit: an effect that asks for a unit or for a spell accepts it. See rule 303.
 Example: A spell unit played from hand through Hooba-Pon's ability counts as playing a spell.
title: CR 204.2a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 204. Type Line
204.3 The words of the type line other than its markers and its card type are subtypes, such as Whale, Squid or Jellyfish. A marker may stand among them. See rule 300.
title: CR 204.3

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 204. Type Line
204.4 An attribute printed on the type line is part of the card's rules. It is an attribute, not an ability. See rules 109, 802.
title: CR 204.4

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 204. Type Line
204.5 Attributes are printed in bold yellow (gold) or purple. Yellow attributes are combat attributes, which are shared by the units in the same column of a formation (see 603 and 802). Purple attributes, such as Burst and Unstable, are non-combat attributes and are not shared in formation. See rules 603, 802, 803.
 Example: Aberrant Statweaver attacking behind Chitin Shredder is Powerful through the column, but Chitin Shredder does not become Unstable: when it dies it is binned, while the Statweaver is erased.
title: CR 204.5

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 204. Type Line
204.6 The order in which a unit's attributes are printed, or in which it gained them, does not decide whether Tough or Balanced applies first: Balanced always applies after Tough (rule 802.1m). See rule 709.
 Example: A Lonely Forager (3/1) given Tough and Balanced is a 3/3, whichever it was given first.
title: CR 204.6

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 204. Type Line
204.7 A timing icon is not an attribute. A card whose only marking is its timing icon has no attributes. See rule 207.
title: CR 204.7

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 205. Text Box and Bracketed Text
205.1 The text box holds the card's abilities, which describe its effects. Most cards have abilities; some have none. See rule 109.
title: CR 205.1

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 205. Text Box and Bracketed Text
205.2 Reminder text, in italics, restates what an attribute or keyword does. An [Augment] mentioned inside reminder text is not an augment symbol (see 208.4a). See rule 208.
 Example: Reconfigure mentions [Augment] in its reminder text, but it cannot be applied as an augment.
title: CR 205.2

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 205. Text Box and Bracketed Text
205.3 Text in square brackets in a text box is either an additional cost or a choice between modes. A bracketed cost must be paid, and a bracketed mode chosen, to play the card. See rules 111, 702.
 Example: Darkblast's [Discard a card] is a cost: with no other card in hand it cannot be cast.
 Example: Retribution Thing's "[lost or gained]" is a mode: X is one of the two, never the sum.
title: CR 205.3

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 205. Text Box and Bracketed Text
(continues 205.3: Text in square brackets in a text box is either an additional cost or a choice between modes. A bracketed cost must be paid, and a bracketed mode chosen, to play the card.)
205.3a The owner of the effect pays a bracketed cost and chooses a bracketed mode, as the card or ability is put on the stack — never on resolution. See rules 702, 703.
 Example: Void Memory's caster declares "unit" or "spell" at cast; each opponent then discards one of that type if able.
205.3b A payment written in prose rather than in brackets, such as "unless its controller pays", is not the owner's: the player it names decides it, when the effect resolves. See rule 111.
205.3c Only bracketed prose is a cost or a mode. Symbols the transcription writes in brackets, such as [Augment], [Switch1], [once] or a cost like [2] or [4bb], are not bracketed text. See rule 111.
title: CR 205.3a–205.3c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 205. Text Box and Bracketed Text
(continues 205.3: Text in square brackets in a text box is either an additional cost or a choice between modes. A bracketed cost must be paid, and a bracketed mode chosen, to play the card.)
205.3d A bracketed additional cost is still paid when an effect lets the card be played for free. See rule 111.
 Example: A card played by Tides of the Cosmos still pays its bracketed cost, and a unit played by the same Tides is not yet in play to pay it.
title: CR 205.3d

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 205. Text Box and Bracketed Text
205.4 On a graft card the graft symbol divides an ability into a cause, before the symbol, and an effect, after it. When the card is grafted onto another, only the text after its graft symbol is added. See rule 722.
 Example: Omniwield Evoker reads "[three]: [Switch] Put a +1/+1 counter on me." Grafted onto another unit, it adds only the +1/+1 counter to the host's ability; the [three] before the symbol is not added, so nothing is paid for it.
title: CR 205.4

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 206. Power and Defense
206.1 A unit's stats are two numbers, printed power/defense. Power is how much damage the unit deals in combat. Defense is how much damage it can take before it dies. See rules 112, 608, 713.
 Example: An unblocked Rune Channeler (4/3) deals 4 damage; a Good Whale (7/5) survives 4 damage and dies to a fifth.
title: CR 206.1

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 206. Power and Defense
206.2 Stats mark a card as a unit. A spell has no stats, and neither does a spell token. Spell units do have stats, and enter play as units with them when they resolve. See rules 301, 303.
 Example: Lonely Forager, a Spell Unit, resolves into play as a 3/1 unit; Resurrect, a plain spell, goes to the bin.
 Example: No spell in the card pool carries a power or a defense.
 Example: A Fireball spell token carries no stats.
title: CR 206.2

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 206. Power and Defense
206.3 A unit's printed stats are the numbers shown on the card. Any difference from the printed stats is a stat change. See rule 709.
 Example: A unit whose base stats an effect has set differently has a stat change, so it is not a "unit with no stat changes" for Leave None Pure.
title: CR 206.3
CR 206.4

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 206. Power and Defense
206.5 An effect that makes a unit "base N/N" replaces its base stats; it does not add to them. Counters and other stat changes still apply on top. When two such effects apply, the later one wins. See rules 113, 709.
 Example: An opponent's Aberrant Statweaver makes their Wisp base 3/3. Body Swap on your 1/1 and that Wisp makes yours base 3/3 and the Wisp base 1/1 until regroup.
 Example: Unmake reads base power, and counters do not count toward it.
title: CR 206.5

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 206. Power and Defense
206.6 A stat change that an effect gives ("gains +1/+1") is temporary: it lasts only as long as the effect says, such as until regroup, or as long as a static ability applies. A +1/+1 or -1/-1 counter is a permanent change. A stat change is a counter only if the effect says it places counters. See rule 506.
 Example: A Good Whale with a +1/+1 counter hit by Jelly ("gains -2/-2 until regroup") is 6/4 in battle and 8/6 after regroup.
206.6a When a unit has both a +1/+1 counter and a -1/-1 counter, the two cancel and both are removed. See rule 706.
 Example: A -1/-1 counter put on a unit with +1/+1 counters removes one of them, and leaves no -1/-1 counter.
title: CR 206.6–206.6a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 206. Power and Defense
(continues 206.6: A stat change that an effect gives ("gains +1/+1") is temporary: it lasts only as long as the effect says, such as until regroup, or as long as a static ability applies. A +1/+1 or -1/-1 counter is a permanent change. A…)
206.6b Every counter is a counter, whatever its sign: a card that speaks of "a counter" counts +1/+1 and -1/-1 counters alike, unless it prints a sign. See rule 112.
 Example: Flux Resonator adds one more to -1/-1 counters too.
title: CR 206.6b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 206. Power and Defense
206.7 A unit with negative power deals 0 damage. See rules 112, 608.
 Example: A -3/1 unit attacking beside a 1/1 in an unblocked column: the column deals 1 damage.
title: CR 206.7

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 207. Timing Glyph
207.1 A timing icon in the top right corner of a card changes when, and how, the card can be played. The icons printed there are Haste, Battle and Virus (207.3–207.5). See rule 500.
 Example: Surly Stalker, a Battle unit, cannot be played in deployment but can be in battle; Ignis Sprite, with no icon, can be played in deployment.
title: CR 207.1

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 207. Timing Glyph
207.2 A card with no timing icon can be played only during deployment. See rule 507.
 Example: A unit with no timing icon cannot be played in battle, except when Tides of the Cosmos lets it ignore timing.
title: CR 207.2

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 207. Timing Glyph
207.3 A card with the Haste icon can be played during the haste step as well as during deployment. See rules 504, 507.
title: CR 207.3

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 207. Timing Glyph
207.4 A card with the Battle icon can be played only while its player is in battle with another player. It cannot be played during deployment. See rule 505.
207.4a Gaining Haste does not let a Battle card be played outside battle. A Battle card that an effect lets be played as if it had Haste can still be played only in battle. See rules 504, 803.
 Example: Dispatch Courier's grant does not let a {Battle} unit be played in the haste step.
title: CR 207.4–207.4a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 207. Timing Glyph
207.5 A card with the Virus icon can also be applied as an augment from hand during battle, as well as being played and augmented normally during deployment (see 723). See rules 721, 723.
 Example: In battle a Virus can be augmented from hand; a card without the Virus icon cannot, unless Rook allows it.
title: CR 207.5

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 207. Timing Glyph
207.6 A timing icon other than Virus does not change when a card can be applied as a mod. A Battle card cannot be applied as a mod during battle, and a Haste card cannot be applied in the haste step. See rule 720.
 Example: Molten Upheaval has Haste, but it can be grafted onto Bellowing Boulder only during deployment: not in the haste step, and not in battle.
title: CR 207.6

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 207. Timing Glyph
207.7 An effect may let a card be played ignoring its timing, as Tides of the Cosmos does ("You may play them now"). A card played that way may be played whatever its timing icon, or lack of one. See rule 701.
 Example: Tides of the Cosmos plays a deployment unit and a deployment spell unit in battle.
title: CR 207.7

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 207. Timing Glyph
(continues 207.7: An effect may let a card be played ignoring its timing, as Tides of the Cosmos does ("You may play them now"). A card played that way may be played whatever its timing icon, or lack of one.)
207.7a An effect that only lets a card be played from somewhere else, such as the bin or the cache, does not waive its timing. Cards that waive timing say so. See rules 403, 405, 803.
title: CR 207.7a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 207. Timing Glyph
207.8 A timing icon printed on one line of a card, rather than on the card, governs only that line. A "Discard me" line with no icon of its own is usable in battle as well as in deployment; one printed with a Battle icon is usable only in battle. See rules 203, 801.
 Example: Nothyr's battle-marked discard-me line is refused outside battle.
title: CR 207.8

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 208. Augment Box
208.1 The augment symbol marks what a card can give to another card when it is applied as an augment. It appears either at the start of a line in the text box, or at the start of the type line, before the card's attributes. See rule 721.
title: CR 208.1

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 208. Augment Box
208.2 An augment symbol in the text box gives all the text in the paragraph after it to the card the augment is applied to. See rule 721.
 Example: Vengeance applied as an augment gives its host "Cards your opponents play during battle gain [Sacrifice a unit]", with the host's controller as "you".
title: CR 208.2

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 208. Augment Box
208.3 An augment symbol on the type line gives the type line's attributes to the card the augment is applied to. An augment gives text, never stats. See rule 721.
 Example: Bubb's type-line augment donates {Unaware} and no stats.
title: CR 208.3

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 208. Augment Box
208.4 A card that prints the augment symbol can be applied as an augment, from hand, bin or cache (see 721), whether or not its augment text does anything a client can carry out. See rule 721.
 Example: A Pile of Rubbish can be applied as an augment from hand, from the bin, or from the cache while a glimpse lets it be played.
208.4a An [Augment] mentioned inside reminder text is not an augment symbol, and does not make the card an augment. See rule 205.
 Example: Reconfigure mentions [Augment] in its reminder text, but it cannot be applied as an augment.
title: CR 208.4–208.4a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 208. Augment Box
208.5 A copy does not have the augment symbol printed on the card it copies. See rule 710.
 Example: A Borrower of Forms that copied Bubb cannot be the first target of Reconfigure, though a real [Augment] unit in play can be.
title: CR 208.5

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 209. Complexity Glyph
209.1 The set symbol shows which expansion a card belongs to. Its colour shows the card's complexity: gold means complex.
title: CR 209.1

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 2. Parts of a Card › 209. Complexity Glyph
209.2 Complexity is used to choose which cards are in a game. The Quick Start suggests that inexperienced players remove the gold-symbol cards from their decks. See rule 902.
title: CR 209.2

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 3. Card Types › 300. General
300.1 Apart from resource cards (106), there are three card types: unit, spell and spell unit. There are two kinds of token: unit tokens and spell tokens. See rules 106, 301, 302, 303, 304.
title: CR 300.1

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 3. Card Types › 300. General
300.2 A card's type line names its type. A unit's type line ends "Unit", a spell's ends "Spell", and a spell unit's ends "Spell Unit". A token's type line also contains the word "Token": "Robot Token Unit" is a unit token, and "Spell Token" a spell token. See rule 204.
title: CR 300.2

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 3. Card Types › 300. General
300.3 Units, unit tokens and spell units have stats: power and defense. Spells and spell tokens have no stats. See rules 206, 301.3, 301.4.
 Example: A Good Whale is 7/5 and a Robot token with two counters is 2/2. A Crystal ("Put X +1/+1 counters on target unit") can target the Whale, but not the Fireball token beside it: a spell token is not a unit and has no stats.
title: CR 300.3

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 3. Card Types › 300. General
300.4 Every unit, spell and spell unit is a card, including a unit that is in play. A token is not a card (see 304). See rule 304.
 Example: Void Mandible, which watches for a nontoken card being played during battle, sees a {Battle} unit being played.
title: CR 300.4

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 3. Card Types › 300. General
300.5 When printed text names a type, the noun it uses decides what it reaches.
 Example: Tranquility ("Spells cost one more") taxes a Crystal token, but Arbiter of Armistice ("Cards played during battle") charges it no life.
title: CR 300.5

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 3. Card Types › 300. General
(continues 300.5: When printed text names a type, the noun it uses decides what it reaches.)
300.5a "Spell" includes spell units and spell tokens. See rules 303.5, 304.
 Example: Emberflame Enlightener gives "your spells" {Powerful}, and that includes your spell tokens.
300.5b "Unit" includes unit tokens and spell units, but not spell tokens. See rules 303.6, 304.9.
 Example: The World Shepherd watches for a unit token being created; a spell token being created does not trigger it.
 Example: Automaton of Abundance copies unit tokens; a spell token in the same batch is not a unit and is not copied.
title: CR 300.5a–300.5b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 3. Card Types › 300. General
(continues 300.5: When printed text names a type, the noun it uses decides what it reaches.)
300.5c "Token" with no other qualifier includes both unit tokens and spell tokens. See rule 304.
 Example: Mycelial Mentor triggers when its controller creates a Fireball, a spell token.
300.5d "Card" never includes a token. A spell token being cast is a spell being played, but not a card being played. See rules 304.2, 701.
 Example: Arbiter of Armistice makes cards played during battle cost 2 life more; casting a spell token costs no life.
300.5e "Nontoken" excludes every token.
 Example: Void Mandible says "nontoken card"; a spell token being cast does not trigger it.
title: CR 300.5c–300.5e

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 3. Card Types › 301. Units
301.1 A unit is a permanent: once it enters play, it stays in play until something removes it. See rule 404.
 Example: A Good Whale stays in play through two turns and their regroups until it is destroyed.
title: CR 301.1

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 3. Card Types › 301. Units
301.2 Units are what players use to build armies, and to attack and defend. See rules 604, 606.
title: CR 301.2

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 3. Card Types › 301. Units
301.3 A unit's power is how much damage it deals in combat. See rules 206, 608.
 Example: An unblocked The Foretold (power 3) deals 3 damage to the defending player.
title: CR 301.3

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 3. Card Types › 301. Units
301.4 A unit's defense is how much damage it can sustain in battle before it dies. See rules 206, 112.
 Example: A Good Whale (defense 5) survives a Fireball 2 with 2 damage on it, then dies to a Fireball 3.
301.4a A unit that has been dealt a total amount of damage greater than or equal to its defense during battle dies. See rules 112, 713.
 Example: A 3/3 dealt exactly 3 dies; dealt 2 it lives.
title: CR 301.4–301.4a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 3. Card Types › 301. Units
301.5 When a unit dies or is deleted, it is put into the bin. See rules 405, 304.10, 803.
title: CR 301.5

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 3. Card Types › 301. Units
301.6 A unit does not have to wait before it can attack or block: as long as a unit is in play, it can attack and block. See rules 604, 606, 301.7.
 Example: A unit that spawned during the attack step may still be declared as a blocker.
title: CR 301.6

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 3. Card Types › 301. Units
301.7 A unit that enters play during battle is placed outside of formation: it is in the region, but it is not attacking or blocking. It enters a formation only if the effect that put it into play says so. See rules 602, 604, 304.8.
 Example: A 2/2 that Tidelurker creates mid-attack stays in the enemy region, in no column, and cannot block the counterattack.
 Example: A spell unit that Hooba-Pon plays spawns into an open position in Hooba-Pon's formation, because Hooba-Pon says so.
title: CR 301.7

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 3. Card Types › 301. Units
301.8 A unit whose text says it spawns with counters enters play already carrying them. This is a fact about the unit as it arrives, not an ability: it does not use the stack, and nothing can respond to it. See rule 708.
 Example: Aethercap Siphoner (printed 4/4, spawns with three -1/-1 counters) is already a 1/1 when an ability that watches allies spawn looks at it.
 Example: Nothing goes on the stack for Powerforge Synergist's or Aethercap Siphoner's spawn counters.
title: CR 301.8

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 3. Card Types › 301. Units
(continues 301.8: A unit whose text says it spawns with counters enters play already carrying them. This is a fact about the unit as it arrives, not an ability: it does not use the stack, and nothing can respond to it.)
301.8a Those counters are put on the unit as it enters, by the player who spawns it. So an ability that triggers when a player puts counters on a unit triggers, and an effect that changes how many counters would be put on a unit changes them. See rules 708, 112.
 Example: A Robot 2 created by Living Forge counts as "you put counters on an ally": its controller's Scrapyard Custodian draws a card.
 Example: Aethercap Siphoner arriving with its counters also counts as "you put counters on an ally".
 Example: With an allied Flux Resonator, Powerforge Synergist enters with three +1/+1 counters instead of two.
title: CR 301.8a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 3. Card Types › 301. Units
301.9 A unit that an effect "puts into play" was not played. A unit that an effect lets a player "play" was played, wherever it came from. See rule 701.
 Example: Bloomcaster creates a 1/1 when its controller plays a unit, but not when a unit is put into play.
 Example: The units Wake the Dead plays out of a bin are played: Bloomcaster and Stalwart Sentinel both see them.
 Example: The unit Gridxlan lets its player play from the bin is played: it is paid for, and only one is allowed each deployment.
title: CR 301.9

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 3. Card Types › 302. Spells
302.1 A spell provides a one-time effect. See rule 702.
 Example: Manufacture creates three Robots once and goes to the bin; it never enters play.
title: CR 302.1

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 3. Card Types › 302. Spells
302.2 When a spell resolves, it goes directly to the bin. See rules 405, 704, 303.3, 304.10.
title: CR 302.2

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 3. Card Types › 302. Spells
302.3 A spell token is a spell. See rule 304.11.
 Example: Emberflame Enlightener's "your spells" includes its controller's spell tokens.
title: CR 302.3

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 3. Card Types › 303. Spell Units
303.1 A spell unit is both a spell and a unit. Like a spell it has a one-time effect; like a unit it has stats. See rule 300.5.
 Example: A played Jelly is a played spell, gives the target -2/-2, and then its body is a 2/1 unit in play.
title: CR 303.1

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 3. Card Types › 303. Spell Units
303.2 A spell unit that has been played goes on the stack. It is not in play while it is on the stack. See rule 406.
 Example: A Jelly that has been played sits on the stack beneath Bloomcaster's trigger; negated there, it never enters play.
title: CR 303.2

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 3. Card Types › 303. Spell Units
303.3 When a spell unit resolves, its spell effect happens first. Then the unit enters play, instead of the card going to the bin. See rules 704, 404.
 Example: Spawntender creates its 8/8, and then its own 2/2 body enters play.
title: CR 303.3

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 3. Card Types › 303. Spell Units
303.4 If a spell unit is prevented from resolving (it is negated, or every one of its targets has become invalid), the unit does not enter play and the card goes to the bin. See rules 704, 405.
 Example: A spell unit played through Hooba-Pon and negated never enters play.
title: CR 303.4

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 3. Card Types › 303. Spell Units
303.5 Playing a spell unit is playing a spell, and while it is on the stack it is a spell: anything that refers to a spell, or to an allied spell, applies to it. See rules 300.5a, 701.
 Example: A spell unit played through Hooba-Pon counts as playing a spell.
 Example: Origon negates a spell unit when it is the first spell a player plays in the battle.
 Example: If Molten Riftbreaker despawns while an allied spell unit is on the stack, its "negate all allied spells" negates that spell unit.
 Example: A Jelly that Wake the Dead plays from a bin is played as a spell: its spell is cast, and its body arrives only after it resolves.
title: CR 303.5

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 3. Card Types › 303. Spell Units
303.6 A spell unit is also a unit card. An effect that lets a player play a unit lets them play a spell unit, and it is played as a spell. See rule 300.5b.
 Example: Hooba-Pon offers a spell unit from the hand; its spell part happens and its body takes the open position.
 Example: Insidious Invitation's "play a unit from hand" lets each player play a spell unit.
 Example: A Jelly that Wake the Dead plays gets its spell part, then its unit body.
title: CR 303.6

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 3. Card Types › 303. Spell Units
303.7 A spell unit played during battle enters play in the region where it resolved, outside of formation, unless its own text or the effect that played it places it in a formation. See rules 301.7, 602.
 Example: Played through Hooba-Pon, a spell unit spawns into Hooba-Pon's formation.
title: CR 303.7

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 3. Card Types › 303. Spell Units
303.8 A spell unit that enters play without being played (for example, one put into play from a bin) does not produce its spell effect. See rules 301.9, 701.
 Example: Exhume puts a Jelly from the bin into play: its -2/-2 does not happen, and Bloomcaster does not trigger, because the Jelly was not played.
title: CR 303.8

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 3. Card Types › 303. Spell Units
303.9 A spell unit that an effect lets a player play from somewhere other than the hand is still played: its spell effect happens, and the unit enters play only if the spell resolves. See rules 301.9, 701.
 Example: A Jelly that Wake the Dead plays from a bin has its spell part happen, and its body enters play only if that spell resolves.
title: CR 303.9

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 3. Card Types › 303. Spell Units
303.10 If a spell unit's own text says that another player gains control of it, it enters play under that player's control. There is no moment when its caster controls it. Its owner does not change. See rules 102, 711.
 Example: Hush Mush negates an opponent's effect and enters play already under that opponent's control; its caster never controls it.
 Example: The caster's Flourishing Flora, which watches allies spawn, does not see Hush Mush arrive.
title: CR 303.10

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 3. Card Types › 303. Spell Units
303.11 If a spell unit's own text says it becomes a copy of something, it enters play already as that copy. Becoming the copy is not a triggered ability. See rule 710.
 Example: Borrower of Forms has the copied unit's name, stats and attributes from the instant it enters play.
title: CR 303.11

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 3. Card Types › 303. Spell Units
(continues 303.11: If a spell unit's own text says it becomes a copy of something, it enters play already as that copy. Becoming the copy is not a triggered ability.)
303.11a While a spell unit is a copy of a unit, it is not a spell unit. See rule 710.
 Example: Cosmic Reversal returns spell units in play to their controllers' hands; a Borrower of Forms copying a unit stays in play.
title: CR 303.11a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 3. Card Types › 304. Tokens
304.1 Tokens are created by effects, directly into play. See rule 404.
 Example: Manufacture creates three Robot tokens straight into play, through no hand, stack or bin.
title: CR 304.1

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 3. Card Types › 304. Tokens
304.2 A token is not a card. See rules 300.4, 300.5d.
title: CR 304.2

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 3. Card Types › 304. Tokens
304.3 A token is either a unit token or a spell token. See rule 300.1.
title: CR 304.3

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 3. Card Types › 304. Tokens
304.4 A unit that an effect creates is a unit token, whether or not the effect calls it a token.
 Example: Spawntender creates an 8/8 unit without calling it a token; it is still a token, so Download ("Gain control of target token") can take it.
304.4a A copy of a unit that an effect creates is a token, even when the unit copied is not. See rule 710.
 Example: The copy Echo of Despair creates of itself is a token.
title: CR 304.4–304.4a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 3. Card Types › 304. Tokens
304.5 A copy of a spell made on the stack, such as one made by Earthbound Replicator or Maelstrom Charger, is not a token. See rule 710.
 Example: Download cannot take a spell copy that Earthbound Replicator made.
title: CR 304.5

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 3. Card Types › 304. Tokens
304.6 A nontoken unit that becomes a copy of a token does not become a token. See rule 710.
 Example: A Borrower of Forms that copies a Robot token is a nontoken unit.
 Example: With that Borrower in play beside a real token, Download can take the token but not the Borrower.
title: CR 304.6

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 3. Card Types › 304. Tokens
304.7 The back face of a card that transforms is not a token. The transformed card is still a card, and in every zone other than play it is its front face. See rule 710.
 Example: A transformed Scholar of the Void that dies goes to the bin as Scholar of the Void.
title: CR 304.7

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 3. Card Types › 304. Tokens
304.8 A token enters play in the region where the source that created it is when the effect resolves. See rules 601, 108.
 Example: Life Plant, attacking in the enemy region, creates its 1/1s there and not at home.
304.8a A unit token created during battle in an enemy region stays in that region, outside of formation. It cannot block a counterattack, and it returns to its controller's home region at regroup. See rules 301.7, 506, 610.
 Example: Tidelurker's 2/2, created mid-attack, stays in the enemy region and cannot block the counterattack.
title: CR 304.8–304.8a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 3. Card Types › 304. Tokens
304.9 A unit token is a unit. It works exactly as a unit card does, except as these rules say otherwise. See rules 301, 304.10.
 Example: A Robot token with two counters attacks unblocked and deals 2 damage.
304.9a Unit tokens stay in play through regroup. See rules 506, 304.13.
 Example: A unit token survives regroup while a spell token beside it is erased.
title: CR 304.9–304.9a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 3. Card Types › 304. Tokens
304.10 A token that leaves play goes to the zone it was sent to: a unit token that dies enters the bin, and a recalled token, unit or spell, enters its controller's hand. It really is there, so abilities that watch that zone see it. It is then erased from the game, before anything that triggered on its arrival resolves. See rules 410, 713, 405, 402.
 Example: A unit token that dies enters the bin, is not trashed, and is then erased.
 Example: Rider of the Tides, which watches cards entering a hand during battle, sees a recalled unit token.
 Example: A Fireball recalled off the stack enters its controller's hand, Rider of the Tides sees it, and it is erased.
title: CR 304.10

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 3. Card Types › 304. Tokens
(continues 304.10: A token that leaves play goes to the zone it was sent to: a unit token that dies enters the bin, and a recalled token, unit or spell, enters its controller's hand. It really is there, so abilities that watch that zone…)
304.10a A token that enters a bin is not trashed. See rules 801, 405.
 Example: A unit token dying in battle does not add to the count of cards trashed in that battle.
304.10b A unit token that dies still dies: abilities that trigger when a unit dies see it, unless they say "nontoken". See rule 713.
title: CR 304.10a–304.10b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 3. Card Types › 304. Tokens
304.11 A spell token is a spell that is in play. Its controller may cast it from play; casting it works the same way as casting a spell from the hand. See rules 302.3, 702.
304.11a A spell token can be cast only in the region it is in. See rule 601.
304.11b Casting a spell token is playing a spell. It is played from play, so it is played from somewhere other than the hand. See rules 701, 702, 300.5d.
 Example: Casting a Fireball token triggers Stalwart Sentinel.
