 Example: Crevice Lurker makes abilities cost [one] more during battle. It taxes both players' abilities in its region, the opponent's as well as its controller's.
601.1e A player cannot sacrifice a unit that is in a different region, even a unit they control, and cannot do so to pay a cost in their current region.
 Example: A player's only units are at home, outside the battle region, when Cull says "Each player sacrifices a unit." They sacrifice nothing.
title: CR 601.1–601.1e

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 601. Regions
601.2 Every unit and every spell token in play is in exactly one region at a time.
 Example: A unit attacks and a Fireball token rides along with it. Both are now in the battle region and no longer in their home region.
601.2a The stack, the bins, the hands and the caches are bound by the regional rule like everything else (rule 101.6). Each region has its own stack. No player owns it: it is shared by the players present in that region, and only they can put effects on it or respond to them. A player's bin, hand and cache are tied to that player: an effect can affect them only in a region where that player is present (rule 601.4c). See rule 601.4c.
 Example: During deployment, an effect that targets a cached card can reach only its controller's own cache. In battle, where both players are present, it can reach either cache.
 Example: Molten Riftbreaker dies in its controller's home region during a battle elsewhere: its "negate all allied spells" leaves the spell on the battle region's stack alone. Dying in the battle region, it negates it.
title: CR 601.2–601.2a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 601. Regions
601.3 The regions are arranged in a circle. Each player's region has two neighbouring regions, one to the left and one to the right, except in a two-player game, where each region has one neighbouring region. See rules 903, 904.
 Example: In a two-player game there is only one region to attack into: the attackers go into the opponent's region, and the counterattack goes into the first attacker's region.
601.3a When a player is eliminated, the regions on either side of theirs become neighbours, and the game continues. See rules 104, 903.
601.3b In a team game, once a player's neighbouring opponents have been eliminated, that player may send attacks through allied regions into the nearest enemy region. See rule 904.
title: CR 601.3–601.3b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 601. Regions
601.4 A player is always present in their own region. A player who attacks into another region becomes present in that region as well, and stays present there until regroup, even if every unit they sent into it is removed. See rule 604.
 Example: A player attacks into the opponent's region. From then until regroup, both players are present there, so a unit that dies in that region dies in front of both of them.
601.4a Attacking is the only way a player enters another player's region. A player who declares no attack does not enter the region they could have attacked. See rule 604.
601.4b Outside the battle phase, every player is alone in their own region. A player cannot interact with any other player, or with another player's units, outside the battle phase. See rules 505, 507.
 Example: During deployment, Prismatic Observer can recall a card from its controller's own cache only. The opponent's cache is out of reach, because the opponent is not in the Observer's region.
601.4c While a player is present in a region, effects in that region can affect that player, and that player's hand, bin, cache and resources. While a player is not present, effects in that region cannot affect any of them.
 Example: In battle, both players are present in the battle region, so Prismatic Observer may recall a card from either player's cache.
601.4d “Each opponent” and “each player” mean each such player who is present in the effect's region. If no such player is present, that part of the effect does nothing. See rule 102.
 Example: A player sacrifices Bloated Manablub during deployment. “Each opponent loses 3 life” reaches nobody, because no opponent is in that player's region.
 Example: Rebalance resolves in a region where no opponent is present. No unit changes hands.
title: CR 601.4–601.4d

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 601. Regions
(continues 601.4: A player is always present in their own region. A player who attacks into another region becomes present in that region as well, and stays present there until regroup, even if every unit they sent into it is removed.)
601.4e An ally is a unit under your control in the region where the effect is happening. An enemy is a unit in that region that is not under your control. A unit in another region is neither. See rule 110.
title: CR 601.4e

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 601. Regions
(continues 601.4: A player is always present in their own region. A player who attacks into another region becomes present in that region as well, and stays present there until regroup, even if every unit they sent into it is removed.)
601.4f At regroup, every player and every unit returns to its own region: a unit returns to its controller's region (see rule 506). See rule 506.
 Example: Life Plant's 1/1s, created in the enemy region during an attack, return to their controller's region at regroup.
title: CR 601.4f

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 601. Regions
601.5 A unit or spell token created by an effect is created in the region where the effect's source is when the effect resolves. That need not be its controller's own region. See rules 602.2a, 304.
 Example: Life Plant attacks into the opponent's region, and its controller loses life there. Its 1/1s are created in the opponent's region, not at home.
 Example: Tidelurker attacks and creates a 2/2 in the enemy region. That 2/2 cannot block the counterattack in its controller's own region.
title: CR 601.5

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 601. Regions
601.6 Battle is resolved one region at a time. Once players have begun interacting inside a region, every step of battle is completed in that region before those players can interact anywhere else. See rules 505, 610.
 Example: The non-initiative player sends a counterattacker at block time. Battle in the first region runs through to its end before the counterattack battle begins in the other region.
601.6a While battle is being resolved in a region, units in any other region are treated as if they don't exist.
 Example: A unit with an “After combat” ability stays at home while its controller attacks. When battle ends in the opponent's region, the ability does not trigger.
601.6b Regions are resolved in clockwise order starting with the region to the left of the initiative player, so the initiative player's region resolves last. In a two-player game, battle is resolved first in the non-initiative player's region and then, if there was a counterattack, in the initiative player's region. See rules 505, 610.
 Example: The initiative player attacks into the non-initiative player's region. After that battle, the counterattack is fought in the initiative player's region.
title: CR 601.6–601.6b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 601. Regions
601.7 An “After combat” ability works for a unit that is present in the region where the battle happened, whether or not that unit is in a formation. It does not trigger in a region where no battle took place. See rule 609.
 Example: A unit with an “After combat” ability is in the battle region but outside the formation. Its ability still triggers after combat.
title: CR 601.7

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 601. Regions
601.8 Regions limit what effects can reach and count. The printed statement that there is “zero information or interaction between regions” is read as a limit on effects: no effect carries information from one region into another. It does not hide anything from players: a player may see what happens in a region they are not present in. See rule 601.1a.
title: CR 601.8

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 602. Formations
602.1 When units attack or block, they are placed in a formation. The units a player attacks with make up that player's attacking formation; the units a player blocks with make up that player's defending formation. See rules 604, 606.
 Example: A player attacks with three units in two columns; those three units are the attacking formation. The two units the defender blocks with are the defending formation.
602.1a A formation has a front row and a back row, and any number of columns. Each column of a formation holds at most two units: one in the front row and one in the back row. See rule 603.1.
 Example: A player may attack five columns wide, but cannot put three units in one column.
602.1b An attacking formation is set during the attack step. A defending formation is set during the block step. See rules 604, 606.
 Example: The defender cannot declare blockers during the attack step, and the attacker cannot change the attack once the block step has begun.
title: CR 602.1–602.1b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 602. Formations
(continues 602.1: When units attack or block, they are placed in a formation. The units a player attacks with make up that player's attacking formation; the units a player blocks with make up that player's defending formation.)
602.1c A player's formation is that player's whole side of the battle in that region: every unit they have arrayed there, in every column. It is not a single column. An effect that targets a formation targets one player's whole side. See rule 110.
 Example: Galactic Germination targets an attacking formation of three units in two columns. It creates three 1/1s.
602.1d A formation remains a formation for as long as its battle lasts, even when every unit in it has been removed. An effect that counts the units in an empty formation counts zero.
 Example: Galactic Germination targets a formation, and every unit in it dies before the spell resolves. It resolves and creates no units.
title: CR 602.1c–602.1d

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 602. Formations
(continues 602.1: When units attack or block, they are placed in a formation. The units a player attacks with make up that player's attacking formation; the units a player blocks with make up that player's defending formation.)
602.1e Once a formation is set, its units are locked in their positions until regroup, when they all leave formation. A unit's position changes only as rules 602.3–602.5 describe, or when an effect moves it. See rules 602.3, 602.4, 602.5, 506.
 Example: Riftwalker's ability switches its position with another ally in its formation.
title: CR 602.1e

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 602. Formations
602.2 A unit can be in a battle region without being in a formation. A unit outside the formation is neither attacking nor blocking.
 Example: A defending unit stands in the battle region but is not declared as a blocker. It blocks nothing, and the unblocked attacker deals its damage to the defending player.
602.2a A unit that spawns during battle, whether created by an effect or played as a spell unit, is placed in its region outside the formation, unless the card says otherwise. See rules 602.6, 602.7.
 Example: Aberrant Populace attacks and creates two Wisps. The Wisps are in the battle region, outside the formation.
602.2b A unit that comes under another player's control during a battle, after the formations are set, leaves its formation, unless the effect that changes its control itself gives it a position. It stays out of every formation for the rest of that battle, attacking and blocking for nobody, and joins its new controller's side at regroup. See rule 711.
 Example: Download steals an enemy Robot token after blocks. The Robot leaves the formation and takes no further part in the battle.
 Example: At regroup, the stolen Robot joins its new controller's side.
 Example: After attacks, the defender casts Organic Exchange on an attacking Bubb and their own 1/1, which is in no formation. The two swap positions as the card says: the 1/1 takes Bubb's attack slot and deals the combat damage, and Bubb is in no formation.
title: CR 602.2–602.2b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 602. Formations
602.3 The front row of a column must be filled before a unit can be placed in its back row. So a column of a formation holds no unit, one unit in its front row, or two units. It never holds a unit in its back row alone.
 Example: While building an attack, a player puts a unit in the back slot of an empty column. When the attack is declared, that unit stands in the front row.
title: CR 602.3

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 602. Formations
602.4 If a unit in the front row of a column leaves the formation, the unit behind it moves up into the front row. This happens whenever it occurs during the battle: before blocks, after blocks and during combat damage.
 Example: Blocks have been declared. The front unit of an attacking column dies; the unit behind it moves to the front of that column.
title: CR 602.4

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 602. Formations
602.5 If the last unit in a column of an attacking formation leaves it before blocks are declared, the columns on either side close in to fill the gap, so the line has no empty column.
 Example: A three-column attack loses the only unit of its middle column during the attack window. The right-hand column moves left, and the line is two columns wide.
602.5a After blocks are declared, columns never move to fill a gap. A column emptied after blocks stays in the line as a hole for the rest of the battle, even if its blockers are removed too. See rule 608.4e.
 Example: After blocks, the only attacker in the middle column dies. The column stays where it is, empty, and the columns to its right do not move.
 Example: Later in the same battle the blockers of that column die too. The hole still does not close.
602.5b Rules 602.4 and 602.5 apply however a unit leaves its formation: it may die, be recalled, cached or erased, or leave in any other way.
 Example: Before blocks, the only unit of a middle column is recalled to its owner's hand. The line closes up just as it would after a death.
title: CR 602.5–602.5b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 602. Formations
(continues 602.5: If the last unit in a column of an attacking formation leaves it before blocks are declared, the columns on either side close in to fill the gap, so the line has no empty column.)
602.5c A formation closes up immediately when a unit leaves it, as a state-based action. An ability that triggers on that unit leaving play sees the formation already closed up. See rule 713.
 Example: Before blocks, the only unit of a middle column dies. By the time any ability that triggers on the death looks at the formation, the gap has already closed.
title: CR 602.5c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 602. Formations
(continues 602.5: If the last unit in a column of an attacking formation leaves it before blocks are declared, the columns on either side close in to fill the gap, so the line has no empty column.)
602.5d A defending formation may have empty columns, and they are never closed up. See rule 606.
 Example: The defender blocks the first and third attacking columns and leaves the second unblocked. The defending formation keeps its gap.
title: CR 602.5d

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 602. Formations
602.6 When an effect creates a unit, or puts one into play, “in my formation” or “in formation” without naming a position, the effect's controller chooses the position as the effect resolves.
 Example: Hooba-Lin's host attacks, and its trigger creates a 1/1 “in my formation”. As the trigger resolves, Hooba-Lin's controller chooses where in the formation the 1/1 goes.
602.6a The positions such a unit may take are: a new column at either end of the line; the back slot of any column that holds exactly one unit; and the front slot of a hole left after blocks (rule 602.5a). A line with no column left has one end, so there the only position is one new column. See rules 602.5a, 602.6k.
 Example: An attacking line has two columns, the first with two units and the second with one. The legal positions are a new column at the left end, the back slot of the second column, and a new column at the right end.
 Example: A lone Hooba-Lin attacks and is killed under its trigger. Its remembered line holds no column, so the 1/1 takes the one new column there.
602.6b “Either side of the existing units” means the two ends of the line. A unit is never put into a new column between two existing columns.
 Example: An attacking line has three columns. A unit placed “in my formation” may open a new column at the left or right end, but never between the first and second columns.
title: CR 602.6–602.6b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 602. Formations
(continues 602.6: When an effect creates a unit, or puts one into play, “in my formation” or “in formation” without naming a position, the effect's controller chooses the position as the effect resolves.)
602.6c A defending formation never gains a new column at its ends this way. A unit placed into a defending formation may go into the back slot of a blocking column that holds one unit. After blocks have been declared, and until combat damage has been dealt, it may also stand in front of an attacking column that still has an attacker and no blocker, and that column is then blocked (see rule 606). See rules 606, 607, 602.6j.
 Example: The defender's only blocking column already holds two units. An effect that puts a unit into the defender's formation has no position for it.
 Example: After blocks, the defender plays Tiderunner Initiate in front of an unblocked attacker. That column is now blocked, and the attacker deals its combat damage to the Tiderunner.
title: CR 602.6c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 602. Formations
(continues 602.6: When an effect creates a unit, or puts one into play, “in my formation” or “in formation” without naming a position, the effect's controller chooses the position as the effect resolves.)
602.6d If exactly one position is legal, the unit goes there and no choice is asked. If no position is legal, the effect places nothing.
602.6e “My formation” means the formation the effect's source is in. If the source is in play but not in any formation when the effect resolves, the effect places nothing and creates nothing. See rule 602.2b.
 Example: Hooba-Lin's host attacks, then is stolen before the trigger resolves, so it is in play but out of the formation. No 1/1 is created.
 Example: Hooba-Bot blocks, and with its trigger waiting, Organic Exchange puts it into the attacking line. The Robot is made in the attacking line, where Hooba-Bot now stands, for the player who controls the trigger.
 Example: The same with Hooba-Pon: the unit it lets its player play goes into the attacking line, where Hooba-Pon now stands.
title: CR 602.6d–602.6e

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 602. Formations
(continues 602.6: When an effect creates a unit, or puts one into play, “in my formation” or “in formation” without naming a position, the effect's controller chooses the position as the effect resolves.)
602.6f If the effect's source has left play while its effect is on the stack, “my formation” means the formation the source was in when it left play, and the effect still places the unit there, even if no unit is left standing in that formation. See rules 714, 602.6k.
 Example: Hooba-Lin attacks and is killed with its trigger on the stack. The 1/1 is still created, in the formation Hooba-Lin was in.
 Example: Hooba-Lin attacks alone and is killed with its trigger on the stack. The attacking line now holds no unit, and the 1/1 is still created in it.
602.6g An effect whose text says “if I am still in formation” does nothing if its source is no longer in the formation when the effect resolves, including when the source has left play.
 Example: Hooba-Nan attacks and is killed with its trigger on the stack. The trigger creates no 1/1s.
602.6h An amount that counts units in “my formation” is counted as the effect resolves. Units that have left the formation by then are not counted. If the source itself has left play, the amount counts the formation it was in. See rule 603.2d.
 Example: Embermaw Fledgling attacks and dies in combat. Its after-combat trigger still counts the attacking units of the formation it was in.
602.6i If an effect lets a player play a spell unit into a formation (as Hooba-Pon does), the spell part happens first. If it resolves, the unit then spawns into the formation. See rule 303.
 Example: Hooba-Pon attacks and its controller plays a spell unit from hand through it. The spell resolves, and then the unit appears in the chosen position.
602.6j After blocks, while the defending formation still holds at least one unit, a unit placed into it may also take the front slot of a blocking column whose blockers have all left it. The unit then blocks that column. See rules 602.6c, 602.6a, 602.6k.
 Example: The defender's only blocker in the second column dies after blocks. An effect that puts a unit into the defender's formation may put it in front of the second attacking column.
title: CR 602.6f–602.6j

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 602. Formations
(continues 602.6: When an effect creates a unit, or puts one into play, “in my formation” or “in formation” without naming a position, the effect's controller chooses the position as the effect resolves.)
602.6k A player with no unit standing in a formation in the battle, because they have not formed one or because every unit in it has left, is offered no position in it, not even a hole, and a unit cannot be played or placed into it. Rules 602.6c and 602.6f are the exceptions. See rules 602.1d, 602.6f, 602.7c, 602.6c.
 Example: The attacker has attacked and the defender has not yet declared blocks. The defender stands in no formation, so an effect that puts a unit into the defender's formation has nowhere to put it.
 Example: After blocks, every attacking unit dies. The attacker then plays Tiderunner Initiate; it cannot be played into the attacking line, not even into a hole, and enters play outside any formation.
 Example: The defender declares no blockers. An effect that puts a unit into the defender's formation may still put it in front of the unblocked attacking column (rule 602.6c); the attacker is offered no such spot.
 Example: A living Hooba-Lin whose line has emptied around it is offered nothing; only a source that has left play keeps its remembered formation.
title: CR 602.6k

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 602. Formations
602.7 Some cards say they may be played into a formation (Tiderunner Initiate, Trench Stalker). The position is chosen as the card is cast, from the positions rule 602.6 allows, and the unit is already in that position when it enters play. See rules 602.6, 702.
 Example: Tiderunner Initiate's spot is asked for while it is being cast, and it enters play already standing in that spot.
 Example: No moment exists in which the Tiderunner is in the region but outside the formation, so the opponent cannot respond to it there.
title: CR 602.7

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 602. Formations
(continues 602.7: Some cards say they may be played into a formation (Tiderunner Initiate, Trench Stalker). The position is chosen as the card is cast, from the positions rule 602.6 allows, and the unit is already in that position when…)
602.7a If the chosen position no longer exists when the card resolves, the unit enters play in the region, outside the formation.
 Example: Tiderunner Initiate is cast to go behind an attacker, and the attacker dies before it resolves. The Tiderunner enters the region outside the formation.
title: CR 602.7a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 602. Formations
(continues 602.7: Some cards say they may be played into a formation (Tiderunner Initiate, Trench Stalker). The position is chosen as the card is cast, from the positions rule 602.6 allows, and the unit is already in that position when…)
602.7b Playing such a card into the formation is optional. Its controller may instead play it so that it enters the region outside the formation.
 Example: When casting Tiderunner Initiate, its controller may choose to have it stay out of the formation.
title: CR 602.7b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 602. Formations
(continues 602.7: Some cards say they may be played into a formation (Tiderunner Initiate, Trench Stalker). The position is chosen as the card is cast, from the positions rule 602.6 allows, and the unit is already in that position when…)
602.7c Such a card can be played into a formation only if its controller has a formation in that battle that still holds at least one unit: they attacked, or they declared blocks, and not every unit in it has left. As an exception, after blocks are declared and until combat damage has been dealt, the defending player may play it in front of an unblocked attacking column (rule 602.6c) even if they declared no blockers. Otherwise it is played normally, outside any formation. See rules 602.6c, 602.6k.
 Example: Before blocks, the defending player has no formation. They cast Tiderunner Initiate; nothing is asked and it enters play outside any formation.
 Example: After blocks, the defender plays a unit in front of an unblocked attacking column. That column is blocked, and stays blocked when the unit is removed.
 Example: After blocks, every attacking unit dies. The attacker plays Tiderunner Initiate; nothing is asked and it enters play outside any formation.
title: CR 602.7c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 603. Columns, Adjacency and Edges
603.1 A column is one file of the battle line: the attacking units in it and the defending units placed in front of it. Each side of a column holds at most two units. A defending unit placed in front of an attacking column blocks that whole column. See rules 602.1a, 606, 608.1c.
 Example: One unit blocks a column of two attackers. Neither attacker deals damage to the defending player.
603.1a Combat attributes are shared by the units in the same column of a formation, and are not shared with units to their left or right (see rule 802.1). See rules 802.1, 712.
 Example: A unit with Flying attacks in the front of a column. The unit behind it has Flying too; the unit in the next column does not.
603.1b A defending unit may also block in a column where there is no attacker (a side-block). Side-block columns stand beside the attacking line, on either side of it (see rule 606). Any number of units may side-block, and each may stand in a column of its own. See rule 606.
 Example: Two defending units block where no attacker is, each in its own column beside the attack.
 Example: A single 2/5 attacks; the defender side-blocks to its left with a 1/1. The 1/1 stands in a new column left of the attack, the attacking column stays unblocked, and it deals 2 to the defender.
title: CR 603.1–603.1b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 603. Columns, Adjacency and Edges
(continues 603.1: A column is one file of the battle line: the attacking units in it and the defending units placed in front of it. Each side of a column holds at most two units. A defending unit placed in front of an attacking column…)
603.1c Two side-blocking units may stand in the same side-block column, one in its front slot and one in its back slot. See rule 603.1b.
title: CR 603.1c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 603. Columns, Adjacency and Edges
603.2 A unit in a formation is adjacent to its left, right, front and back neighbours in that formation.
 Example: Inspiration gives +2/+2 to its controller's units adjacent to it in formation, and to no others.
 Example: The defender blocks the first and third attacking columns and leaves the second unblocked. The two blockers are not neighbours, so an Inspiration in one does not buff the other.
603.2a A unit in a formation has at most three adjacent positions: the same row of the column to its left, the same row of the column to its right, and the other slot of its own column. The other row of a neighbouring column is diagonal, and is not adjacent. Where a line ends, there is a position past the end only as rule 603.3 allows. See rule 603.3.
 Example: Hooba-Nan stands in the front row of a middle column. Its adjacent slots are the front rows of the columns on either side and the slot behind it, and nothing diagonal.
 Example: A blocker stands next to an unblocked attacking column. It has no adjacent position in that column.
603.2b Adjacency exists only in a formation. A unit that is not in a formation has no adjacent units and no adjacent slots.
 Example: During deployment, Throwing Boulder stands in its region beside an allied unit, but neither is in a formation. Its ability (“only if I have an adjacent ally”) cannot be activated.
603.2c An amount based on adjacency, such as the number of adjacent allies, is counted as the effect resolves. See rule 706.
 Example: Flamebreath Initiate attacks with one ally in the column beside it. X is 1, so it creates a Fireball 2. Attacking alone, X is 0 and the Fireball is 1.
 Example: Flamebreath Initiate attacks beside an ally, and the ally is destroyed while the trigger waits. X is 0 when the trigger resolves.
603.2d A unit that has left play has no adjacent units. If it left play with its effect on the stack, an amount counting the units adjacent to it is 0. See rules 602.6f, 714.
 Example: Flamebreath Initiate attacks and is removed with its trigger on the stack. X is 0, so the trigger still creates a Fireball 1.
title: CR 603.2–603.2d

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 603. Columns, Adjacency and Edges
603.3 The empty column just past each end of an attacking line exists. For a unit in the front row at either end of an attacking line, the front-row slot of a new column past that end is an adjacent slot.
 Example: Hooba-Nan stands alone in an attacking line. Its trigger creates three 1/1s: one in a new column on each side and one behind it.
 Example: Hooba-Nan is at the right end of a longer line, with a unit to its left. Its trigger creates two 1/1s: one in a new column past the right end and one behind it.
603.3a Past the end of the line, only the front-row slot is adjacent. A unit in the back row at the end of the line has no adjacent slot past that end, because the front row must be filled first (rule 602.3). See rule 602.3.
 Example: Hooba-Nan stands in the back row of the column at the end of the line. Its trigger creates no 1/1 past the edge.
603.3b A defending formation has no adjacent slots past its ends.
title: CR 603.3–603.3b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 603. Columns, Adjacency and Edges
603.4 Text that names positions relative to the unit itself, such as “my empty adjacent slots” or “the empty slot behind me”, refers to exactly those positions. Its controller does not choose among positions as they do under rule 602.6. See rule 602.6.
 Example: Rousing Spirit attacks, and a cheap unit from its controller's bin is put into the empty slot behind it.
title: CR 603.4

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 603. Columns, Adjacency and Edges
603.5 A formation can grow at either end without limit.
title: CR 603.5

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 603. Columns, Adjacency and Edges
(continues 603.5: A formation can grow at either end without limit.)
603.5a When the columns of a line move (a new column opens at the left end, or the line closes up under rule 602.5), each block and each effect that applies to a particular column moves with that column.
 Example: A new column opens at the left end of a line that has already been blocked. Every blocker still blocks the same attackers as before.
 Example: A Swift column led by Dune Drifter has already dealt its damage first. Its controller then plays Tiderunner Initiate into a new column on the left; the Drifter's column shifts right but still counts as having struck, so it does not deal damage again.
title: CR 603.5a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 604. Attacking
604.1 Attacking is how a player brings units, and the spell tokens that travel with them, into a neighbouring enemy region for battle. Attacks are declared in the attack step, the first step of a battle round (see 505). See rules 505, 601.
 Example: The initiative player declares an attack with one unit. That unit moves into the other player's region, and at regroup it returns home.
604.1a Units attack players directly. They do not attack individual units unless a spell directs them to. See rule 608.
604.1b In a two-player game and in team games, each team gets one chance to attack per turn. In the first battle round the initiative player attacks into the non-initiative player's region; in the second battle round the non-initiative player attacks with the units it sent to counterattack or, if the first round had no attack, with any of its units (see 505, 610 and rule 604.4a). See rules 505, 610, 604.4a.
 Example: The initiative player attacks with a 2/2. The non-initiative player sends a 4/3 to counterattack while declaring blocks. After the first round's combat, the 4/3 attacks in the second round.
title: CR 604.1–604.1b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 604. Attacking
604.2 To attack, the attacking player chooses which of its units go and places them in an attacking formation (see 602). The attacking formation is set in the attack step, and from then on its units are locked in position. See rule 602.
 Example: A player with three units attacks with two of them, side by side in two columns. The third stays at home.
604.2a Attacking is optional: a player may declare no attack. The exception is a counterattack: a sent counterattacker that is still able to attack must attack (see rule 610.4e). See rule 604.4.
 Example: The initiative player has a unit that could attack and declares no attack. The battle moves to the second round.
 Example: The non-initiative player sent three units to counterattack. In round 2, declaring no attack is refused.
604.2b There is no summoning sickness. A unit may attack, or block, however recently it entered play. See rules 504, 606.2a.
 Example: A 2/2 enters play during the battle phase, just before attacks are declared. It may attack at once, and it deals 2 to the defending player.
604.2c Spell tokens may go with an attack, but only together with at least one unit, and only spell tokens the attacking player controls in the region the attack leaves from. Spell tokens sent with a counterattack are not optional in round 2: they must ride (see rule 610.3). See rules 304, 606.5a.
 Example: A player sending a counterattack names a Poison token and no unit when declaring blocks. The declaration is refused.
 Example: A player declares an attack naming a Poison token and no unit. The Poison does not go: with no unit, the declaration is no attack at all.
604.2d Bringing a spell token into another region with an attack cannot be undone. See rule 304.
 Example: A Poison token goes along with an attack into the enemy region. In the counterattack, fought in its owner home region, the token is still in the enemy region and cannot be cast.
title: CR 604.2–604.2d

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 604. Attacking
(continues 604.2: To attack, the attacking player chooses which of its units go and places them in an attacking formation (see 602). The attacking formation is set in the attack step, and from then on its units are locked in position.)
604.2e A unit targeted by an Alluring trigger may not be declared as an attacker, or sent to counterattack, for the rest of the battle phase (see 802.15). See rules 802.15, 610.
 Example: An Alluring attacker targets a defending unit. That unit cannot be sent out to counterattack when blocks are declared.
title: CR 604.2e

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 604. Attacking
(continues 604.2: To attack, the attacking player chooses which of its units go and places them in an attacking formation (see 602). The attacking formation is set in the attack step, and from then on its units are locked in position.)
604.2f In the second battle round, the attacking player may attack only with the units it sent to counterattack in the first round, unless the first round had no attack (see 604 and 610). Every sent unit still there and able to attack must be in the formation, and every spell token sent with them must ride along; only the formation's shape is chosen (see rule 610.4b). See rules 610, 604.4a.
 Example: The non-initiative player sent one unit to counterattack and kept another at home. In the second round, only the sent unit may attack.
 Example: Three units were sent. Attacking with only two of them is refused; any formation holding all three is accepted.
 Example: A Fireball token sent with the counterattack is left behind: the declaration is refused.
title: CR 604.2f

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 604. Attacking
604.3 When an attack is declared, the attacking units, and the spell tokens with them, move into the region attacked. They remain there until the regroup phase, when they return to their own region (see 506). See rules 506, 601.
 Example: A unit that counterattacked into the initiative player's region is back in its own region once regroup is over.
604.3a Once a player has sent attacking units into an enemy region, that player is present there and may interact with things in that region using spells and effects (see 601). See rule 601.
 Example: After an attack, both players are present in the battle region, so each sees every death in it.
604.3b The units in the attacking formation are the attacking units. A unit that arrives in the battle region outside the formation, such as one created there during the battle, is not attacking. See rules 602, 607.2.
 Example: Aberrant Populace attacks and creates two Wisps. The Wisps are in the battle region but not in the formation, so they are not attacking.
604.3c Abilities that trigger when a unit attacks trigger as the attack is declared. They are put on the stack before the attack window opens, so players can respond to them in that window (see 605 and 706). See rules 605, 706, 802.15.
 Example: Tempest Wrangler attacks and its Alluring trigger goes on the stack. In the attack window the defending player negates it with Containment Protocol, and no unit is lured.
604.3d A unit attacks alone when it is the only unit in its attacking formation. Spell tokens that travel with it do not count as company. See rule 802.14.
 Example: Whispering Mantid (Sneaky) attacking by itself cannot be blocked; attacking beside another unit, it can.
title: CR 604.3–604.3d

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 604. Attacking
604.4 If the attacking player declares no attack, there is no combat in that round: no attack window, no block step, no block window, no combat damage step and no after combat step. A counterattack cannot be declined this way while a sent counterattacker is able to attack (see rule 610.4e). See rules 505, 609.
 Example: Both players decline to attack. The whole battle phase passes with no priority window at all.
604.4a If the initiative player declares no attack in the first battle round, the non-initiative player may still attack in the second battle round, and may attack with any of its units. See rule 610.
 Example: The initiative player declines to attack. The non-initiative player, who sent nobody to counterattack, attacks in the second round with a unit that stayed at home.
title: CR 604.4–604.4a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 605. Attack Window
605.1 The attack window is the priority window that follows the declaration of an attack, in the region attacked. See rule 703.
 Example: An attack is declared. Priority goes to the initiative player, then to the other player; when both pass, the step moves on.
605.1a The initiative player receives priority first in the attack window (see 703). See rule 703.
605.1b When all players pass priority in succession with the stack empty, the attack window ends and the block step begins (see 606). See rules 606, 703.
 Example: Luminous Arc is cast in the attack window; two passes resolve it and a new window opens. Two more passes on the empty stack end the attack window.
605.1c Until blocks are declared, a column of the attacking formation that loses its last unit closes up: the columns on its sides move in to fill the gap (see 602). See rules 602, 607.1b.
 Example: The middle column of a three-column attack is killed in the block step, before blocks are declared. The right-hand column slides left into the gap, and the attack is two columns wide.
605.1d If every attacking unit is removed during the attack window, the attacking player is still present in the region for the rest of the battle phase. See rules 601, 606.7.
 Example: The only attacker is destroyed in the attack window. Its controller may still cast spells in that region later in the battle phase.
title: CR 605.1–605.1d

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 606. Blocking
606.1 Blocking is how a player who has been attacked defends. In the block step, the defending player may place its units in front of the attacking formation. See rules 602, 608.
 Example: Two columns attack, a 3/5 and a 4/5; the defending player places a 2/5 in front of the 3/5. That column is blocked and the two units deal damage to each other; the unblocked 4/5 hits the player.
606.1a The blocking units form the defending formation. Like any formation, it has a front row and a back row (see 602). See rule 602.
 Example: Two units block one attacking column, one in the front row and one behind it. The attacker damages the front one.
606.1b Unlike an attacking formation, the defending formation may have empty columns: the defending player need not block every attacking column, and an empty blocking column is never closed up. See rule 602.
 Example: Against a three-column attack, the defending player blocks only the third column. The first two columns are unblocked, and the attack stays three columns wide.
606.1c The defending player may declare no blockers at all.
 Example: The defending player declares no blocks and sends a unit to counterattack; the attacker's unblocked column hits the defending player.
606.1d Blocks are declared once. Once declared, the defending formation is set and its units are locked in position. A unit can join it later only by an effect that puts a unit into formation (see 607). See rules 602, 607.2.
 Example: After declaring blocks, the defending player cannot declare them again to move a blocker from one column to another.
606.1e A blocking unit stands in one slot of the defending formation, so it blocks only the attacking column it stands in front of. See rule 602.
 Example: One blocker cannot block two attacking columns at once; to block both, the defending player needs a unit in front of each.
606.1f An empty blocking column keeps its place in the defending formation. Two blockers with an empty blocking column between them are not neighbours, so they are not adjacent (see 603). See rules 603, 606.4g.
 Example: Against a three-column attack, the defending player blocks the first and third columns. The two blockers are not adjacent: the empty middle blocking column lies between them.
title: CR 606.1–606.1f

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 606. Blocking
606.2 The defending player may block with units it controls in the battle region. See rule 601.
 Example: A unit created in the enemy region during the first round's attack is not in its controller's region when the counterattack arrives, so it cannot block it.
606.2a A unit may block however recently it entered play (see 604). See rule 604.2b.
 Example: A unit that entered the defending player's region during the attack window may be declared as a blocker.
title: CR 606.2–606.2a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 606. Blocking
(continues 606.2: The defending player may block with units it controls in the battle region.)
606.2b Whether a unit is able to block a column depends only on that unit and that column. It never depends on what the defending player chose to do with its other units, except where two Alluring duties name the same unit (see 802.15). See rule 802.15.
 Example: An Alluring column lures a defending unit. The defending player cannot excuse it by putting it on another column instead; it is still able to block the Alluring column, so it must.
title: CR 606.2b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 606. Blocking
(continues 606.2: The defending player may block with units it controls in the battle region.)
606.2c These attributes change which units may block a column, or how many it takes: Flying (802.2), Feeble (802.12), Evasive (802.13), Sneaky (802.14), Alluring (802.15) and Pure (802.25). See rules 802.2, 802.12, 802.13, 802.14, 802.15, 802.25.
 Example: Only a Flying unit can block a Flying column, but a Pure unit ignores Flying and can block it too.
 Example: Wisps are Feeble and cannot block.
 Example: Curio Drifter is Evasive, so its column needs two blockers.
606.2d A unit sent to counterattack leaves the region and is treated as if it does not exist until the first battle round is over, so it cannot also block (see 610). See rules 610, 606.5.
 Example: The defending player has one unit. It may block, or it may be sent to counterattack, but not both.
606.2e A unit targeted by an Alluring trigger must block that Alluring column if it is able to. If the column is blocked at all, the lured unit must be one of its blockers (see 802.15). See rules 802.15, 802.13.
 Example: An Alluring column lures unit A. The defending player tries to block that column with unit B instead. The declaration is refused.
 Example: The Alluring column is also Evasive and the defending player has only the lured unit. It cannot block an Evasive column alone, so it need not block it, and may block another column.
title: CR 606.2c–606.2e

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 606. Blocking
(continues 606.2: The defending player may block with units it controls in the battle region.)
606.2f Alluring duties never leave the defending player without a legal block declaration. However many Alluring triggers have resolved, the game offers the defending player at least one block declaration, and every declaration it offers is legal. See rule 802.15.
 Example: Two attacking columns both have Alluring, and their triggers targeted the same defending unit. The defending player is still offered a legal declaration.
title: CR 606.2f

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 606. Blocking
606.3 An attacking column is blocked once a defending unit has been placed in front of it. The whole column is blocked, however many attacking units it holds. See rule 608.
 Example: A column of two attackers is blocked by one unit. Neither attacker deals combat damage to the defending player.
606.3a A blocked column stays blocked for the rest of the battle round, even if every unit blocking it leaves, whether it dies, is recalled, is erased or changes control. See rules 608, 607.2a.
 Example: The only blocker dies in the block window. The vanilla attacker's column is still blocked and deals no damage to the defending player.
 Example: The only blocker is stolen by Download mid-combat. The column is still blocked.
606.3b A blocked column deals no combat damage to the defending player, except as Piercing allows (see 608 and 802.16). See rules 608, 802.16.
 Example: A blocked non-Piercing column whose blocker died before damage deals nothing to the defending player.
title: CR 606.3–606.3b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 606. Blocking
606.4 A defending unit may be placed blocking where no attacker is, as long as at least one attacking unit is left in the attacking formation (see rule 606.7). This is a side-block, and the blocking column it makes is a side-blocking column. See rules 602, 603.
 Example: One unit attacks. The defending player places two units to the side of it, each in its own column, and leaves the attacker unblocked.
 Example: The only attacker is destroyed before blocks: a side-block beside the empty attack is refused.
title: CR 606.4

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 606. Blocking
(continues 606.4: A defending unit may be placed blocking where no attacker is, as long as at least one attacking unit is left in the attacking formation (see rule 606.7). This is a side-block, and the blocking column it makes is a…)
606.4a Side-blocks may stand on either side of the attacking formation.
 Example: A unit side-blocks to the left of a one-column attack. A new column opens before the attacking column, and the attacking column is still unblocked.
title: CR 606.4a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 606. Blocking
(continues 606.4: A defending unit may be placed blocking where no attacker is, as long as at least one attacking unit is left in the attacking formation (see rule 606.7). This is a side-block, and the blocking column it makes is a…)
606.4b Any number of units may side-block, each as its own column.
 Example: Two units side-block beside a one-column attack; each makes its own side-blocking column.
title: CR 606.4b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 606. Blocking
(continues 606.4: A defending unit may be placed blocking where no attacker is, as long as at least one attacking unit is left in the attacking formation (see rule 606.7). This is a side-block, and the blocking column it makes is a…)
606.4c A block declaration may reach no further out from the attacking formation than it has blocking columns, so a single side-block stands next to the attacking formation.
 Example: Against a one-column attack, a single side-block may stand right beside the attack on either side, but not three columns out.
title: CR 606.4c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 606. Blocking
(continues 606.4: A defending unit may be placed blocking where no attacker is, as long as at least one attacking unit is left in the attacking formation (see rule 606.7). This is a side-block, and the blocking column it makes is a…)
606.4d A side-blocking column counts as a blocked column.
 Example: Roving Quillback attacks alone and two units side-block beside it. Quillback deals 1 damage to the defending player for each blocked column: 2, for the two side-blocking columns.
title: CR 606.4d

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 606. Blocking
(continues 606.4: A defending unit may be placed blocking where no attacker is, as long as at least one attacking unit is left in the attacking formation (see rule 606.7). This is a side-block, and the blocking column it makes is a…)
606.4e A side-block blocks no attacker. It does not count as blocking a lone Sneaky attacker, and no Flying or Evasive rule applies to it. See rules 802.2, 802.13, 802.14.
 Example: A lone Sneaky unit attacks. A unit side-blocking beside it is allowed, and the Sneaky unit is still unblocked.
title: CR 606.4e

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 606. Blocking
(continues 606.4: A defending unit may be placed blocking where no attacker is, as long as at least one attacking unit is left in the attacking formation (see rule 606.7). This is a side-block, and the blocking column it makes is a…)
606.4f A side-blocking column deals no combat damage, Piercing included, because no attacker stands in front of it (see 608). See rules 608, 802.16.
 Example: A 5/5 Piercing unit side-blocks. It deals no combat damage to the attacking player.
606.4g Side-blocking units are part of the defending formation, so they are adjacent to their neighbours in it (see 603). See rule 603.
 Example: A unit side-blocks next to a unit blocking the attacking column. The two are adjacent, which matters to cards that count adjacent units.
title: CR 606.4f–606.4g

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 606. Blocking
606.5 In the first battle round, the defending player declares at the same time as its blocks which of its units it sends to counterattack (see 610). See rule 610.
 Example: The non-initiative player declares no blocks and sends one unit; that unit takes no part in the first round and attacks in the second.
title: CR 606.5

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 606. Blocking
(continues 606.5: In the first battle round, the defending player declares at the same time as its blocks which of its units it sends to counterattack (see 610).)
606.5a Spell tokens may go with the counterattacking units, under the same conditions as with an attack (see 604). A spell token sent this way must then ride with the counterattack in round 2 (see rule 610.3). See rules 604.2c, 610.
 Example: The defending player sends a unit to counterattack and names a Poison token to go with it. The token leaves with the unit and arrives with it for round 2.
title: CR 606.5a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 606. Blocking
(continues 606.5: In the first battle round, the defending player declares at the same time as its blocks which of its units it sends to counterattack (see 610).)
606.5b In the second battle round the defending player declares blocks only. There are no further counterattacks. See rule 610.
 Example: In the second round the initiative player blocks the counterattack; it cannot send units to attack back.
title: CR 606.5b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 606. Blocking
606.6 Abilities that trigger when a unit blocks trigger as blocks are declared. They are put on the stack before the block window opens (see 607 and 706). See rules 607, 706.
 Example: Spewing Mushroom says 'When I attack or block'. Declared as a blocker, it creates its Poison.
 Example: Palewing blocks and its controller discards a card.
title: CR 606.6

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 606. Blocking
606.7 If no attacking unit is left when the block step begins, nothing can be blocked: no defending unit may be placed blocking, in front of the attack or to the side of it. In the first battle round the defending player may still send units to counterattack; otherwise the block declaration is empty. The battle round then continues. See rule 605.1d.
 Example: The only attacker is destroyed before blocks. The defending player cannot block, not even to the side, but may still send a unit to counterattack, or declare nothing; the block window follows.
 Example: With the attack emptied, a side-block on either side is refused, with or without a unit sent to counterattack.
 Example: In the second battle round the lone counterattacker is destroyed before blocks: the initiative player can neither block nor send anything.
title: CR 606.7

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 607. Block Window
607.1 The block window is the priority window that follows the declaration of blocks. See rule 703.
607.1a When all players pass priority in succession with the stack empty, the block window ends and the combat damage step begins (see 608). See rule 608.
 Example: After blocks, the first pass deals no damage; the second pass starts the combat damage step.
607.1b Once blocks have been declared, a column that loses its last unit is not closed up; the columns stay where they are for the rest of the battle round (see 602). See rules 602, 605.1c.
 Example: After blocks, the middle attacking column dies. It stays as a hole, and the columns beside it do not move.
607.1c A unit behind a removed unit still moves up to the front row after blocks have been declared (see 602). See rule 602.
 Example: After blocks, the front unit of a column dies; the unit behind it moves to the front.
title: CR 607.1–607.1c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 607. Block Window
607.2 After blocks have been declared, a unit that joins the defending formation (for example Tiderunner Initiate, played into an open spot) may be placed in front of an attacking column that has no blocker. That column is then blocked. See rules 602, 702.
 Example: The defending player declares no blocks, then plays Tiderunner Initiate in front of the unblocked attacker. The attacker deals its damage to the Tiderunner, not to the player.
607.2a A column blocked this way stays blocked if that unit later leaves, like any blocked column (see 606). See rule 606.3a.
 Example: Tiderunner Initiate is played in front of an unblocked attacker and is then removed. The column is still blocked.
title: CR 607.2–607.2a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 607. Block Window
(continues 607.2: After blocks have been declared, a unit that joins the defending formation (for example Tiderunner Initiate, played into an open spot) may be placed in front of an attacking column that has no blocker. That column is…)
607.2b The defending player may block this way even if it declared no blockers.
 Example: The defending player declared no blocks; Tiderunner Initiate is still offered the spot in front of the attacker.
607.2c Only a unit joining the defending formation can be placed this way. A unit joining the attacking formation is never placed in a blocking position.
 Example: After blocks, the attacking player is offered no blocking spot; the defending player is offered one, in front of the unblocked column.
607.2d A unit can be placed this way from the block window until the combat damage step is over. See rule 608.
 Example: In the window between the Swift and normal damage sub-steps, the defending player plays Tiderunner Initiate in front of an unblocked attacking column. The column is blocked for the normal sub-step.
607.2e A unit placed this way was not declared as a blocker, so the events of the block declaration do not happen for it. See rule 606.6.
 Example: After blocks, the defending player plays Tiderunner Initiate in front of an unblocked attacker. It now blocks that column, but it was never declared as a blocker, so nothing that happens when blocks are declared happens for it.
title: CR 607.2b–607.2e

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 607. Block Window
607.3 An ability that triggers "after the blocking step" triggers once blocks have been declared, and resolves in the block window. See rule 706.
 Example: Roving Quillback attacks and two units side-block. Once both players pass in the block window, its trigger resolves and the defending player loses 2 life, before any combat damage.
title: CR 607.3

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 608. Combat Damage Step
608.1 The combat damage step is the step of a battle in which the units in formation deal combat damage. It begins once blocks have been declared and all players have passed priority in the window that follows them, and it is followed by the after combat step (see rule 609). See rules 607, 609.
 Example: A 2/5 attacks and is blocked by a 2/5. After blocks, the block window opens; once both players pass, each deals 2 to the other, and then the after combat step begins.
608.1a The combat damage step takes place separately in each region where a battle takes place. A region that was not attacked has no combat damage step. See rules 601, 609.
 Example: The first attacker declares no attack, so the defending player's region has no combat damage step. The second player then attacks, and the only combat damage step of the turn is in the first player's region.
608.1b All combat damage is dealt simultaneously, unless an ability changes when a column deals its damage. Swift and Sluggish are the attributes that do (see rule 608.2). See rules 608.2, 802.4, 802.5.
 Example: A 3/3 attacks and is blocked by a 3/3. Both are dealt 3 at the same time, so both die.
608.1c Combat damage is dealt by columns. The attacking units of one column deal their combat damage together, as one source, and so do the blocking units of one column. In this section, each of these two groups is called a half-column: a column has an attacking half and a blocking half. See rules 603, 802.20.
 Example: Two Slinks (Thieving) attack in one column and are not blocked. The column is one source of combat damage, so its controller draws one card, not two.
title: CR 608.1–608.1c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 608. Combat Damage Step
608.2 The combat damage step has three damage sub-steps, taken in this order: the Swift sub-step, the normal sub-step and the Sluggish sub-step. Each half-column strikes (deals its combat damage) only in the sub-steps that rule 608.2a gives it. The two halves of one column are scheduled separately. See rules 802.4, 802.5.
 Example: Dune Drifter (2/1, Swift) is blocked by a 1/5, and Ambling Mountaintop (Sluggish) attacks unblocked. The Drifter deals 2 in the Swift sub-step, the 1/5 strikes back in the normal sub-step and kills it, and the Mountaintop deals its damage last.
608.2a A half-column that has Swift strikes in the Swift sub-step. A half-column that has Sluggish strikes in the Sluggish sub-step. A half-column that has neither strikes in the normal sub-step. See rules 802.4, 802.5.
 Example: Dune Drifter (2/1, Swift) and Rune Channeler (4/3) attack in one column and are blocked by a 2/2. The attacking half deals its 6 damage in the Swift sub-step; when that sub-step ends the 2/2 has been destroyed and the attackers are undamaged.
608.2b Whether a half-column has Swift or Sluggish depends on the combat attributes its units share: an attribute of any unit in a column is shared by every unit in that column (see rule 603). When a unit leaves a column, the other units in it lose the attributes that unit was sharing at once. See rules 603, 802.1.
 Example: Dune Drifter (Swift) and Lithoghul attack in one column, so Lithoghul would strike in the Swift sub-step. If Dune Drifter is recalled, Lithoghul at once strikes in the normal sub-step instead.
608.2c A half-column that has both Swift and Sluggish strikes twice: once in the Swift sub-step and once in the Sluggish sub-step. It does not strike in the normal sub-step. See rules 802.4, 802.5.
 Example: Rime Wraith (2/1, Swift and Sluggish) and Vroot (4/4) attack in one column and are not blocked. The column deals 6 in the Swift sub-step and 6 more in the Sluggish sub-step.
 Example: Rime Wraith attacks alone and is not blocked. It deals 2 in the Swift sub-step, nothing strikes in the normal sub-step, and it deals 2 more in the Sluggish sub-step.
title: CR 608.2–608.2c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 608. Combat Damage Step
(continues 608.2: The combat damage step has three damage sub-steps, taken in this order: the Swift sub-step, the normal sub-step and the Sluggish sub-step. Each half-column strikes (deals its combat damage) only in the sub-steps that…)
608.2d If either half of a column contains a Pure card, neither half of that column has Swift or Sluggish for that exchange, so both halves strike in the normal sub-step. An unblocked column that contains a Pure card has no Swift or Sluggish either: it strikes the player in the normal sub-step. See rule 802.25.
 Example: A printed Swift column blocked by a Pure unit strikes in the normal sub-step.
 Example: An unblocked Pure column strikes the player in the normal sub-step, and does not double or draw.
608.2e A half-column that has struck in the Swift sub-step does not strike in the normal sub-step, even if the unit that gave it Swift has since left the column, and even if a new unit has since been put into that column. A half-column that has struck in the normal sub-step does not strike in the Sluggish sub-step, even if it has since gained Sluggish. A half-column that struck in the Swift sub-step and has Sluggish in the Sluggish sub-step strikes again then (rule 608.2c). This record belongs to the half-column, not to the units in it, and it stays with that column if the columns are renumbered (for example, when a new column is opened to its left). See rule 603.
 Example: Dune Drifter (2/1, Swift) and a 3/3 attack in one column; a 1/1 attacks in another. The Swift column deals 5 in the Swift sub-step. Dune Drifter is then recalled. In the normal sub-step only the 1/1's column strikes.
 Example: After Dune Drifter's column strikes in the Swift sub-step, Dune Drifter is recalled and Tiderunner Initiate is played into the emptied column. Tiderunner Initiate deals no normal combat damage.
608.2f Whether a half-column strikes in a sub-step is determined as that sub-step begins, from the units then in the column and the attributes they then share. See rule 603.
 Example: A column strikes in the Swift sub-step and then gains Sluggish. It strikes again in the Sluggish sub-step.
title: CR 608.2d–608.2f

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 608. Combat Damage Step
608.3 A combat damage step is split if, when the step begins, half-columns are scheduled to strike in two or more different sub-steps. Otherwise it is unsplit. Only Swift and Sluggish can split a step. See rules 802.4, 802.5.
 Example: Dune Drifter (Swift) is blocked by a unit without Swift or Sluggish. The attacking half strikes in the Swift sub-step and the blocking half in the normal one, so the step is split.
608.3a In an unsplit step, all combat damage is dealt at once, as one step. No player receives priority during it, and abilities that trigger during it wait until the after combat step (see rule 608.9b). See rules 609, 703.
 Example: Lithoghul (4/4) and Geode (1/1) attack in separate columns and are not blocked. Neither has Swift or Sluggish, so the step is unsplit; the 5 damage is dealt at once and the game goes straight to the after combat step.
608.3b In a split step, each scheduled sub-step (rule 608.3d) is a separate step. After each such sub-step except the last scheduled one, the abilities that triggered during it are put on the stack and players receive priority; the next sub-step deals no damage until that stack has resolved and all players have passed priority in succession with it empty. State-based changes (deaths, back-row units moving forward, lost shared attributes) have already happened when this window opens. See rules 703, 706.
 Example: Bripp (4 power) and Bloated Manablub (2 power) attack in normal columns, and Adversary of the Deep (2/2, Sluggish; 'Whenever a player loses life, put that many +1/+1 counters on me') attacks in a third column. None are blocked. The normal sub-step deals 6; the step stops, Adversary's trigger resolves with priority, and Adversary strikes in the Sluggish sub-step for 8.
 Example: At the boundary, the stack holds Adversary of the Deep's trigger. Its controller has the initiative and receives priority first; the other player may respond once they pass.
title: CR 608.3–608.3b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 608. Combat Damage Step
(continues 608.3: A combat damage step is split if, when the step begins, half-columns are scheduled to strike in two or more different sub-steps. Otherwise it is unsplit. Only Swift and Sluggish can split a step.)
608.3c A sub-step in which no half-column is scheduled to strike (rule 608.3d) is not a separate step: no window opens after it. A scheduled sub-step keeps its window even if every half-column scheduled for it has since been destroyed; only the Sluggish sub-step is decided again, as 608.3d says. No window opens after the last scheduled sub-step; the after combat step begins.
 Example: Dune Drifter (Swift) and Lithoghul attack in separate columns and are not blocked. Half-columns strike in the Swift and normal sub-steps and nothing strikes in the Sluggish sub-step, so there is exactly one window, between the Swift and normal sub-steps.
608.3d Which sub-steps are scheduled, and so are separate steps, is determined when the combat damage step begins, with one revision: when the window after the Swift sub-step ends, the Sluggish sub-step is scheduled if, and only if, a half-column will then strike in it. So a half-column that gains Sluggish in that window gets the window before the Sluggish sub-step; and if no half-column has Sluggish when that window ends, the normal sub-step is the last scheduled one and the after combat step follows it. Without a Swift sub-step there is no such window, and the schedule is not revisited. Nothing else unsplits a split step: a unit that dies, leaves or loses an attribute during the step does not remove the Swift or the normal sub-step.
 Example: Dune Drifter (Swift) attacks beside Lithoghul and is blocked by another Dune Drifter. Both Swift units destroy each other in the Swift sub-step; the window before the normal sub-step still opens.
 Example: A column is given Sluggish in the window after the Swift sub-step. The normal sub-step's triggers resolve in a window before the Sluggish sub-step, and then the column strikes.
 Example: The only Sluggish striker is gone before the window after the Swift sub-step ends. No window opens before a Sluggish sub-step; after the normal sub-step the after combat step begins.
title: CR 608.3c–608.3d

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 608. Combat Damage Step
(continues 608.3: A combat damage step is split if, when the step begins, half-columns are scheduled to strike in two or more different sub-steps. Otherwise it is unsplit. Only Swift and Sluggish can split a step.)
608.3e Between sub-steps, the game's state is updated before anything else: units with lethal damage are destroyed, a unit behind a removed unit moves to the front row, and attributes shared by a removed unit are lost. A unit destroyed in an earlier sub-step deals no damage in a later one, and damage in a later sub-step is assigned to the formation as it then stands. Columns do not close gaps after blocks have been declared. See rules 602, 603.
 Example: Dune Drifter (2/1, Swift) is blocked by a 2/2 in front of a 4/3. Its Swift damage destroys the 2/2; the 4/3 is already in front when the boundary window opens, and in the normal sub-step it destroys Dune Drifter while taking no damage.
 Example: A blocking column whose attacker was destroyed in an earlier sub-step deals nothing in a later sub-step.
title: CR 608.3e

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 608. Combat Damage Step
608.4 Each attacking half-column deals its combat damage either to the defending player or to the blocking half-column in front of it, and each blocking half-column deals its combat damage to the attacking half-column it blocks. Piercing can also carry combat damage to a player (see rule 802.16). An attacking column is blocked once a blocking unit has been placed in front of it, normally in the block step (see rule 606) or later as rule 608.4d allows. See rules 606, 802.16.
 Example: A 3/5 and a 4/5 attack in two columns; a 2/5 blocks the 3/5. The 3/5 deals 3 to the blocker, the blocker deals 2 to the 3/5, and the 4/5 deals 4 to the defending player.
608.4a An attacking half-column that is not blocked deals its combat damage to the defending player.
 Example: Slink (2/3) attacks and is not blocked. The defending player is dealt 2 combat damage.
608.4b An attacking half-column that is blocked deals its combat damage to the units of the blocking half-column in front of it, and that blocking half-column deals its combat damage to the units of the attacking half-column. A blocked attacking half-column deals no combat damage to the defending player, except as Piercing allows (see rule 802.16). See rule 802.16.
 Example: The column of Living Forge and A Pile of Rubbish deals a combined 3 damage to the Tiderunner Initiate blocking it; the Tiderunner deals 2 back, all to Living Forge because it is in the front. (from the Manual p.23)
608.4c Once an attacking column is blocked, it remains blocked for the rest of the battle, however its blockers leave the blocking half-column: destroyed, recalled, erased or stolen. If no blocking unit remains when that column strikes, an attacking half-column without Piercing deals no combat damage at all, and one with Piercing deals all of its damage to the defending player (see rule 802.16). See rules 606, 802.16.
 Example: A vanilla attacker is blocked; the blocker is then recalled before damage. The column stays blocked and the defending player is dealt no damage.
 Example: Good Whale (7/5, Piercing) is blocked by a 1/1 that dies before damage. All 7 of its damage is dealt to the defending player.
 Example: A 7/5 without Piercing is blocked by a 1/1 that dies before damage. It deals nothing to the defending player.
title: CR 608.4–608.4c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 608. Combat Damage Step
(continues 608.4: Each attacking half-column deals its combat damage either to the defending player or to the blocking half-column in front of it, and each blocking half-column deals its combat damage to the attacking half-column it…)
608.4d If, after blocks have been declared and before combat damage is over, a unit is put into the defending formation in front of an unblocked attacking column, that column becomes blocked, and it stays blocked if that unit later leaves. The defending player may do this even if they declared no blockers. See rules 606, 607.
 Example: Tiderunner Initiate is played in front of an unblocked attacker after blocks; the attacker deals its damage to the Tiderunner instead of the defending player.
608.4e A blocking half-column with no attacking unit left in front of it when it would strike deals no combat damage, even if it has Piercing. See rule 802.16.
 Example: Good Whale (7/5, Piercing) blocks a column whose only attacker is destroyed in the block window. Good Whale deals no damage to the attacking player and takes none.
608.4f A unit blocking where no attacking unit is (a side-block) forms a blocking half-column with no attacker in front of it. It deals no combat damage, even if it has Piercing, and it never makes the combat damage step split. See rules 606, 802.16.
 Example: A Piercing unit side-blocks. It deals no combat damage to the attacking player.
title: CR 608.4d–608.4f

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 608. Combat Damage Step
608.5 A half-column's combat damage is the combined power of the units in it when it strikes, counted as rule 608.5c describes. See rule 206.
 Example: A 1/1 and a 2/2 attack in one column beside a Swift column. In the window after the Swift sub-step the 1/1 gets two +1/+1 counters, so the column deals 3 + 2 = 5 in the normal sub-step.
title: CR 608.5

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 608. Combat Damage Step
(continues 608.5: A half-column's combat damage is the combined power of the units in it when it strikes, counted as rule 608.5c describes.)
608.5a A unit with 0 power deals no damage, but it does not stop its column from dealing the combined power of the other units in it. A half-column whose combined power is 0 deals no combat damage.
 Example: Zephyrzoa, reduced to 0 power, is in a column with a powered unit. The column deals combat damage and Zephyrzoa's 'when my column deals combat damage' ability triggers.
 Example: Zephyrzoa, reduced to 0 power, attacks alone. Its column deals no combat damage and its ability does not trigger.
title: CR 608.5a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 608. Combat Damage Step
(continues 608.5: A half-column's combat damage is the combined power of the units in it when it strikes, counted as rule 608.5c describes.)
608.5b Powerful doubles a half-column's combined power once, before that damage is divided among its recipients (see rule 802.10). Vulnerable does not change the amount a half-column deals; it doubles what a Vulnerable unit is dealt (see rule 802.11). See rules 802.10, 802.11.
 Example: Chitin Shredder (Powerful) attacks unblocked; the defending player is dealt double its column's power.
608.5c When a half-column's combined power is counted, a unit with negative power counts as 0: it deals no damage and does not reduce its column's damage. In an exchange in which Unaware applies, each unit's printed power is used. See rule 802.9.
 Example: Lithoghul (4/4) and a -2/3 token attack in one column and are not blocked. The column deals 4.
 Example: A Robot token with nine +1/+1 counters (a 9/9) attacks and is blocked by Bubb, which is Unaware. In that exchange both read their printed stats: the Robot is a 0/0, so it dies and deals Bubb no damage.
title: CR 608.5b–608.5c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 608. Combat Damage Step
608.6 When a half-column deals combat damage to the units of the opposing half-column, its damage is divided among those units, starting with the front unit and then the unit behind it. See rule 602.
 Example: Living Forge and A Pile of Rubbish attack in one column and are blocked by Tiderunner Initiate. All 2 of the Tiderunner’s damage goes to Living Forge, in front; none goes to A Pile of Rubbish behind it. (from the Manual p.23)
608.6a The controller of the half-column dealing the damage divides it: the attacking player divides an attacking half-column's damage among the blocking units, and the defending player divides a blocking half-column's damage among the attacking units. See rule 608.6.
 Example: A 4-power attacker is blocked by two 1/1s. The attacking player is asked how to divide the 4.
