 Example: The defending player divides a blocking half-column's damage and may put all of it on the front attacker.
608.6b Lethal damage (rule 608.6e) must be assigned to a unit before any damage is assigned to the unit behind it.
 Example: Rune Channeler (4 power) is blocked by a 2/3 in front of a 1/1. Its controller may put 3 or 4 on the 2/3, but not less than 3, since 3 is the 2/3's lethal damage.
608.6c A unit may be assigned more than lethal damage. The dealing player may assign all of a half-column's damage to the front unit and none to the unit behind it, even if there is enough to destroy both.
 Example: A 4-power attacker is blocked by a 1/1 in front of a 1/1. The attacking player assigns all 4 to the front 1/1; the back 1/1 is untouched.
608.6d All combat damage assigned to a unit is dealt to that unit, including any beyond its lethal damage; none of it is lost. A half-column without Piercing that has at least one unit to deal damage to assigns all of its damage to those units, so none of it reaches the player; any of its damage still unassigned when the last unit is reached is assigned to that unit. See rules 802.16, 608.4c.
 Example: Rune Channeler (4/3, no Piercing) is blocked by a 1/1. All 4 damage is dealt to the 1/1; none is lost and none reaches the player.
 Example: An overkill combat hit on Mirage Scuttler marks the whole amount, not only the lethal part.
title: CR 608.6–608.6d

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 608. Combat Damage Step
(continues 608.6: When a half-column deals combat damage to the units of the opposing half-column, its damage is divided among those units, starting with the front unit and then the unit behind it.)
608.6e Lethal damage, for assignment, is the smallest amount of the half-column's damage that would destroy the unit, given the damage already marked on it: its remaining defense; half of that, rounded up, if the unit is Vulnerable; 1 if the half-column has Deadly. In an exchange in which Unaware applies, the unit's printed defense, less the damage already marked on it, is used. In an exchange involving a Pure card, neither Vulnerable nor Deadly changes lethal damage. See rules 802.3, 802.9, 802.11, 802.25.
 Example: A 10-power Piercing half-column blocked by a Vulnerable 3/8 must assign 4 to it, and the other 6 may go to the player.
608.6f If the opposing half-column has only one unit, all of the damage is assigned to that unit; with Piercing, the dealing player may instead send damage beyond that unit's lethal damage to its controller (see rule 802.16). See rule 802.16.
 Example: A Piercing attacker with 10 power is blocked by a lone Vulnerable 3/8. It may assign all 10 to that unit (dealt as 20), and then none reaches the player.
608.6g Damage prevention on a unit does not change its lethal damage. Lethal damage is worked out as if the unit were not protected, and the prevention applies when the damage is dealt (rule 608.7a). See rule 708.
 Example: A shielded 0/5 Awoken Tomb is in front of a 5/6. At least 5 must be assigned to the Tomb before any is assigned to the 5/6.
title: CR 608.6e–608.6g

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 608. Combat Damage Step
(continues 608.6: When a half-column deals combat damage to the units of the opposing half-column, its damage is divided among those units, starting with the front unit and then the unit behind it.)
608.6h In each sub-step, every half-column's damage is divided before any damage in that sub-step is dealt.
 Example: Two 10/20 attackers are each blocked by two 1/3s. Both attackers are asked how to divide their damage, and no damage is dealt until both have answered.
title: CR 608.6h

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 608. Combat Damage Step
608.7 All the combat damage of one sub-step is dealt simultaneously. Damage dealt to a unit is marked on it; a Vulnerable unit is dealt double the damage assigned to it (see rule 802.11), and a Poisonous source deals its damage to units in the form of -1/-1 counters (see rule 802.18). See rules 802.11, 802.18.
 Example: Crumbling Ancient (Vulnerable) is marked with double the combat damage assigned to it.
608.7a Prevention applies as combat damage is dealt. Damage that is prevented is not dealt: it is not marked, it places no -1/-1 counters, it does not trigger abilities that trigger on a unit being dealt damage, and it cannot destroy a unit through Deadly. See rule 708.
 Example: A 12-power half-column is blocked by an Awoken Tomb under Phytochemical Protection in front of a 5/6. The 5 combat damage assigned to the Tomb is prevented: none is marked, and the Tomb’s “when I am dealt damage” ability does not trigger.
 Example: A Deadly half-column cannot destroy a unit whose damage is prevented.
title: CR 608.7–608.7a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 608. Combat Damage Step
(continues 608.7: All the combat damage of one sub-step is dealt simultaneously. Damage dealt to a unit is marked on it; a Vulnerable unit is dealt double the damage assigned to it (see rule 802.11), and a Poisonous source deals its…)
608.7b After a sub-step's damage has been dealt, units with lethal damage, and units dealt damage by a Deadly source, are destroyed before the next sub-step begins. See rules 713, 802.3.
 Example: A Swift half-column destroys its 2/2 blocker in the Swift sub-step; the blocker never strikes back in the normal sub-step.
title: CR 608.7b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 608. Combat Damage Step
(continues 608.7: All the combat damage of one sub-step is dealt simultaneously. Damage dealt to a unit is marked on it; a Vulnerable unit is dealt double the damage assigned to it (see rule 802.11), and a Poisonous source deals its…)
608.7c Damage marked on units remains until the regroup phase, when it is removed. See rule 506.
 Example: An attacker and its blocker each have 2 damage marked in the first battle of the turn. Both still have 2 damage marked when the second battle begins; it is removed in the regroup phase.
title: CR 608.7c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 608. Combat Damage Step
608.8 Combat damage is dealt to a player in two ways: by an unblocked attacking half-column (rule 608.4a), and as Piercing excess from an attacking half-column, or from a blocking half-column with an attacker in front of it (see rule 802.16). Combat damage dealt to a player causes that player to lose that much life, unless an effect replaces that damage or changes the life lost. See rules 112, 802.16.
 Example: A Piercing attacker is not blocked; all of its damage is dealt to the defending player.
 Example: A blocking Piercing half-column with an attacker in front of it deals its excess to the attacking player.
title: CR 608.8

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 608. Combat Damage Step
(continues 608.8: Combat damage is dealt to a player in two ways: by an unblocked attacking half-column (rule 608.4a), and as Piercing excess from an attacking half-column, or from a blocking half-column with an attacker in front of it…)
608.8a Combat damage to a player that an effect replaces but still deals to that player (for example, Blightsea Polyp's rot) was still dealt. An ability that triggers when a column deals combat damage to a player still triggers, and reads the damage dealt, even if the player lost no life. Damage redirected to a unit instead is not dealt to the player (rule 608.8c). See rules 708, 112.
 Example: A fully replaced combat hit still counts as dealt: Vroot, which counts all the combat damage its column deals, pays out the damage dealt to the player, not the life the player lost.
 Example: Blightsea Polyp turns a Lethal hit into rot. That is still damage dealt to the player, so the player is killed.
title: CR 608.8a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 608. Combat Damage Step
(continues 608.8: Combat damage is dealt to a player in two ways: by an unblocked attacking half-column (rule 608.4a), and as Piercing excess from an attacking half-column, or from a blocking half-column with an attacker in front of it…)
608.8b Damage dealt by an ability that a source's combat damage causes, such as Resonant's extra damage, is not combat damage, even when it is dealt during or because of combat. See rule 802.19.
 Example: Resonant's extra damage to a player is not combat damage, so Oorblak does not take it; the player does.
title: CR 608.8b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 608. Combat Damage Step
(continues 608.8: Combat damage is dealt to a player in two ways: by an unblocked attacking half-column (rule 608.4a), and as Piercing excess from an attacking half-column, or from a blocking half-column with an attacker in front of it…)
608.8c If combat damage that would be dealt to a player is dealt to a unit instead (as Oorblak's ability does), the replacement applies to that damage once. Without Piercing, all of that damage is dealt to the unit. With Piercing, the damage beyond the unit's lethal damage is still combat damage that would be dealt to the player: another such effect that has not applied (a second Oorblak) may take it, the same one may not, and what none takes is dealt to the player. A redirect applies before an effect that changes how combat damage is dealt to a player (Blightsea Polyp); that effect applies only to damage actually dealt to the player, such as Piercing excess no redirect took. Damage a redirect takes is not dealt to the player. If all of a column's combat damage to a player is redirected, the column has dealt that player no combat damage: Lethal kills no one, Thieving draws nothing, and nothing that triggers when a column deals combat damage to a player triggers. If some of it gets past the redirects (Piercing excess), the column has dealt the player that much. An ability that triggers when its column deals combat damage, with no player named (Vroot), does trigger on a redirected hit: the column dealt that damage to the unit that took it (see rule 608.9a). See rules 708, 802.16.
 Example: 10 Piercing combat damage that would be dealt to a player is redirected into a 2/4 Oorblak. 4 destroy it, and the other 6 are dealt to the player.
 Example: A non-Piercing overkill redirected into Oorblak is absorbed whole; nothing reaches the player.
 Example: 10 Piercing combat damage and two 2/4 Oorblaks: 4 destroy the first, the 6 left are still combat damage and the second takes 4 of them, and 2 reach the player.
 Example: With three 2/4 Oorblaks the third takes the last 2, and nothing reaches the player.
 Example: Blightsea Polyp and Oorblak, in either order: Oorblak takes the column's damage, and no rot is gained. With a Piercing column, the excess past the Oorblak reaches the player and is dealt as 1 rot.
 Example: Blightsea Polyp beside two Oorblaks: the player chooses only between the Oorblaks, and no rot is gained.
 Example: Gublin (Lethal) attacks and all of its combat damage is redirected into Oorblak. The player is dealt nothing and lives.
 Example: A wholly redirected hit raises no "deals combat damage to a player" trigger and costs the player no life.
 Example: A partly redirected hit is dealt as what got past Oorblak.
 Example: Vroot's 10-power Piercing column puts 4 into Oorblak and 6 past it: each opponent gains 10, all the combat damage its column dealt.
title: CR 608.8c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 608. Combat Damage Step
608.9 An ability that triggers on combat damage, or on something combat damage causes (such as a unit being destroyed), triggers when that event happens, during the combat damage step, and its trigger condition is checked then. It is put on the stack later, as rules 608.9b and 608.9c describe, and only then are its targets chosen. See rules 706, 703.
 Example: Lithoghul attacks and is blocked by a Geode. In the damage step the Geode deals 1 to Lithoghul, and Lithoghul's 'whenever I am dealt damage' ability triggers then; nothing goes on the stack or resolves until the after combat step.
608.9a An ability that triggers 'when my column deals combat damage' triggers in each sub-step in which its own column deals combat damage, and only for damage its own column dealt; another column's damage does not trigger it. A 0-power unit with such an ability triggers if its column's combined power is greater than 0. Such an ability counts combat damage its column deals to anything: to the units blocking it, to a unit that a redirect deals the damage to instead (Oorblak), and to a player. "That much" counts all of it. See rule 706.
 Example: A Swift and Sluggish column with Vroot strikes twice, and Vroot's ability triggers twice.
 Example: Vroot's 'that much' is its own column's damage, not the total dealt to the player by every column.
 Example: Vroot is blocked by a 0/20 unit: its column deals the blocker 4, and each opponent gains 4.
 Example: Vroot's column is wholly redirected into Oorblak: the column dealt Oorblak 4, and each opponent gains 4.
608.9b In an unsplit step, every ability that triggered during the combat damage step is put on the stack in the after combat step, together with the abilities that trigger at the start of the after combat step, as one batch. The initiative player puts all of theirs on the stack first, in the order they choose, and then the other player puts theirs; each player may interleave the two kinds in any order. All players may respond to them. See rules 609, 706.
 Example: One player's combat-damage trigger and after-combat trigger are put in order together, in one choice.
 Example: The initiative player's triggers go on the stack first and sit at the bottom.
title: CR 608.9–608.9b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 608. Combat Damage Step
(continues 608.9: An ability that triggers on combat damage, or on something combat damage causes (such as a unit being destroyed), triggers when that event happens, during the combat damage step, and its trigger condition is checked…)
608.9c In a split step, the abilities that triggered during a sub-step other than the last scheduled one are put on the stack, in the same order as in rule 608.9b, at the window after that sub-step, and resolve before the next sub-step deals damage (rule 608.3b). The abilities that trigger during the last sub-step in which damage is dealt join the after combat batch as in rule 608.9b. See rules 609, 706.
 Example: In a split step, a death trigger from the Swift sub-step resolves at the window before the normal sub-step, not after combat.
 Example: With Sluggish last, a death in the Sluggish sub-step joins the after combat batch.
608.9d Abilities that trigger during the combat damage step trigger during battle, so an effect that makes abilities cost more to trigger during battle applies to them. See rules 111, 706.
 Example: Crevice Lurker taxes a combat-damage trigger; on the same board without the Lurker there is no tax.
608.9e An ability that works only while its card is in the bin can trigger on combat damage only if the card is already in the bin when that damage is dealt. A unit destroyed by combat damage is not in the bin while that same damage is dealt, but a unit destroyed in an earlier sub-step is. See rules 405, 706.
 Example: Cinder Scuttler is destroyed in the same sub-step in which another of its controller's columns deals combat damage to the opponent. It does not return.
 Example: A Swift unit destroys Cinder Scuttler in the Swift sub-step; in the normal sub-step its controller deals combat damage to the opponent, and it returns.
title: CR 608.9c–608.9e

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 609. After Combat
609.1 The after combat step is the last step of a battle round. It follows the combat damage step, in the region where that battle is fought, and it is the last priority window for interaction in that region before regroup. See rules 505.2, 608.
609.1a A region in which no battle takes place has no after combat step. A battle round in which no attack is declared has no after combat step. See rules 505.2a, 604.4.
 Example: Both players decline to attack. Neither region has a combat damage step or an after combat step, and the battle phase opens no priority window at all.
609.1b In a game with two battle rounds, each round that has a battle has its own after combat step, in the region where that round is fought: the first round's in the non-initiative player's region, and the second round's in the initiative player's region. See rules 505.3, 505.4b, 610.
title: CR 609.1–609.1b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 609. After Combat
609.2 The after combat step is a priority window. The initiative player receives priority first, then priority passes to the non-initiative player in the region. When all players pass priority in succession with the stack empty, the after combat step ends. See rule 703.
 Example: After combat, the initiative player passes, the non-initiative player casts a spell, and both then pass. The spell resolves and the initiative player receives priority again. When both pass with the stack empty, the step ends.
609.2a When the after combat step of the first battle round ends and units were sent to counterattack, the battle phase does not end: the second battle round begins (see rule 610). See rule 610.
 Example: With counterattackers sent, passing in round 1's after-combat window does not end the battle.
609.2b When the after combat step of the last battle round ends, the battle phase ends and regroup begins. The last battle round is the second round, or the first round if no units were sent to counterattack. See rules 506, 610.4.
 Example: When the last player passes in the final after-combat window, the game goes through regroup and into deployment; no one is given priority in between.
title: CR 609.2–609.2b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 609. After Combat
609.3 An ability that triggers "after combat" triggers when the after combat step begins. It is put on the stack in the after combat step, and players may respond to it there. See rules 109.3, 706.
 Example: Smouldering Inferno, played as a unit, sacrifices itself after combat.
609.3a An "after combat" ability of a unit triggers if that unit is present in the region where the battle is happening. The unit need not be in a formation. See rule 601.7.
 Example: A unit with an after-combat ability that stands in the battle region outside the formation still triggers.
609.3b An "after combat" ability does not trigger in a region where no battle took place. A unit in a region other than the one where the battle is fought does not trigger. See rules 505.4c, 601.7.
 Example: A unit with an after-combat ability that stays in another region does not trigger.
609.3c Abilities that triggered during the combat damage step and are still waiting are put on the stack in the after combat step together with the "after combat" abilities, as one batch. The initiative player puts all of theirs on the stack first, then the non-initiative player puts theirs, so the non-initiative player's resolve first. Each player chooses the order of their own and may interleave the two kinds. See rules 608.9b, 706.
 Example: One player's combat-damage trigger and after-combat trigger are put in order together, in one choice.
 Example: The initiative player's triggers go on the stack first and sit at the bottom.
609.3d When Swift or Sluggish splits the combat damage step, only the abilities that triggered in the last sub-step in which damage is dealt join the after combat batch. Those that triggered in an earlier sub-step have already resolved before the next sub-step (see rule 608.9c). See rules 608.3, 608.9c.
 Example: With Swift in the battle, a unit that dies in the last (normal) sub-step has its death trigger in the after-combat batch.
 Example: With Sluggish last, a death in the Sluggish sub-step joins the after-combat batch.
 Example: In a split damage step a death trigger from an earlier sub-step resolves at the boundary, not after combat.
title: CR 609.3–609.3d

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 610. Counterattacks and Later Battle Rounds
610.1 A counterattack is the non-initiative team's attack in a battle phase with two battle rounds. The non-initiative team sends its counterattacking units out during the block step of the first battle round, and they attack in the second battle round. See rules 505.3, 606.5.
610.1a Units are sent to counterattack only in the first battle round, at the same time as the non-initiative team declares its blocks. Sending counterattackers is optional. See rules 606.5, 606.5b.
title: CR 610.1–610.1a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 610. Counterattacks and Later Battle Rounds
610.2 Counterattacking units leave their region as soon as they are sent. From then until the first battle round ends they are in no region, and they are treated as if they do not exist. See rules 505.3b, 606.2d.
610.2a A sent counterattacker's static abilities apply to nothing while it is away, not even to itself. See rule 707.
 Example: Bubb carries Towering Colossus ("Enemies gain +2/+2"), so an enemy 1/1 attacking into Bubb's region is a 3/3. When Bubb is sent to counterattack, the attacker is a 1/1 again at once.
 Example: A sent Prickly Protector ("I gain +1/+1 for each other ally") does not give itself that bonus while it is away.
610.2b A sent counterattacker cannot be targeted and cannot be sacrificed while it is away. See rule 110.
 Example: The initiative player casts a spell that targets a unit in the round-1 battle region. A unit that was sent to counterattack is not offered as a target.
610.2c A sent counterattacker does not count as a unit in the region it left. A unit that stays behind does not count a sent counterattacker as an ally. See rule 601.
 Example: Prickly Protector, carrying a -1/-1 counter, is alive only because it has one other ally. When that ally is sent to counterattack, the Protector stays home, no longer counts it, and dies.
610.2d Spell tokens sent with counterattackers are away with them, and cannot be cast until they return. See rule 610.3.
title: CR 610.2–610.2d

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 610. Counterattacks and Later Battle Rounds
(continues 610.2: Counterattacking units leave their region as soon as they are sent. From then until the first battle round ends they are in no region, and they are treated as if they do not exist.)
610.2e A sent counterattacker is not checked for death while it is away. It is checked as soon as it returns at the start of the second battle round. See rule 713.
 Example: Prickly Protector with a -1/-1 counter, alive only through its own static, survives being declared as a counterattacker.
 Example: A Prickly Protector sent out alone survives the send, and dies on arrival in the enemy region, where it has no ally to count.
title: CR 610.2e

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 610. Counterattacks and Later Battle Rounds
610.3 Spell tokens may go with counterattacking units, under the same conditions as with an attack (see rule 604.2c). A counterattack made only of spell tokens is not allowed: spell tokens need at least one counterattacking unit to go with. A spell token sent with a counterattack is committed as the units are: in round 2 it must ride with the counterattacking formation, with the formation as a whole rather than with any one unit. If every unit sent with it has died, it cannot ride and is not owed: it reaches no priority window, and is erased unused at regroup. See rules 604.2c, 606.5a.
 Example: Three units and a Fireball token were sent. In round 2 a formation that leaves the Fireball behind is refused.
 Example: The only unit sent with a Fireball token dies before round 2: no attack is possible, the battle phase ends with no window, and the token is erased at regroup.
title: CR 610.3

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 610. Counterattacks and Later Battle Rounds
610.4 The second battle round begins only once the first battle round has completely finished, its after combat step included. In a two-player game it is fought in the initiative player's region. See rules 505.4b, 609.2.
610.4a When the second battle round begins, the sent counterattackers, and the spell tokens sent with them, reappear in the region they are attacking. See rule 610.2.
 Example: The non-initiative player sent two units. When round 1's after combat step ends, both appear in the initiative player's region, ready to be put into formation.
610.4b If the first battle round had a battle, only the units sent to counterattack can attack in the second battle round, and every one of them still there and able to attack must attack. In its attack step the non-initiative team puts all of them into formation, in any shape; the shape is chosen then, not when the units are sent. Every spell token sent with them that is still there rides along too (see rule 610.3). A sent unit that died on its return is not owed. See rule 604.2f.
 Example: The non-initiative player sent Conduit of Pain at block time. In round 2 it is the only unit they can attack with, and it must attack: declining is refused.
 Example: Three units were sent. Declining, or leaving one off to the side, is refused; any shape that holds all three is accepted.
 Example: Two units were sent and one dies on its return: the other alone is owed, and it forms by itself.
610.4c If the first battle round had a battle and no units were sent to counterattack, there is no second battle round. The battle phase ends after the first round's after combat step. See rules 505.3f, 609.2b.
 Example: With no counterattack sent, no battle is fought in the initiative player's region.
610.4d If the initiative team declared no attack in the first battle round, the non-initiative team may still attack in the second battle round. It may attack with any of its units, since it never had a block step in which to send counterattackers. See rules 505.3e, 604.4a.
 Example: The initiative player could attack and declines; the non-initiative player may then attack with any unit.
title: CR 610.4–610.4d

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 610. Counterattacks and Later Battle Rounds
(continues 610.4: The second battle round begins only once the first battle round has completely finished, its after combat step included. In a two-player game it is fought in the initiative player's region.)
610.4e The non-initiative team may decline to attack in the second battle round only when no unit it sent to counterattack is still there and able to attack, or when the first battle round had no attack (see rule 610.4d). A counterattack with such a unit cannot be declined. A declined second round has no battle and opens no priority window, and the battle phase ends. See rules 604.2a, 604.4.
 Example: Two units were sent. In round 2 declining is refused, and so is leaving one of them behind; every formation offered holds both.
 Example: The initiative player declined to attack in round 1. In round 2 the non-initiative player may decline too, and the battle phase ends.
 Example: The initiative player's spell tokens at home cannot be cast in any round-1 window. If the non-initiative player's only counterattacker then dies on its return, round 2 has no attack, and those tokens never become castable this battle.
610.4f In the second battle round the initiative team declares blocks only. It cannot send units to counterattack, because each team gets only one chance to attack. See rules 505.3d, 606.5b.
610.4g In every priority window of the second battle round, the initiative player receives priority first, although it is now the defending player. See rules 605.1a, 703.
610.4h While the second battle round is resolved, units in the region where the first round was fought are treated as if they do not exist. They include the units the initiative team attacked with and any unit created there during the first round, so none of them can block in the second round. See rules 505.4c, 304.8a.
 Example: Tidelurker's 2/2, created mid-attack in the enemy region, stays there and cannot block the counterattack.
 Example: A spell token the initiative player keeps at home cannot be cast in any round-1 window, and can be cast in round 2's windows.
title: CR 610.4e–610.4h

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 610. Counterattacks and Later Battle Rounds
610.5 A battle phase has at most two battle rounds. After the second round's after combat step, battle ends and regroup begins. See rules 505.3d, 506.
 Example: In round 2 the initiative player cannot send units out to counterattack, and the battle phase ends after round 2.
title: CR 610.5

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 6. Regions, Formations and Battle › 610. Counterattacks and Later Battle Rounds
610.6 In team games, combat is first resolved completely in every region the initiative team attacked. Then combat is resolved in the regions the non-initiative team counterattacked. See rules 505.4, 904.
 Example: In a 2v2 game the initiative team attacks both non-initiative regions. Both of those battles are resolved, one region at a time, before any counterattack battle in an initiative region begins.
title: CR 610.6

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 700. General
700.1 An effect is anything on the stack. Whenever a card is played, or an ability is activated or triggered, it is added to the stack as an effect. A unit or spell unit on the stack is an effect too. See rule 703.
 Example: a {Battle} unit being played sits on the stack and can be chosen by an effect that says "target effect" (Dematerialize).
700.1a A spell effect is an effect that is a spell: a spell, a spell unit or a spell token on the stack. A unit on the stack is an effect but not a spell effect, and neither is an Ambush, since the card played as an Ambush is a unit: a card that says "spell effect" cannot affect either of them.
 Example: Null Drone ("target spell effect") cannot choose a plain unit on the stack, but can choose a spell unit.
 Example: Dreadwave Devourer ("Negate target spell effect") cannot target an Ambush on the stack, and the Ambush resolves.
 Example: A spell unit and a spell token on the stack are spell effects; an Ambush is not.
700.1b A nonspell effect is any effect that is not a spell effect: a triggered ability, an activated ability, a Virus being applied, a unit on the stack, or an Ambush.
 Example: Nothyr ("negate up to one target nonspell effect") can choose a {Battle} unit on the stack.
 Example: Nothyr can also choose an Ambush on the stack.
title: CR 700.1–700.1b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 700. General
700.2 Casting a spell is playing it. The printed rules use "cast" and "play" for the same act, and casting a spell token is playing a spell. See rule 701.
title: CR 700.2

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 700. General
700.3 Players interact by playing cards and activating abilities in response to one another. All interaction uses the stack (rule 703). See rule 703.
title: CR 700.3

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 701. Playing and Applying
701.1 Only units and spells are played, whatever zone they are played from. Applying a modification is not playing a card (701.2).
 Example: Godray and Monke played from hand, and Trench Stalker played from the bin, are plays; a Virus applied to the attacker is not.
701.1a Playing a spell unit is playing a spell.
 Example: a spell unit played through Hooba-Pon counts as a spell played.
701.1b Casting a spell token is playing a spell. A spell token is never in a hand; it is cast from play, so it is played from somewhere other than the hand. See rule 702.7.
 Example: casting a Fireball token triggers Stalwart Sentinel ("when you play a card from anywhere other than your hand").
title: CR 701.1–701.1b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 701. Playing and Applying
(continues 701.1: Only units and spells are played, whatever zone they are played from. Applying a modification is not playing a card (701.2).)
701.1c A token is not a card. An ability or cost modifier that refers to a "card" being played does not apply to a spell token being cast; one that refers to a "spell" does; one that refers to a "nontoken spell" does not. See rule 108.
 Example: Arbiter of Armistice ("Cards played during battle gain [Pay 2 life]") does not make a spell token cost life.
701.1d Creating a token is not playing it. See rule 304.
701.1e An ability that triggers whenever its controller plays a unit works only while its card is in play. A card that is being played is on the stack, not in play, so its own play does not trigger it, whether or not the ability says "another". See rule 706.
title: CR 701.1c–701.1e

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 701. Playing and Applying
(continues 701.1: Only units and spells are played, whatever zone they are played from. Applying a modification is not playing a card (701.2).)
701.1f An ability that triggers when a player plays a unit triggers as the unit is played, not when it enters play. It goes on the stack above the unit and resolves before it, and it triggers even if the unit is negated and never enters play. See rule 706.
 Example: Proph is in play and its controller plays Good Whale from the cache. Proph's draw goes on the stack above Good Whale and resolves first; only then does Good Whale spawn.
 Example: A unit played from the cache is negated before it resolves. It never enters play, but it was played, so Proph still draws.
title: CR 701.1f

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 701. Playing and Applying
701.2 Applying a modification (an augment, a graft, or a Virus) is not playing a card. A modification is applied, whether it comes from a hand, a bin, a cache or elsewhere. Applying a modification is a special action. See rule 720.
701.2a An ability that triggers when a player plays a unit, a spell or a card does not trigger when a modification is applied, including one applied from the bin.
 Example: Ravenous Fireslinger does not trigger when its controller applies an augment, and does trigger on a real spell.
 Example: Applying a Virus during battle is not playing a card, so Void Mandible does not react to it.
701.2b A modifier to the cost of playing cards does not change the cost of applying a modification. A modification still needs its own affinity and its own mana cost to be applied. See rule 111.
701.2c Tides of the Cosmos is the one exception. Although it says "play", it may put a Virus card onto a unit as a Virus, and it may play a card as an Ambush or a Prophecy. It cannot graft a card or apply a non-Virus augment.
 Example: a Virus card that Tides of the Cosmos plays as a Virus is attached to a unit and never enters play.
title: CR 701.2–701.2c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 701. Playing and Applying
701.3 Putting a card into play is not playing it. Whether an effect plays a card or puts it into play is decided by the verb the effect prints.
 Example: Covenant of the Damned puts a unit from the bin into play; only Covenant itself was played.
701.3a A spell unit that enters play without being played (for example, one put into play from a bin) does not produce its spell effect.
 Example: Covenant of the Damned puts Lonely Forager into play from the bin; Forager does not draw a card.
title: CR 701.3–701.3a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 701. Playing and Applying
701.4 A card played during the resolution of another effect is played. During battle it is put on the stack and can be responded to (rule 703.5), and abilities that trigger on a play see it. See rule 703.5.
 Example: Tides of the Cosmos plays a unit, and Bloomcaster's "Whenever you play a unit" triggers on it.
 Example: A unit Wake the Dead plays waits on the stack and can be answered; a negated one never arrives.
 Example: A card an effect plays where nobody can respond is still announced as played, for a unit and for a spell.
title: CR 701.4

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 701. Playing and Applying
(continues 701.4: A card played during the resolution of another effect is played. During battle it is put on the stack and can be responded to (rule 703.5), and abilities that trigger on a play see it.)
701.4a A card played by an effect is played from the zone it came out of. If it came out of a hand, it is played from the hand. If it came out of the cache, a bin, the deck or anywhere else, it is not played from the hand.
 Example: Tides of the Cosmos plays a card off the top of the deck, so Proph and Stalwart Sentinel see a play from somewhere other than the hand.
 Example: Hooba-Pon plays a unit from its controller's hand, so neither Proph nor Stalwart Sentinel triggers.
title: CR 701.4a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 701. Playing and Applying
701.5 A copy of a spell is not played. It does not trigger abilities that trigger on playing, and it is not counted as a played spell. See rule 710.
 Example: Earthbound Replicator does not copy its own copy.
title: CR 701.5

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 702. Casting Spells
702.1 To play a card, a player must meet its affinity requirement, pay its mana cost, select its targets as it is played, and resolve whatever is inside its brackets (an additional cost to pay or a mode to choose). See rules 105, 110, 111.
 Example: Arc Lightning (rr, cost 4) cannot be played with four water resources (no affinity) or with only two fire resources (not enough mana); with two fire and two water it can.
702.1a A player must meet a card's affinity requirement to be able to play it, unless an effect lets it be played ignoring affinity. See rule 105.
 Example: Tides of the Cosmos plays a fire unit for a player who has only water resources.
702.1b To pay a card's mana cost, the player expends a number of unexpended resources equal to that cost. See rule 106.
 Example: playing Arc Lightning, cost 4, expends four of the player’s unexpended resources.
702.1c A card can be played only when its timing allows (rule 207). A card with no timing icon can be played only during deployment. See rules 207, 504.
 Example: Lonely Forager has no timing icon: it can be played in deployment but not in battle.
title: CR 702.1–702.1c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 702. Casting Spells
702.2 A card in the cache under a live permission may be played in every way it could be played from the hand. It is still not in the hand. See rule 403.
 Example: a glimpsed Virus in the cache can be applied onto an enemy unit in battle.
title: CR 702.2

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 702. Casting Spells
(continues 702.2: A card in the cache under a live permission may be played in every way it could be played from the hand. It is still not in the hand.)
702.2a A card played from the cache or a bin under a permission still obeys its own printed timing; the permission itself never waives timing. Apart from the timing grants that also work from the cache (rule 702.2d), only an effect that says the card may be played now, such as Tides of the Cosmos, lets it ignore its timing. See rules 207, 405.
 Example: Tides of the Cosmos plays a deploy-timing unit in battle.
702.2b A card that says it can't be played from your hand is restricted from that zone only. It may still be played from another zone that allows it.
702.2c Permission to play a card "as if it had [Haste]" does not let a {Battle} card be played outside battle. See rule 504.
 Example: Dispatch Courier cannot let a {Battle} spell unit be played in the haste step.
title: CR 702.2a–702.2c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 702. Casting Spells
(continues 702.2: A card in the cache under a live permission may be played in every way it could be played from the hand. It is still not in the hand.)
702.2d The rules that widen a card's timing when it is played from hand also widen it when it is played from the cache: a haste grant such as Dispatch Courier's, the erase-funded haste play of Writhing Host, Ambush, and the battle {Virus} augment window. See rules 504, 702.2c.
 Example: a glimpsed {Virus} card in the cache can be augmented onto a unit in a battle window, as it could from hand.
 [Verification of 702.2d was only partial.]
title: CR 702.2d

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 702. Casting Spells
702.3 Playing a card follows the steps below, in order. Everything the play needs is declared and paid before the card is put on the stack, so no player can respond to an undeclared or unpaid play.
 Example: while Sacrificial Burst’s target and sacrifice are being chosen, nothing is on the stack and the opponent has no action; it reaches the stack only once both are done.
title: CR 702.3

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 702. Casting Spells
(continues 702.3: Playing a card follows the steps below, in order. Everything the play needs is declared and paid before the card is put on the stack, so no player can respond to an undeclared or unpaid play.)
702.3a Step 1: if the card has an X, the player chooses X. A variable additional cost (one whose amount is X) is paid at this step, and the amount paid is X. The card's mana cost is paid at the start of the play. See rule 107.
702.3b Step 2: the player chooses any {Modular} modifications for the card. See rule 724.
 Example: Spellbind asks for its {Modular} mods as it is played; the chosen mod goes on the stack with it.
title: CR 702.3a–702.3b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 702. Casting Spells
(continues 702.3: Playing a card follows the steps below, in order. Everything the play needs is declared and paid before the card is put on the stack, so no player can respond to an undeclared or unpaid play.)
702.3c Step 3: the player declares every target the card's text names (rule 110). See rule 110.
title: CR 702.3c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 702. Casting Spells
(continues 702.3: Playing a card follows the steps below, in order. Everything the play needs is declared and paid before the card is put on the stack, so no player can respond to an undeclared or unpaid play.)
702.3d Step 4: if a bracket in the card's text offers a choice of modes, the owner of the effect chooses one. See rule 702.5.
 Example: Wither and Bloom declares which half it is before anyone may respond.
702.3e Step 5: a card that may be played into a formation has its place in the formation chosen. See rule 602.
 Example: Tiderunner Initiate’s place in the formation is chosen as it is played, before it is on the stack.
702.3f Step 6: the player pays the card's fixed additional costs, after everything else has been declared. See rule 111.
 Example: Sacrificial Burst asks for its target before its sacrifice; Trench Stalker asks for its formation spot before its two discards.
title: CR 702.3d–702.3f

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 702. Casting Spells
(continues 702.3: Playing a card follows the steps below, in order. Everything the play needs is declared and paid before the card is put on the stack, so no player can respond to an undeclared or unpaid play.)
702.3g Step 7: options that a card offers "as you play" a spell (Maelstrom Charger) are taken. Such an option is not an effect: it never goes on the stack and cannot be responded to. See rule 710.
 Example: the Maelstrom Charger option is asked while the spell is played and never reaches the stack.
702.3h Step 8: the card is put on the stack as an effect (rule 703). See rule 703.
 Example: once Arc Lightning has been declared and paid, it is on the stack as a spell effect controlled by its player, and no longer in hand.
title: CR 702.3g–702.3h

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 702. Casting Spells
702.4 Every cost of playing a card is paid before the card is put on the stack. No player can respond to the payment, or between a cost and the effect it pays for. See rule 111.
title: CR 702.4

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 702. Casting Spells
(continues 702.4: Every cost of playing a card is paid before the card is put on the stack. No player can respond to the payment, or between a cost and the effect it pays for.)
702.4a A card whose costs cannot all be paid cannot be played.
 Example: with nothing to sacrifice, Tides of the Cosmos does not offer Volatile Toxicity.
702.4b Negating a card does not refund the costs paid to play it. See rule 704.4.
title: CR 702.4a–702.4b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 702. Casting Spells
(continues 702.4: Every cost of playing a card is paid before the card is put on the stack. No player can respond to the payment, or between a cost and the effect it pays for.)
702.4c A unit sacrificed to pay a cost is gone before the card is played, so it does not see that card being played.
 Example: Ravenous Fireslinger sacrificed to pay for Sacrificial Burst does not trigger on it.
702.4d A cost cannot be paid with something that does not exist yet: not with units the effect itself would create, and not with a unit played by the same effect, which is on the stack and not in play.
 Example: Volatile Toxicity played by Tides of the Cosmos cannot sacrifice a Towering Colossus played by the same Tides.
title: CR 702.4c–702.4d

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 702. Casting Spells
(continues 702.4: Every cost of playing a card is paid before the card is put on the stack. No player can respond to the payment, or between a cost and the effect it pays for.)
702.4e A card played during another effect's resolution pays its bracketed additional cost exactly as if it were played from a hand.
 Example: a Trench Stalker played through Hooba-Pon discards two cards.
title: CR 702.4e

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 702. Casting Spells
702.5 A printed square bracket in a card's text is either an additional cost or a choice of modes. The owner of the effect pays that cost or chooses that mode, when the effect is played or put on the stack, and at no other time. See rules 205, 111.
title: CR 702.5

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 702. Casting Spells
(continues 702.5: A printed square bracket in a card's text is either an additional cost or a choice of modes. The owner of the effect pays that cost or chooses that mode, when the effect is played or put on the stack, and at no other…)
702.5a A payment an effect's text asks for without brackets, such as "unless its controller pays [x]", is not a cost of playing. It is made while the effect resolves, by the player the text names (rule 704.1). See rule 704.1.
title: CR 702.5a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 702. Casting Spells
702.6 X is chosen when the card is played, before it is put on the stack. Only values the player can pay may be chosen, and responses see the X already fixed. When X counts targets ("X target units"), all X targets are required: only an X that many legal targets can fill may be chosen, and at X = 0 the card needs no target. See rule 107.
 Example: Blight's End ("Augment a Wight onto X target units") with one unit in the battle offers X of 0 or 1, and at X = 1 it must take that unit.
 Example: Blight's End cast for X = 2 with two units asks for both and never offers a stop after one.
 Example: Torrential Reclamation ("Recall X target nontoken allies") with no ally in the fight can be cast only for X = 0.
702.6a If a card says X can't be zero, X must be at least 1. A player with less open mana than the smallest legal X cannot play the card.
title: CR 702.6–702.6a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 702. Casting Spells
(continues 702.6: X is chosen when the card is played, before it is put on the stack. Only values the player can pay may be chosen, and responses see the X already fixed. When X counts targets ("X target units"), all X targets are…)
702.6b A variable additional cost sets X. The player adds to it one unit at a time until they stop, and the amount they stop at is X. A variable life cost is then lost all at once, as one loss of X life (see rule 112.1a).
 Example: a player removes two +1/+1 counters for Discharge, one at a time, then stops; X is 2 and Discharge deals 2 damage.
 Example: Every variable life cost in the pool is lost as one change of X.
title: CR 702.6b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 702. Casting Spells
(continues 702.6: X is chosen when the card is played, before it is put on the stack. Only values the player can pay may be chosen, and responses see the X already fixed. When X counts targets ("X target units"), all X targets are…)
702.6c An X spell released for free by a fulfilled prophecy is cast with X = 0. A variable bracketed cost on it is still collected. See rule 803.
 Example: a fulfilled prophecy releases an X spell; no X is asked, X is 0 and no mana is paid.
title: CR 702.6c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 702. Casting Spells
702.7 A spell token is cast from play, and only in the region the token is in. Otherwise it is cast the same way as a spell from the hand. See rule 304.
 Example: In the attack window the defending player casts their Fireball 3 token in the battle region. They choose its target, the attacking player, and it goes on the stack, where the attacker may respond; when both pass it deals 3.
title: CR 702.7

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 702. Casting Spells
(continues 702.7: A spell token is cast from play, and only in the region the token is in. Otherwise it is cast the same way as a spell from the hand.)
702.7a A modifier to the cost of playing spells applies to casting a spell token, and a spell token cast counts as a spell played. See rule 111.
 Example: Tranquility makes a spell token cost [1] more in battle.
title: CR 702.7a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 702. Casting Spells
(continues 702.7: A spell token is cast from play, and only in the region the token is in. Otherwise it is cast the same way as a spell from the hand.)
702.7b A spell token with Burst is cast together with all of its controller's spell tokens of the same name in the same region as it. They are still separate spells. See rules 803, 703.4.
 Example: A player with two Fireballs in the battle region casts one; both go on the stack. A Fireball the same player has in another region is not cast.
title: CR 702.7b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 702. Casting Spells
702.8 A card or ability that needs targets can be played only if every target it requires can be chosen at the same time, each one legal and different from the others. Every target is required unless the card says "up to" or "any number". A triggered ability's targets are required in the same way: if a legal target exists, it must take one, even one of its controller's own units. A triggered ability whose "you may" governs its target ("you may recall target ally") offers the decline at the time its targets are chosen: its controller chooses a target or declines, and a declined ability does nothing. Once it has one target, every other target it needs is required. Choosing a target is choosing to use it, so no second "you may" is asked as it resolves; a payment its text asks for is still asked then (see rule 111.9). See rule 110.
 Example: Fight cannot be played unless the region holds an ally and another unit.
 Example: Tidal Reversion cannot be played while one player has no unit to recall.
 Example: Unstable Singularity ("When I die, Delete target unit.") dies in deployment with only its controller's other unit on the board: its trigger must target that unit, with no option to choose none, and deletes it.
 Example: Shoreline Specter ("After combat, you may recall target ally. If you do, each opponent loses 2 life.") offers the decline beside its allies as its trigger goes on the stack. Declined, nothing is recalled and no opponent loses life.
 Example: Shoreline Specter given a target recalls that ally and each opponent loses 2 life, with no further question as it resolves.
 Example: Chombot ("You may move up to two counters from target unit onto another target unit") may be declined before its first target; once one is chosen, the second is required.
702.8a A card that targets nothing has no target requirement.
 Example: Rebalance can be played by a player with no unit.
702.8b A triggered graft composite whose targeted part has no legal target is not put on the stack at all, and its untargeted parts do not happen either. See rules 722, 706.
 Example: Megadeath grafted with Resurrect, and no unit of cost 2 or less in the bin: no Poison 5 is made.
 Example: Megadeath with Resurrect grafted, and no unit of cost 2 or less in the bin: the composite never reaches the stack.
 Example: With a cost 2 unit in the bin, the composite goes on the stack.
title: CR 702.8–702.8b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 703. The Stack and Priority
703.1 The stack is "first in, last out". A new effect is put on top of the effects already there. When it is time to resolve, the top effect resolves first, so the effect put on last resolves first.
 Example: Mycelial Mentor is played with Bloomcaster out. Bloomcaster's trigger goes on the stack above the Mentor, so its 1/1 is made before the Mentor arrives and the Mentor never sees it.
703.1a An effect put on the stack does not resolve immediately. This gives the other players in the region a chance to respond to it.
 Example: Luminous Arc is cast at a unit; the unit is undamaged while the Arc waits on the stack, and the other player may respond.
703.1b New effects can be added on top of the stack after it has started resolving, between the resolutions of the effects on it.
 Example: two Luminous Arcs are on the stack; after the top one resolves, a third Arc is cast and resolves before the one still waiting.
703.1c A triggered ability put on the stack can be responded to like any other effect. See rule 706.
 Example: Xenopod Progenitor's trigger is negated on the stack, and its controller is never asked to pay its [1].
title: CR 703.1–703.1c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 703. The Stack and Priority
703.2 Priority is the ability to take game actions such as playing cards or activating abilities. A player with priority can take such actions; a player without priority cannot.
 Example: In the attack window only the initiative player, who holds priority, may play a card; the other player cannot until they receive priority.
703.2a A player who uses priority to take an action may keep priority and take further actions. Each action goes on the stack as an effect; none of them happens immediately. See rules D2.9, 703.7.
 Example: A player casts a spell and keeps priority, then casts a second spell on top of it before the opponent can respond. When the player passes, the opponent receives priority.
 Example: A player who keeps priority and then passes hands the window over, and the items wait for both players to pass.
703.2b When a player passes priority after taking one or more actions, each other player receives priority, so that they can respond. This continues until all players pass priority in succession.
 Example: after a cast the other player receives priority and responds; the first player then receives priority again, and the top item resolves only after both pass in succession.
703.2c A player cannot respond to another player passing priority. A player who passes may not get another chance to act.
 Example: the defender passes on an Arc and the attacker passes; the Arc resolves at once, with no further chance for the defender.
703.2d All players on a team share priority and can act in whichever order they choose among themselves. Teams pass and receive priority as one. See rule 904.
title: CR 703.2–703.2d

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 703. The Stack and Priority
703.3 A priority window is a sequence in which the players (or teams) each receive priority in order.
 Example: in an empty attack window the initiative player receives priority, then the other player; when both have passed the step ends.
703.3a In a priority window the initiative player receives priority first. If they decline to act, priority passes clockwise to the next non-initiative player in the region. If the initiative player is not in the region, priority begins with the player nearest to the initiative player, clockwise. See rules 508, 903.
 Example: the defender casts a spell, which resolves; the new window opens with the initiative player, not the caster.
703.3b In each region, the attack step, the block step and the after combat step each have a priority window. The combat damage step has a priority window only between its sub-steps, and only when Swift or Sluggish units split it (rule 608). See rules 604, 605, 607, 608, 609.
703.3c When all players pass priority in succession with an effect on the stack, the top effect resolves. All players then receive priority in order again, which is a new priority window. When all players pass priority with the stack empty, the game moves to the next step.
 Example: two passes resolve Luminous Arc; a new window opens in the same step with the initiative player; two passes on the empty stack end the step.
title: CR 703.3–703.3c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 703. The Stack and Priority
703.4 When several effects are put on the stack at the same time, each player chooses the order of their own. The initiative player puts all of theirs on first, then the non-initiative player, so the non-initiative player's effects resolve first. See rule 706.
 Example: with one trigger per player, the initiative player's trigger is at the bottom of the stack.
703.4a Cards played by one effect at the same time are separate effects, put on the stack at the same time in an order their controller chooses.
title: CR 703.4–703.4a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 703. The Stack and Priority
(continues 703.4: When several effects are put on the stack at the same time, each player chooses the order of their own. The initiative player puts all of theirs on first, then the non-initiative player, so the non-initiative player's…)
703.4b A Burst group of spell tokens goes on the stack all at once. Its caster chooses the order, one token at a time, and aims each; the token chosen first resolves first. The other players receive priority only when the whole group is on the stack. See rule 803.
 Example: the first Fireball picked ends on top of the stack.
title: CR 703.4b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 703. The Stack and Priority
703.5 A card played during another effect's resolution waits on the stack until that resolution has finished. Only then do players receive priority, and they may respond to the played card before it resolves. See rule 701.4.
 Example: a card Tides of the Cosmos plays for free can be answered on the stack.
 Example: A unit Wake the Dead plays waits on the stack until Wake the Dead has finished resolving, and can be answered before it resolves.
title: CR 703.5

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 703. The Stack and Priority
703.6 Once an effect has begun to resolve, no player can respond to it. It can no longer be targeted, negated or augmented.
 Example: while Premonition is resolving, the other player is offered nothing, it is not a legal target, and a negation or a Virus aimed at it is refused.
title: CR 703.6

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 703. The Stack and Priority
703.7 Deployment uses the stack, but each player has a stack of their own there, which only that player sees; no other player can respond to it or is made to wait on it. No player holds priority in deployment: a player cannot keep priority there or respond to an item on their own deployment stack. Otherwise that stack works exactly as the battle stack does: a player's plays, activated abilities and spell tokens go on it, an ability triggered by an item goes on it above that item and resolves first, and it resolves on its own, top first. See rule 507.
 Example: In deployment a player plays a deploy-timing spell at their Earthbound Replicator; the spell goes on that player's own stack, so the Replicator can copy it.
 Example: In deployment a player asks to keep priority as they play a card. The ask is refused: nobody can hold priority there.
 Example: In deployment a player activates Lilbot and sacrifices Seer of Empty Spaces to pay for it. Seer's death trigger goes on the stack above Lilbot's ability and resolves first, as it would in battle.
title: CR 703.7

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 703. The Stack and Priority
703.8 There is no priority in the haste step. Haste cards are played there as special actions. See rule 504.
 Example: Molten Upheaval played in the haste step makes its Fireball at once; no one has priority and nothing waits on a stack.
title: CR 703.8

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 703. The Stack and Priority
703.9 During battle, a region where only one player is present has its own stack too (rule 601.2a), and nobody holds priority over it. An item put on that stack resolves on its own, top first, with no priority window, and the battle's priority window is not changed by it. See rules 601, 703.7.
 Example: Molten Riftbreaker dies in its controller's home region during a battle elsewhere. Its trigger resolves there on its own, and does not reach the spell on the battle region's stack.
title: CR 703.9

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 704. Resolution and Fizzling
704.1 When an effect resolves, its instructions are carried out in the order printed, and a later instruction sees the results of an earlier one. The exception is target legality: it is judged once, as the effect begins to resolve (rule 704.5), so an earlier instruction cannot make a later instruction's target illegal. See rule 704.5.
 Example: Finality ("Negate all other effects. Erase all cards in bins.") erases the cards it has just negated, because they are in bins by its second sentence.
 [Verification of 704.1 was only partial.]
704.1a Choices an effect makes that are not targets (how to divide damage among a player's units, which card to discard, whether to pay an optional amount inside the effect) are made while it resolves. See rule 702.5.
 Example: Xenopod Progenitor's trigger goes on the stack with no payment asked; its [1] is asked as it resolves.
title: CR 704.1–704.1a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 704. Resolution and Fizzling
(continues 704.1: When an effect resolves, its instructions are carried out in the order printed, and a later instruction sees the results of an earlier one. The exception is target legality: it is judged once, as the effect begins to…)
704.1b No priority window opens around a payment or choice made while an effect resolves.
 Example: while Premonition asks its controller which card to cache, the other player has no action; the choice made, Premonition finishes without any pass.
title: CR 704.1b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 704. Resolution and Fizzling
704.2 When a spell resolves it goes to its controller's bin. When a spell unit resolves it enters play as a unit instead. See rule 405.
 Example: a resolved Luminous Arc is in its controller’s bin; a resolved Jelly is in play as a unit.
title: CR 704.2

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 704. Resolution and Fizzling
(continues 704.2: When a spell resolves it goes to its controller's bin. When a spell unit resolves it enters play as a unit instead.)
704.2a A card that goes to a bin from the stack is not trashed. See rule 801.
 Example: two Luminous Arcs reach the bin from the stack, one resolved and one fizzled; neither is trashed.
title: CR 704.2a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 704. Resolution and Fizzling
(continues 704.2: When a spell resolves it goes to its controller's bin. When a spell unit resolves it enters play as a unit instead.)
704.2b A spell token never goes to a bin; it is erased. See rule 304.
title: CR 704.2b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 704. Resolution and Fizzling
(continues 704.2: When a spell resolves it goes to its controller's bin. When a spell unit resolves it enters play as a unit instead.)
704.2c A spell that is Unstable, or that carries a Virus applied to it on the stack, is erased instead of going to a bin, whether it resolves, fizzles or is negated. See rule 723.
 Example: a spell played from the bin under Abyssal Evocation is Unstable, so it is erased and not put back in the bin.
 Example: a spell played from the bin under Abyssal Evocation that fizzles is erased too.
704.2d A copy of a spell has no card. When it resolves or leaves the stack, nothing goes to a bin. See rule 710.
 Example: a resolved copy of Suspend bins nothing, and its "Erase me." erases nothing.
title: CR 704.2c–704.2d

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 704. Resolution and Fizzling
704.3 A spell unit's spell effect happens first; if it resolves, the unit then enters play. If the spell unit is prevented from resolving (negated, or with its targets made invalid), the unit does not enter play and the card goes to the bin. See rule 303.
 Example: a spell unit played through Hooba-Pon has its spell part happen, then spawns into the formation.
title: CR 704.3

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 704. Resolution and Fizzling
704.4 A negated effect is removed from the stack at once, when the effect that negates it resolves. It does not resolve.
 Example: one mass negate removes all its victims from the stack together, with no extra priority rounds.
title: CR 704.4

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 704. Resolution and Fizzling
(continues 704.4: A negated effect is removed from the stack at once, when the effect that negates it resolves. It does not resolve.)
704.4a A negated spell, spell unit, unit, ambush or Virus goes to its controller's bin, and a negated Virus cannot be used as a Virus again. A negated spell token is erased. A negated triggered or activated ability just leaves the stack, because it has no card of its own.
704.4b A negated unit or spell unit never enters play.
title: CR 704.4a–704.4b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 704. Resolution and Fizzling
704.5 As an effect begins to resolve, each target it declared is checked again by the rule it was chosen under: its kind, its printed restriction, its region, and being different from the other targets. A target that fails the check is lost, exactly like a target that has left play. See rule 110.
 Example: an Ambush whose ally was stolen in response recalls nothing.
title: CR 704.5

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 704. Resolution and Fizzling
(continues 704.5: As an effect begins to resolve, each target it declared is checked again by the rule it was chosen under: its kind, its printed restriction, its region, and being different from the other targets. A target that fails…)
704.5a The check is made once, as the effect begins to resolve. An earlier part of the effect cannot make a later part's target illegal in the middle of its resolution.
 Example: Minor Kraken is grafted under a part that grows its target past 5 defense. The target was judged legal as the item began to resolve, so it is still recalled.
 Example: A target already past 5 defense when the item begins to resolve is still refused.
title: CR 704.5a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 704. Resolution and Fizzling
(continues 704.5: As an effect begins to resolve, each target it declared is checked again by the rule it was chosen under: its kind, its printed restriction, its region, and being different from the other targets. A target that fails…)
704.5b A target remains the same object while it stays where it is. A target that changes zone (to a hand, a bin, and so on) is gone, and the effect does not follow it to a new object. A target that stays put is still a legal target even if another effect also targets it. See rule 410.
 Example: Organic Exchange may target two of its controller's own units, and another spell aimed at one of them still resolves.
title: CR 704.5b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 704. Resolution and Fizzling
(continues 704.5: As an effect begins to resolve, each target it declared is checked again by the rule it was chosen under: its kind, its printed restriction, its region, and being different from the other targets. A target that fails…)
704.5c Several effects may target the same unit, even if together they would do more than destroying it takes. If an earlier one removes it, the later ones lose that target.
title: CR 704.5c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 704. Resolution and Fizzling
(continues 704.5: As an effect begins to resolve, each target it declared is checked again by the rule it was chosen under: its kind, its printed restriction, its region, and being different from the other targets. A target that fails…)
704.5d Changing an effect's targets before it resolves can save it from fizzling. See rule 110.
title: CR 704.5d

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 704. Resolution and Fizzling
704.6 An effect fizzles if, as it resolves, it has lost all of its targets. A fizzled effect does nothing, and a fizzled spell goes to the bin. See rule 110.
 Example: Arc Lightning’s only target dies before it resolves; Arc Lightning fizzles, deals no damage and goes to the bin.
704.6a When an effect fizzles, none of it happens, including parts of it that had no target.
 Example: Spewing Mushroom carries the grafts Biotoxicity ("create three Poison 1") and Technological Superiority, which targets the Mushroom itself. The Mushroom attacks, and the opponent deletes it with Leaping Lillik before its trigger resolves. Its only target is gone, so the whole trigger fizzles: not even Biotoxicity's Poisons are made.
704.6b If an effect has lost some but not all of its targets, it resolves as best it can against those that remain, untargeted parts included.
 Example: Tidal Reversion still recalls the other unit when one of its targets is removed.
 Example: Twin Flame loses one of its two targets before it resolves; the remaining target still takes its 2 damage.
 Example: Spewing Mushroom carries Biotoxicity and two Technological Superiority grafts; when it attacks, the two targeted parts aim at the Mushroom and at an enemy 1/1. The 1/1 dies before the trigger resolves. One target remains, so it still resolves: all four Poison tokens are made.
704.6c An effect that needs two of its targets together (a fight or an exchange) does nothing if it loses one of them. It does not fizzle.
 Example: Fight that loses one of its two targets does nothing to the survivor.
 Example: Organic Exchange that loses one of its two targets exchanges nothing; the survivor stays with its controller.
title: CR 704.6–704.6c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 704. Resolution and Fizzling
(continues 704.6: An effect fizzles if, as it resolves, it has lost all of its targets. A fizzled effect does nothing, and a fizzled spell goes to the bin.)
704.6d An effect that has no targeting part anywhere cannot fizzle. Nor can a part whose target was optional ("up to") and was left empty: declaring no target was a legal choice, and the rest of the effect still happens. See rule 704.6g.
title: CR 704.6d

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 704. Resolution and Fizzling
(continues 704.6: An effect fizzles if, as it resolves, it has lost all of its targets. A fizzled effect does nothing, and a fizzled spell goes to the bin.)
704.6e An ambush is a targeted effect. If its target is removed, the ambush fizzles and the ambushing unit is put into the bin. See rule 803.
 Example: the ally targeted by Lurking Slimebeast’s ambush dies; the ambush fizzles and Slimebeast goes to the bin.
704.6f A Virus whose target has become invalid when it resolves is put into the bin, and cannot be used as a Virus again. See rule 723.
 Example: a Virus’s host dies before the Virus resolves; the Virus goes to the bin and is not offered as a Virus from there.
title: CR 704.6e–704.6f

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 704. Resolution and Fizzling
(continues 704.6: An effect fizzles if, as it resolves, it has lost all of its targets. A fizzled effect does nothing, and a fizzled spell goes to the bin.)
704.6g An effect with a required target that never had a legal candidate fizzles, although it declared no target. See rule 704.6d.
title: CR 704.6g

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 704. Resolution and Fizzling
704.7 An effect stays on the stack, and still resolves, if its source leaves play. See rule 714.
704.7a Where such an effect reads its source (its attributes, power, defense, or the formation it stood in), it uses the source's last-known state: what the source was at the moment it left play. See rule 714.
 Example: Bellowing Boulder dies with its ping on the stack; the ping is still Deadly, from its last state.
704.7b An effect that acts on its source itself, or that says "if I am still in formation", does nothing if the source is gone. See rule 714.
 Example: Hooba-Nan dies with its attack trigger on the stack; the trigger creates no 1/1s.
title: CR 704.7–704.7b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 705. Activated Abilities
705.1 An activated ability is written with a colon (":"). Everything before the colon is the cost of activating the ability; everything after it is the effect the ability has. See rule 109.2.
 Example: Glook's "[once] Discard X cards: Glimpse 1, X times" — discarding X cards is the cost, and glimpsing X times is the effect.
title: CR 705.1

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 705. Activated Abilities
705.2 An activated ability may print a timing icon of its own. An ability marked {Battle} can be activated only during battle, and one marked {Deployment} only during deployment. The icon is checked when the ability is activated. See rules 109.2a, 109.2b.
 Example: Grox's ability is marked {Battle}, so it cannot be activated during deployment.
 Example: Cadaverous Cultivator's {Battle} ability is refused when activated outside battle, rather than doing nothing when it resolves.
title: CR 705.2

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 705. Activated Abilities
705.3 To activate an ability, the player takes the steps below, in order. Everything is chosen and paid before the ability is put on the stack, so no player can respond between the payment of its cost and the ability going on the stack. See rules 111.7, 703.
705.3a Step 1: the game checks that the ability can be activated: its timing allows it, any printed condition on it ("Activate this ability only if …") is met, every part of its cost can be paid, and every target it requires has a legal choice. If any check fails, the ability cannot be activated and nothing is paid. See rules 111.6a, 111.7b.
 Example: Instrument of Reassignment costs [x] and "sacrifice another nontoken unit". With only a token beside it, it cannot be activated, and the 3 open mana are not spent either.
705.3b Step 2: if the cost has a variable part (a printed [x], "Discard X cards", "Sacrifice X units"), the player pays it, one at a time, until they stop. The amount paid is X. See rules 111.7, 702.6b.
 Example: Celestial Shifter's "[x]" is paid while activating, so the opponent sees X before deciding whether to respond.
705.3c Step 3: the player declares the ability's targets. See rule 110.
 Example: Slag Spewer's target is declared before its mod is erased to pay the cost.
705.3d Step 4: the player pays the rest of the cost: its mana, including any tax on activating abilities (rule 111.10f), and any life, debt, sacrifice or other fixed part. See rules 111.7, 111.10f.
 Example: Auric Ascendant's "Recall another ally" is paid before the ability is on the stack, so the opponent already knows which ally left.
705.3e Step 5: the ability is put on the stack as an effect, and players receive priority as rule 703 describes. See rule 703.
 Example: Infernal Cultivator's sacrificed units are gone while the ability waits on the stack, so negating it refunds nothing.
title: CR 705.3–705.3e

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 705. Activated Abilities
705.4 If a part of an ability's cost names something that is not there to pay with (no other ally to recall, no mod to erase), the ability cannot be activated. Nothing is paid, and a [once] on the ability is not used. See rules 111.6, 109.9b.
 Example: Auric Ascendant with no other ally cannot be activated, so its [one] is not paid and its [once] is kept.
title: CR 705.4

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 705. Activated Abilities
705.5 An activated ability that a mod gives its host is an ability of the host. The host's controller activates it, and "I" and "me" in it mean the host. See rule 720.
 Example: Living Forge augmented onto another unit lets that unit's controller activate "[three]: create a Robot 2" through the mod.
 Example: Aurozoa's "[Augment] Pay 1 life: Recall me" recalls the host when Aurozoa is a mod.
title: CR 705.5

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 7. Spells, Abilities and Effects › 705. Activated Abilities
