802.9a An Unaware card's own power and defense are always the ones printed on it, for every purpose, including whether it has died. Counters, temporary changes, continuous effects and the other stat attributes do not change them. See rules 206.4, 713.
 Example: A +1/+1 counter on Bubb (5/6, Unaware) leaves it a 5/6.
 Example: Bubb survives 100 -1/-1 counters.
 Example: Tough donated onto Bubb does nothing.
 Example: Reconfigure moves Bubb onto a Robot token, which gains Unaware: it ignores its own +1/+1 counters and dies as a 0/0.
title: CR 802.9–802.9a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.9: Unaware is an attribute. An Unaware card, and every card interacting with it, ignores all stat changes: each is read at the stats printed on it.)
802.9b Setting a unit's base stats is a stat change too. An Unaware unit whose base stats an effect sets is still read at its printed stats. See rule 206.5.
 Example: Aberrant Statweaver ("your units are base 3/3") leaves Bubb a 5/6.
title: CR 802.9b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.9: Unaware is an attribute. An Unaware card, and every card interacting with it, ignores all stat changes: each is read at the stats printed on it.)
802.9c When an Unaware card deals damage or is dealt damage, every card in that interaction is read at its printed stats: the other card as well as the Unaware one. See rule 112.6.
 Example: Unaware Bubb squishing a Robot 10 kills it: the Robot is read as its printed 0/0.
 Example: A Robot 10 squishing Unaware Bubb deals its printed defense, 0.
 Example: Two units fight: Bubb reads a Robot 7 as a 0/0 and kills it.
title: CR 802.9c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.9: Unaware is an attribute. An Unaware card, and every card interacting with it, ignores all stat changes: each is read at the stats printed on it.)
802.9d In combat, the interaction is the exchange between an attacking half-column and the half-column blocking it. If a unit on either side is Unaware, every unit on both sides deals and is dealt combat damage at its printed stats. See rules 608.5c, 608.6e.
 Example: Bubb blocks a 3/3 pumped to 5/5 and takes 3, the attacker's printed power.
802.9e A unit dealt damage in such an interaction is destroyed if the damage is lethal for its printed defense, even if the stats it has outside the interaction would let it survive. See rule 713.
 Example: Bubb blocking a Robot token kills it, however many +1/+1 counters it has.
 Example: Haboob's 1 damage kills any unit with a printed defense of 1.
802.9f Outside such an interaction, an Unaware card does not change the stats of the other cards.
802.9g A spell can be Unaware. A spell has no stats of its own, so its Unaware only makes the cards it deals damage to be read at their printed stats. See rule 302.
 Example: Haboob (an Unaware spell) deals 1 damage to each unit and kills every unit with a printed defense of 1.
title: CR 802.9d–802.9g

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.9: Unaware is an attribute. An Unaware card, and every card interacting with it, ignores all stat changes: each is read at the stats printed on it.)
802.9h Unaware does not stop a card being targeted. An effect can put counters or other stat changes on an Unaware card; they stay on it but do not change its stats while it is Unaware. See rule 110.
 Example: Poison with X = 6, targeting Bubb (a 5/6, Unaware), puts six -1/-1 counters on it; Bubb is still a 5/6.
 Example: A Robot 10 may Squish Unaware Bubb, targeting Bubb. The Robot, interacting with Unaware Bubb, is read at its printed 0/0, so it deals 0 and Bubb takes no harm.
title: CR 802.9h

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
802.10 Powerful. Powerful is a combat attribute. Its reminder text reads "Powerful sources deal double damage".
 Example: When Chitin Shredder (1/2, Powerful) is the source of 3 damage from an effect, 6 is dealt; attacking unblocked, it costs the defending player 2 life.
802.10a A Powerful half-column's combat damage is doubled once, as a whole, before it is divided among its recipients, whether they are units or a player. A unit without Powerful in a Powerful column has its damage doubled along with the rest (see rule 608.5b). See rule 608.5b.
 Example: Chitin Shredder (Powerful) deals double combat damage to a player.
 Example: A vanilla unit in front of Chitin Shredder has its damage doubled too.
802.10b If a modifier that adds to the damage also applies, the addition is made first and Powerful doubles the result (see rule 112.9). See rule 112.9.
 Example: A Powerful Bellowing Boulder's 1 damage with Conduit of Pain is (1+1)x2 = 4 to each unit.
802.10c Powerful also doubles damage its source deals through spells and abilities, to units and players alike. See rule 112.9.
802.10d A spell can have Powerful. Damage a Powerful spell deals is doubled. See rule 302.
 Example: With Emberflame Enlightener in its region, a player's spell deals double damage.
802.10e When a spell makes a unit deal damage, as Squish, Fight and Battle do, the unit is the source: the unit's own Powerful, including Powerful it shares from its column, applies, and Powerful on the spell does not (see rule 112.6). See rule 112.6.
 Example: Squish makes a Powerful ally deal double its defense.
 Example: A Powerful Squish does not double.
 Example: Squish on a 1/3 that shares Powerful from Chitin Shredder in its column deals 6.
802.10f Powerful does not apply in an interaction with a Pure card (see rule 802.25). See rule 802.25.
title: CR 802.10–802.10f

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
802.11 Vulnerable. Vulnerable is an attribute. A Vulnerable unit is dealt double the damage that would be dealt to it.
 Example: Crumbling Ancient (Vulnerable) is dealt double the combat damage assigned to it.
802.11a Because the damage is doubled when it is dealt, lethal damage for a Vulnerable unit, when assigning, is half its remaining defense, rounded up (see rule 608.6e). See rule 608.6e.
 Example: Arc Lightning (6 damage, Electric) on a Vulnerable 3/8: 4 of the 6 destroy it, and the other 2 may jump on.
 Example: A 10-power Piercing column blocked by a Vulnerable 3/7 assigns it 4 (half of 7, rounded up), and 6 go through.
 Example: A Vulnerable 3/8 with 2 damage marked needs 3, so a 10-power Piercing column sends 7 through.
802.11b Damage assigned to a Vulnerable unit counts as that much of the source's damage; the unit is then dealt double that amount. Any damage the source keeps on a Vulnerable unit, including the rest of a column's damage, is doubled on that unit. See rules 608.6d, 608.7.
 Example: A Piercing attacker may put all 10 of its damage into a lone Vulnerable 3/8, which is dealt 20.
802.11c Piercing excess past a Vulnerable unit is measured in the source's damage before the doubling: only the source damage beyond what the unit needs is excess (see rule 802.16). See rule 802.16.
 Example: A 10-power Piercing column blocked by a Vulnerable 3/8 assigns 4 to it, and 6 goes to the player.
title: CR 802.11–802.11c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.11: Vulnerable is an attribute. A Vulnerable unit is dealt double the damage that would be dealt to it.)
802.11d If a Powerful source deals damage to a Vulnerable unit, both apply: the source's damage is doubled, and the unit is dealt double that. See rule 112.9.
title: CR 802.11d

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.11: Vulnerable is an attribute. A Vulnerable unit is dealt double the damage that would be dealt to it.)
802.11e A Pure Vulnerable unit, and a Vulnerable unit in an interaction with a Pure card, is not dealt double damage. See rule 802.25.
 Example: Chitin Shredder (Powerful), made Pure, deals 2 damage to Crumbling Ancient (Vulnerable, 3/8). It is dealt 2: neither Powerful nor Vulnerable doubles it, and the Ancient survives.
 Example: Crumbling Ancient (Vulnerable) made Pure is dealt 2 by a 2-damage effect, not 4.
 Example: A Pure, Vulnerable Oorblak takes a redirected hit from a column that is not Pure. It is dealt the damage once, not doubled.
title: CR 802.11e

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
802.12 Feeble. Feeble is an attribute. A Feeble unit can't block.
 Example: Spectrogenesis creates three Wisps (Feeble); none of them can block.
title: CR 802.12

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.12: Feeble is an attribute. A Feeble unit can't block.)
802.12a Whether a unit can block depends on its own Feeble only. A Feeble unit can't block even if it shares a column with units that are not Feeble, and Feeble that a unit would share from its column does not stop it blocking. See rules 802.1, 606.2.
title: CR 802.12a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.12: Feeble is an attribute. A Feeble unit can't block.)
802.12b A Pure unit that is Feeble can block: Pure makes it ignore its own Feeble (see rule 802.25). See rule 802.25.
 Example: Just a Unit (Pure) granted Feeble can still be declared as a blocker.
title: CR 802.12b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.12: Feeble is an attribute. A Feeble unit can't block.)
802.12c A Feeble unit is not able to block, so an Alluring trigger that targets it cannot compel it to block (see rules 606.2e and 802.15). See rules 606.2e, 802.15.
title: CR 802.12c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
802.13 Evasive. Evasive is an attribute. Its reminder text, printed under the type line, reads "Evasive units require two blockers." See rules 802.1, 606.2c.
802.13a A column with Evasive cannot be blocked by a single unit. To block it, the defending player must place two units in front of it. See rules 606.2c, 602.
 Example: An Evasive Curio Drifter attacks. The defender may block it with two units placed in front of it, one behind the other, but not with one.
title: CR 802.13–802.13a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.13: Evasive is an attribute. Its reminder text, printed under the type line, reads "Evasive units require two blockers.")
802.13b Evasive does not apply if either the Evasive column or the units blocking it include a Pure card. A single Pure unit can block an Evasive column on its own (see rule 802.25). See rule 802.25.
 Example: Just a Unit (Pure) blocks an Evasive column by itself.
title: CR 802.13b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
802.14 Sneaky. Sneaky is an attribute. Its reminder text, printed under the type line, reads "Sneaky units can't be blocked if attacking alone." See rules 802.1, 606.2c.
title: CR 802.14

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.14: Sneaky is an attribute. Its reminder text, printed under the type line, reads "Sneaky units can't be blocked if attacking alone.")
802.14a An attacking column with Sneaky cannot be blocked if its unit is the only attacking unit in the attacking formation. Whether it is alone is judged when blocks are declared: if the other attacking units have left play by then, it cannot be blocked. See rule 606.
 Example: Whispering Mantid attacks alone and cannot be blocked. Attacking with another unit, it can be.
 Example: Whispering Mantid attacks beside Lonely Forager, and the Forager is sacrificed before blocks: the Mantid is now attacking alone and cannot be blocked.
title: CR 802.14a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.14: Sneaky is an attribute. Its reminder text, printed under the type line, reads "Sneaky units can't be blocked if attacking alone.")
802.14b Spell tokens that go with an attack do not count as attacking units for Sneaky. A Sneaky unit attacking with only spell tokens beside it is attacking alone. See rule 604.2c.
 Example: A Sneaky unit attacks together with two Fireball spell tokens. It is still attacking alone and cannot be blocked.
802.14c Two Sneaky units attacking together are not alone. Both can be blocked.
 Example: Two Whispering Mantids attack in different columns. The defender may block either or both.
802.14d A side-block does not block a lone Sneaky attacker. The defending player may side-block beside it, and it stays unblocked (see rule 606.4e). See rule 606.4e.
802.14e A Pure unit ignores Sneaky, so it can block a lone Sneaky attacker (see rule 802.25). See rule 802.25.
 Example: A lone Sneaky unit attacks. The defender can block it with Just a Unit (Pure), and with no other unit.
title: CR 802.14b–802.14e

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
802.15 Alluring. Alluring is an attribute. Its reminder text, printed under the type line, reads "When an alluring column attacks, target enemy can't attack and must block it this combat if able." See rules 802.1, 604.2e, 606.2e.
802.15a When an attacking column with Alluring is declared, Alluring triggers. The trigger goes on the stack and targets one enemy unit, chosen by the attacking player from the enemy units in the battle region as the trigger is put on the stack. See rules 706, 110.
 Example: Two attacking columns, one Alluring, against one possible blocker: the Alluring trigger targets that blocker, which then must block the Alluring column.
802.15b Alluring does not stack. An attacking column with Alluring has one Alluring trigger, however many of its units have Alluring.
 Example: Two Alluring units attack in one column. Alluring triggers once.
802.15c Each attacking column with Alluring has its own trigger. Two Alluring columns make two triggers, which may target the same unit or different units.
 Example: Two Alluring columns attack. Each triggers, and both triggers may target the same defending unit.
 Example: Two Alluring columns target two different units. Each of those units must block its column.
802.15d Alluring is shared by the units of its column, but the column's Alluring trigger comes from the unit that has Alluring itself, not from the units it is shared with. See rule 802.1.
 Example: Tempest Wrangler attacks in a column with a vanilla unit. The trigger is Tempest Wrangler's.
802.15e When the Alluring trigger resolves, its target cannot attack: it cannot be declared as an attacker or sent to counterattack for the rest of the battle phase (see rule 604.2e). See rules 604.2e, 610.
 Example: A lured unit cannot be sent out to counterattack when blocks are declared.
title: CR 802.15–802.15e

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.15: Alluring is an attribute. Its reminder text, printed under the type line, reads "When an alluring column attacks, target enemy can't attack and must block it this combat if able.")
802.15f When the Alluring trigger resolves, its target must block the Alluring column in that battle round if it is able to. If the column is blocked at all, the target must be one of its blockers (see rule 606.2e). See rule 606.2e.
 Example: The defender has two units able to block and tries to leave the Alluring column unblocked by putting both on other columns. That is not allowed: the lured unit must block the Alluring column.
802.15g Whether the target is able to block the Alluring column depends only on that unit and that column. If the target could not block the column by itself (because the column is Evasive and needs two blockers, the target is Feeble, the column has Flying and the target does not, or the column is a lone Sneaky attacker), the defending player may leave the column unblocked, and the target may block another column. See rules 606.2b, 802.13.
 Example: A lone lured unit cannot block an Alluring and Evasive column by itself, so it need not block it, and it may block another column.
802.15h An Alluring and Evasive column can be blocked only by two units, one of which is the target. The defending player chooses between blocking it with the target and one other unit, and not blocking it at all; blocking it with two other units is not allowed. See rule 802.13.
 Example: The target is A and the defender also has B and C. A+B and A+C may block the column; B+C may not.
 Example: The defender has only A and B. They block the column with A+B, or leave it unblocked.
title: CR 802.15f–802.15h

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.15: Alluring is an attribute. Its reminder text, printed under the type line, reads "When an alluring column attacks, target enemy can't attack and must block it this combat if able.")
802.15i If, when the Alluring trigger would resolve, the unit with Alluring is no longer in an attacking column, or its column no longer has Alluring, the trigger does nothing.
 Example: The attacker's Alluring unit is killed while its trigger is on the stack. The trigger does nothing, and the targeted unit may attack and block freely.
802.15j Once the Alluring trigger has resolved, removing the unit with Alluring does not undo it: its target still cannot attack. If the Alluring column ceases to exist, the duty to block it ends with it.
 Example: After the trigger resolves, the Alluring attacker is killed in the attack window. The lured unit may block another column, but it still cannot be sent to counterattack.
802.15k If two Alluring triggers have targeted the same unit, it cannot block both columns. Blocking either of those columns with it satisfies both triggers, and the other column may then be blocked by other units or left unblocked.
 Example: Two Alluring columns both target unit A. A blocks the first column. The second column may be blocked by B alone, or left unblocked.
802.15m An Alluring trigger from a lone Sneaky attacker compels no unit, because no unit is able to block that attacker (see rule 802.14), unless its target is Pure. See rule 802.14.
 Example: A lone Sneaky and Alluring unit attacks. The defender declares no blocks, and that is legal.
802.15n An Alluring column that contains a Pure card does not trigger at all (see rule 802.25). See rule 802.25.
 Example: An Alluring column with Just a Unit in it attacks. No Alluring trigger is put on the stack.
802.15p A Pure unit ignores the attributes that would stop it blocking, so a Pure target is able to block any Alluring column: it must block even a Flying Alluring column, and it satisfies an Evasive Alluring column by itself. See rule 802.25.
 Example: A lured Pure unit must block a Flying Alluring column.
 Example: A lured Pure unit blocks an Evasive Alluring column alone.
title: CR 802.15i–802.15p

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.15: Alluring is an attribute. Its reminder text, printed under the type line, reads "When an alluring column attacks, target enemy can't attack and must block it this combat if able.")
802.15q The Alluring trigger is a triggered ability. It can be negated while it is on the stack, and an effect that makes triggered abilities cost more to trigger (Crevice Lurker) applies to it: if that cost is not paid, the trigger does not happen. See rules 111.10f, 706.
 Example: Crevice Lurker is in play. The attacker declines to pay for the Alluring trigger, and nothing is lured.
 Example: Containment Protocol negates a waiting Alluring trigger.
title: CR 802.15q

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
802.16 Piercing. Piercing is an attribute. Its reminder text reads "Excess damage from piercing sources is dealt to the recipient's controller." See rules 802.1, 608.
802.16a Excess damage, for Piercing, is the damage a source deals to a unit beyond that unit's lethal damage. A unit's lethal damage is worked out after Powerful has doubled the source's damage; it is reduced for a Vulnerable unit, which is dealt double what reaches it; it is 1 if the source has Deadly; and damage already dealt to the unit counts towards it, including damage dealt to it earlier by the same effect (see rule 608.6e). See rules 608.6e, 802.3, 802.10, 802.11.
 Example: A Powerful Piercing source deals 3 to a 1/1. The 3 is doubled to 6; 1 is lethal; 5 is excess.
 Example: A 10-power Piercing column is blocked by a Vulnerable 3/8. Lethal damage is 4, which is dealt as 8; the other 6 is excess.
 Example: One effect names the same unit twice with Piercing. The unit is given its lethal damage once, and the rest of both hits is excess.
802.16b A half-column with Piercing that deals combat damage to the units of the opposing half-column must assign lethal damage to each of those units, front to back. Any of its damage that is not assigned to a unit is dealt to the player who controls those units. See rules 608.6, 608.8.
 Example: A Piercing column with 10 power is blocked by a 1/2 in front of a 1/3. It must assign 2 to the front unit and 3 to the back unit; the other 5 may be dealt to the defending player.
802.16c Excess is elective. After each unit has been assigned its lethal damage, the dealing player may assign any part of the remaining damage to those units, including all of it, and only the damage no unit is assigned is dealt to the player. See rule 608.6c.
 Example: A 10-power Piercing attacker is blocked by a lone Vulnerable 3/8. The attacker may put all 10 into it (dealt as 20), and none reaches the player.
802.16d An unblocked attacking half-column with Piercing deals its combat damage to the defending player, as any unblocked half-column does. See rule 608.4a.
title: CR 802.16–802.16d

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.16: Piercing is an attribute. Its reminder text reads "Excess damage from piercing sources is dealt to the recipient's controller.")
802.16e If an attacking half-column with Piercing is blocked but no blocking unit is left in front of it when it strikes, all of its damage is excess and is dealt to the defending player. A blocked half-column without Piercing deals no damage in that case (see rule 608.4c). See rules 608.4c, 606.3a.
 Example: A Piercing column's only blocker dies before damage. The column is still blocked, and its full power is dealt to the defending player.
 Example: The same position without Piercing deals nothing to the player.
802.16f A blocking half-column with Piercing deals excess combat damage to the attacking player only if there is an attacking unit in front of it when it strikes. If no attacking unit is in front of it (its attackers are all gone, or it is a side-block), it deals no combat damage at all (see rules 608.4e and 608.4f). See rules 608.4e, 608.4f.
 Example: A Piercing side-blocker deals no combat damage to the attacking player.
802.16g If the Piercing source also has Deadly, lethal damage is 1 for each unit, so all damage beyond 1 for each unit may be excess. See rule 802.3.
 Example: A Deadly and Piercing column is blocked by two units. It assigns 1 to each, and the rest may go to the player.
 Example: A 10-power Deadly and Piercing column is blocked by one unit: 1 kills it and the other 9 may pierce.
802.16h Damage prevention on a unit does not change how much must be assigned to it before there is excess. Excess is worked out as though the unit were unprotected. See rules 608.6g, 708.
 Example: A Piercing column is blocked by a shielded 0/5 in front of a 5/6. It must assign 5 to the shielded unit and 6 to the unit behind; the rest may go to the player.
title: CR 802.16e–802.16h

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.16: Piercing is an attribute. Its reminder text reads "Excess damage from piercing sources is dealt to the recipient's controller.")
802.16i Piercing excess is dealt as part of the same damage as the rest, at the same time. It is not a triggered ability, and no player can act between the damage dealt to the units and the excess dealt to the player.
 Example: A Piercing effect deals 5 to a 1/1. The unit's 1 and the 4 to its controller are dealt together, with nothing on the stack in between.
title: CR 802.16i

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.16: Piercing is an attribute. Its reminder text reads "Excess damage from piercing sources is dealt to the recipient's controller.")
802.16j Piercing applies to noncombat damage too. A Piercing source that deals noncombat damage to a unit must deal that unit its lethal damage first. The dealing player may then keep any of the excess on that unit; the rest of the excess is dealt to that unit's controller. See rule 112.7.
 Example: Squish makes Bubb, in a column with Good Whale (Piercing), deal 6 to a 1/1. The dealing player may keep all 6 on the 1/1, or send up to 5 to its controller.
title: CR 802.16j

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.16: Piercing is an attribute. Its reminder text reads "Excess damage from piercing sources is dealt to the recipient's controller.")
802.16k For noncombat damage, the dealing player is the controller of the source unit, even if another player controls the spell that made it deal damage (for Squish, Fight and Battle the unit is the source; see rule 112.6). If the source is not a unit in play (a spell, or a unit that has left play), the controller of the effect decides. See rule 112.6.
 Example: A Battle makes an opponent's Piercing unit fight. The opponent, who controls that unit, places its excess.
title: CR 802.16k

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.16: Piercing is an attribute. Its reminder text reads "Excess damage from piercing sources is dealt to the recipient's controller.")
802.16m Each unit's excess is dealt to that unit's controller. If one effect deals Piercing damage to units controlled by different players, each player is dealt the excess from their own units.
802.16n A unit in a column with a Piercing unit has Piercing while that column exists, for the noncombat damage it deals as well as for combat damage (see rule 802.1). See rule 802.1.
 Example: Bubb, in a column with Good Whale, squishes with Piercing: the excess reaches the player.
802.16p If Piercing combat damage that would be dealt to a player is dealt to a unit instead (as Oorblak's ability does), that unit is dealt its lethal damage and the rest is still Piercing excess. That excess is still combat damage that would be dealt to the player: another such effect that has not applied (a second Oorblak) may take it, the same one may not, and what none takes is dealt to the player (see rule 608.8c). See rule 608.8c.
 Example: 10 Piercing combat damage is redirected into a 2/4 Oorblak. 4 kill it and the other 6 reach the player.
 Example: 5 Piercing combat damage is redirected into Oorblak on a 1/1 host. 1 kills the host and the remaining 4 reach the player.
 Example: 10 Piercing combat damage and two 2/4 Oorblaks: each takes 4 and dies, and 2 reach the player.
title: CR 802.16m–802.16p

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.16: Piercing is an attribute. Its reminder text reads "Excess damage from piercing sources is dealt to the recipient's controller.")
802.16q If a source has both Electric and Piercing, excess that reaches a unit with no further unit to jump to is Piercing excess: the dealing player may keep any of it on that unit, and the rest is dealt to that unit's controller (see rule 802.17). See rule 802.17.
 Example: A 6-damage Electric and Piercing hit lands on a lone 1/2 with no neighbour. The dealing player chooses how much of the 4 excess stays on it; the rest goes to its controller.
title: CR 802.16q

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.16: Piercing is an attribute. Its reminder text reads "Excess damage from piercing sources is dealt to the recipient's controller.")
802.16r Piercing does not apply in an interaction involving a Pure card (see rule 802.25). See rule 802.25.
 Example: A 6-power Piercing column is blocked by Just a Unit (Pure). All 6 are dealt to Just a Unit; none reaches the defending player.
title: CR 802.16r

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
802.17 Electric. Electric is an attribute. Its reminder text reads "Excess damage from electric sources can be directed to an adjacent unit, recursively." It applies to combat damage as it does to damage from effects: the excess combat damage an Electric unit deals to a unit may jump on too. See rule 802.1.
 [The online client currently plays 802.17 differently; a fix is filed.]
802.17a When an Electric source deals a unit more than its lethal damage, the excess may be dealt to a unit adjacent to that unit instead. The unit the excess jumps to is dealt the lethal damage it needs, and any excess beyond that may jump again, to a unit adjacent to it. See rules 603.2, 802.16.
 Example: Arc Lightning (6, Electric) hits a Vulnerable 3/8. 4 kill it (dealt as 8), and the other 2 may jump to an adjacent unit.
title: CR 802.17–802.17a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.17: Electric is an attribute. Its reminder text reads "Excess damage from electric sources can be directed to an adjacent unit, recursively." It applies to combat damage as it does to damage from effects: the excess combat…)
802.17b The excess never jumps to a unit it has already been dealt to in that chain.
802.17c The Electric source's controller chooses where the excess goes at each jump.
 Example: A Fight makes the opponent's Electric unit the source. Its controller, not the caster, chooses where the excess goes.
 Example: The source's controller's answer steers the excess onto the chosen neighbour.
title: CR 802.17b–802.17c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.17: Electric is an attribute. Its reminder text reads "Excess damage from electric sources can be directed to an adjacent unit, recursively." It applies to combat damage as it does to damage from effects: the excess combat…)
802.17d Each jump is optional. At any jump, the source's controller may instead keep all the remaining excess on the unit it has reached; it is then all dealt to that unit and goes no further. This is so even when there is only one unit to jump to.
 Example: Arc Lightning hits a Vulnerable 3/8 with a unit beside it. Its controller keeps all 6 on the 3/8 (dealt as 12), and nothing jumps.
802.17e Excess that has no unit to jump to is dealt to the last unit it reached; it is not lost. If the source also has Piercing, that excess is Piercing excess instead (see rule 802.16). See rule 802.16q.
 Example: Arc Lightning hits a lone Vulnerable 3/8 with nothing beside it. All 6 land on it, dealt as 12.
802.17f Adjacency for Electric is adjacency in a formation (see rule 603.2). A unit that is not in a formation has no adjacent unit, so Electric excess dealt to it has nowhere to jump. See rule 603.2b.
 Example: During the deployment phase no unit is in a formation, so an Electric spell's excess stays on the unit it hit.
title: CR 802.17d–802.17f

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.17: Electric is an attribute. Its reminder text reads "Excess damage from electric sources can be directed to an adjacent unit, recursively." It applies to combat damage as it does to damage from effects: the excess combat…)
802.17g The whole Electric chain is part of one damage event. No formation changes happen while the excess is distributed. See rule 112.8.
 Example: An Electric chain of three units is dealt in one damage event; the units it kills die together afterwards.
title: CR 802.17g

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.17: Electric is an attribute. Its reminder text reads "Excess damage from electric sources can be directed to an adjacent unit, recursively." It applies to combat damage as it does to damage from effects: the excess combat…)
802.17h Lethal damage along the chain is worked out as it is for Piercing (see rule 802.16): a Vulnerable unit needs only half, and damage already dealt to it by the same effect counts. See rule 802.16a.
802.17i Envoy of Lightning makes "your spell effects with a single target" Electric. A spell effect has a single target if it was cast with exactly one target.
 Example: Twin Flame cast with one target under Envoy of Lightning is Electric.
802.17j A spell effect cast with two targets does not have a single target, even if one of its targets has become illegal by the time it resolves. See rule 110.
 Example: Twin Flame is cast with two targets and one is removed. It is not Electric under Envoy of Lightning.
title: CR 802.17h–802.17j

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
802.18 Poisonous. Poisonous is an attribute. Its reminder text reads "Poisonous sources damage units in the form of -1/-1 counters." See rule 802.1.
802.18a Damage a Poisonous source deals to a unit is put on that unit as that many -1/-1 counters instead of being marked on it. See rule 112.5.
 Example: Noxious Sporefiend deals 2 combat damage to a unit; the unit gets two -1/-1 counters and no marked damage.
802.18b Poisonous damage is damage dealt. Abilities that trigger when a unit is dealt damage trigger on it (see rule 112.10). See rule 112.10.
title: CR 802.18–802.18b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.18: Poisonous is an attribute. Its reminder text reads "Poisonous sources damage units in the form of -1/-1 counters.")
802.18c For damage assignment and for Piercing, a unit's lethal damage is the same whether the source is Poisonous or not. See rules 802.16a, 608.6e.
 Example: A Poisonous and Piercing effect deals 5 to a 1/1. One counter is lethal, and the other 4 may pierce.
802.18d A source with both Deadly and Poisonous destroys the unit it damages and also puts the -1/-1 counters on it. See rule 802.3.
 Example: Deadly and Poisonous damage kills the unit, and the -1/-1 counter lands on it before it dies.
802.18e Powerful doubles a Poisonous source's damage, and so doubles the -1/-1 counters it puts on a unit. See rule 802.10.
 Example: A Powerful Poisonous effect hit of 2 becomes 4 counters and kills a 4/3.
title: CR 802.18c–802.18e

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.18: Poisonous is an attribute. Its reminder text reads "Poisonous sources damage units in the form of -1/-1 counters.")
802.18f If a Poisonous source's damage to a unit is prevented, no damage is dealt and no -1/-1 counters are put on it. See rules 112.11, 708.
 Example: Sporebloom Siren (2/2, Poisonous) attacks; the defender casts Phytochemical Protection on Jollyglop and blocks with it. The 2 damage is prevented: Jollyglop gets no -1/-1 counters and makes no 1/1s, and Phytochemical Protection puts two +1/+1 counters on it.
802.18g Poisonous changes only damage dealt to units. Damage a Poisonous source deals to a player is ordinary damage.
 Example: An unblocked Poisonous column with 3 power makes the defending player lose 3 life.
title: CR 802.18f–802.18g

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.18: Poisonous is an attribute. Its reminder text reads "Poisonous sources damage units in the form of -1/-1 counters.")
802.18h Poisonous damage triggers Resonant like any other damage (see rule 802.19). See rule 802.19.
 Example: A Poisonous and Resonant source deals 2 to a unit. The unit gets two -1/-1 counters, and the Resonant trigger deals 2 to its controller.
title: CR 802.18h

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.18: Poisonous is an attribute. Its reminder text reads "Poisonous sources damage units in the form of -1/-1 counters.")
802.18i Poisonous does not apply in an interaction involving a Pure card (see rule 802.25). See rule 802.25.
 Example: A Poisonous column is blocked by Just a Unit. Just a Unit is dealt ordinary marked damage, not -1/-1 counters.
802.18j The -1/-1 counters a Poisonous source's combat damage puts on a unit are put by that source's controller (see rule 708.8b). See rule 708.8b.
 Example: A Poisonous blocker deals combat damage to the attacker: its -1/-1 counters on the attacker are put by the defending player, so the defender's Wandering Blightshell ("When you put a counter on an enemy, [Switch1] Draw a card.") draws a card.
 Example: A Poisonous attacker's -1/-1 counters on its blocker are put by the attacking player, and the attacker's Wandering Blightshell draws.
title: CR 802.18i–802.18j

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
802.19 Resonant. Resonant is an attribute. Its reminder text, printed under the type line, reads "Whenever a resonant source deals damage to a unit, it deals that much damage to that unit's controller." See rule 802.1.
 Example: Resonant Form's combat damage to a unit also hits that unit's controller.
802.19a Resonant is a triggered ability of the Resonant source. When the source deals damage to a unit, the trigger goes on the stack, and when it resolves the source deals that much damage to that unit's controller. See rule 706.
 Example: The Resonant trigger from combat damage waits on the stack after combat, as its source's trigger, and can be negated.
 Example: A Resonant effect deals 1 to a unit; the trigger then deals 1 to its controller as damage from the source.
802.19b The damage Resonant deals to the controller is not combat damage, even when the damage that triggered it was (see rule 608.8b). See rules 608.8b, 112.7.
 Example: Oorblak, which takes combat damage that would be dealt to its controller, does not take Resonant's extra damage; the player does.
title: CR 802.19–802.19b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.19: Resonant is an attribute. Its reminder text, printed under the type line, reads "Whenever a resonant source deals damage to a unit, it deals that much damage to that unit's controller.")
802.19c "That much damage" is the damage the unit was dealt: after Vulnerable doubled it and after any prevention. If all of the damage to the unit is prevented, Resonant does not trigger. See rules 802.11, 112.11.
 Example: A Resonant source deals 2 to a Vulnerable unit, which is dealt 4. The Resonant trigger deals 4 to that unit's controller.
title: CR 802.19c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.19: Resonant is an attribute. Its reminder text, printed under the type line, reads "Whenever a resonant source deals damage to a unit, it deals that much damage to that unit's controller.")
802.19d Resonant's damage is damage from the Resonant source, so everything that changes that source's damage applies to it: an allied Conduit of Pain adds 1 to it, and Powerful doubles it, even though the damage that triggered it was already doubled. See rules 802.10, 112.9.
 Example: A Powerful Resonant 2/4 deals 4 combat damage to a unit, and then 8 to that unit's controller.
 Example: With Conduit of Pain, a Resonant 2/4 deals 2 combat damage to a unit and then 3 to its controller.
802.19e When both apply to Resonant's damage, an added amount (Conduit of Pain's 1) is added before Powerful doubles (see rule 112.9). See rule 112.9.
 Example: A Powerful Resonant 2/4 with Conduit of Pain deals 4 combat damage, then (4+1)x2 = 10 to the controller.
802.19f Resonant triggers for each unit the source deals damage to. An effect that damages several units makes one Resonant trigger for each damaged unit.
 Example: A Resonant, Powerful Bellowing Boulder with Conduit of Pain deals 4 to each unit, then 10 to a controller for each damaged unit.
802.19g Resonant triggers only on damage dealt to a unit. Damage a Resonant source deals to a player does not trigger it.
 Example: An unblocked Resonant column deals 3 combat damage to the defending player. Resonant does not trigger.
802.19h Because Resonant is a triggered ability, an effect that makes triggered abilities cost more to trigger (Crevice Lurker) applies to it, and if that cost is not paid the trigger does not happen. It can be negated while it is on the stack. See rule 111.10f.
title: CR 802.19d–802.19h

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.19: Resonant is an attribute. Its reminder text, printed under the type line, reads "Whenever a resonant source deals damage to a unit, it deals that much damage to that unit's controller.")
802.19i A Resonant trigger caused by combat damage is put on the stack and resolved as other triggers caused by combat damage are (see rules 608 and 609). See rule 609.
802.19j If the Resonant source has left play by the time its trigger resolves, the trigger still deals its damage, reading the source as it last was in play. See rule 714.
 Example: A Powerful Resonant unit deals 1 to a unit, which is dealt 2, and then leaves play with its Resonant trigger waiting. The trigger still deals double damage, 4, because the unit was Powerful when it left play.
title: CR 802.19i–802.19j

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.19: Resonant is an attribute. Its reminder text, printed under the type line, reads "Whenever a resonant source deals damage to a unit, it deals that much damage to that unit's controller.")
802.19k Resonant does not apply in an interaction involving a Pure card (see rule 802.25). See rule 802.25.
 Example: A Resonant column is blocked by Just a Unit. No Resonant trigger happens for the damage dealt to Just a Unit.
title: CR 802.19k

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
802.20 Thieving. Thieving is an attribute. Its reminder text, printed under the type line, reads "Whenever a thieving source deals combat damage to an opponent, draw a card." See rule 802.1.
802.20a When a column with Thieving deals combat damage to an opponent, the column's controller draws a card.
 Example: Slink attacks unblocked and deals combat damage to the defending player. Its controller draws a card.
title: CR 802.20–802.20a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.20: Thieving is an attribute. Its reminder text, printed under the type line, reads "Whenever a thieving source deals combat damage to an opponent, draw a card.")
802.20b The column is the source of the combat damage, so a Thieving column draws one card each time it deals combat damage to an opponent, however many Thieving units it holds and however much damage it deals.
 Example: Two Thieving units in one column deal combat damage to a player. Their controller draws one card.
title: CR 802.20b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.20: Thieving is an attribute. Its reminder text, printed under the type line, reads "Whenever a thieving source deals combat damage to an opponent, draw a card.")
802.20c Piercing excess counts: a blocked Thieving column whose Piercing excess is dealt to the opponent draws a card. See rule 802.16.
 Example: A Thieving and Piercing column is blocked by a 1/1 and deals 3 of excess to the defending player. Its controller draws a card.
802.20d If combat damage a Thieving column deals to an opponent is replaced by an effect that still deals it to that player (for example, Blightsea Polyp, which deals it as rot), the damage was still dealt, and the column's controller still draws a card (see rule 608.8a). If all of it is redirected to a unit instead (Oorblak), the column dealt the opponent nothing and draws no card (see rule 608.8c). See rules 608.8a, 112.12.
 Example: Blightsea Polyp turns a Thieving column's combat damage to the defending player into 1 rot. The attacker still draws a card.
 Example: A Thieving column's combat damage is all redirected into Oorblak. Its controller draws no card.
802.20e Thieving applies only to combat damage. Noncombat damage a Thieving source deals to an opponent does not draw a card.
 Example: A Thieving unit deals 2 noncombat damage to an opponent. No card is drawn.
title: CR 802.20c–802.20e

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
802.21 Reaping. Reaping is an attribute. Its reminder text, printed under the type line, reads "When a reaping source kills one or more units, draw a card. It loses reaping until regroup." See rule 802.1.
802.21a When a Reaping source kills one or more units, its controller draws one card, however many units it killed.
 Example: Flame of History kills a unit and its controller draws a card.
 Example: Seismomancy kills a unit by damage and draws exactly once.
802.21b A unit counts as killed by a Reaping source however the source killed it: by damage, by -1/-1 counters, by changing its stats, or by destroying it outright.
 Example: Invasive Reassignment swaps a 0/4 into a 4/0, which dies. Reaping draws a card.
 Example: Noxious Demise kills a 1/1 with a -1/-1 counter. Reaping draws a card.
802.21c After a Reaping source's kill has drawn a card, the source loses Reaping until regroup.
 Example: If a unit had Reaping and killed a blocker in the first battle round, it would draw a card and then have no Reaping in the second round.
 [The online client currently plays 802.21c differently; a fix is filed.]
title: CR 802.21–802.21c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
802.22 Blessed. Blessed is an attribute. Its reminder text reads "Damage dealt by a blessed source causes its controller to gain that much life." See rule 802.1.
 Example: Godray deals 3 damage to any target, and Blessed gains its controller 3.
802.22a When a Blessed source deals damage, its controller gains that much life. This applies to combat and noncombat damage, and to damage dealt to units and to players.
title: CR 802.22–802.22a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.22: Blessed is an attribute. Its reminder text reads "Damage dealt by a blessed source causes its controller to gain that much life.")
802.22b The life is gained at the same time as the damage is dealt. It is not a triggered ability and does not use the stack, and it is gained before it is checked whether any player has reached 0 life.
 Example: A player at low life is dealt lethal damage by an opponent at the same moment their own Blessed source deals damage. They gain the life first, and survive if it is enough.
802.22c A Blessed source cannot kill its own controller with its own damage: damage it deals to its own controller is matched by the life that player gains at the same time.
 Example: Godray aimed at a player damages them and heals its controller on the same check.
802.22d Blessed applies only to damage dealt. A kill without damage, and damage that is prevented, gain no life. See rule 112.11.
 Example: Noxious Demise carrying a Blessed Thing virus kills a unit with a -1/-1 counter. No life is gained.
802.22e A unit in a column with a Blessed unit has Blessed while that column exists, so damage its abilities deal gains its controller life too (see rule 802.1). See rule 802.1.
 Example: Lithoghul attacks in a column with Flzzz (Blessed) and uses an ability to deal 3 damage. Lithoghul has Blessed from its column, so its controller gains 3 life.
title: CR 802.22b–802.22e

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.22: Blessed is an attribute. Its reminder text reads "Damage dealt by a blessed source causes its controller to gain that much life.")
802.22f Blessed does not apply in an interaction involving a Pure card (see rule 802.25). See rule 802.25.
title: CR 802.22f

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
802.23 Afflicting. Afflicting is an attribute. Its reminder text reads "When an afflicting source kills one or more units, those units' controllers gain a rot." See rules 802.1, 112.13.
802.23a When an Afflicting source kills one or more units, each player who controlled one of those units gains one rot.
 Example: Umbral Decay kills a unit with its counters. That unit's controller gains a rot.
 Example: Umbral Decay's target survives, shrunk. Nobody gains a rot.
title: CR 802.23–802.23a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.23: Afflicting is an attribute. Its reminder text reads "When an afflicting source kills one or more units, those units' controllers gain a rot.")
802.23b A player gains one rot for each kill, however many of their units the source killed at once.
 Example: An Afflicting source kills two units of one player at once. That player gains one rot.
802.23c A unit counts as killed by an Afflicting source however the source killed it: by damage, by -1/-1 counters, by changing its stats, or by destroying it outright.
 Example: Umbral Decay's counter kill gives a rot and draws nothing.
title: CR 802.23b–802.23c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.23: Afflicting is an attribute. Its reminder text reads "When an afflicting source kills one or more units, those units' controllers gain a rot.")
802.23d Afflicting applies to kills by combat damage as well. An Afflicting column that kills units in combat gives their controllers rot.
802.23e Afflicting does not apply in an interaction involving a Pure card (see rule 802.25). See rule 802.25.
 Example: An Afflicting column kills Just a Unit (Pure) in combat. Its controller gains no rot.
title: CR 802.23d–802.23e

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
802.24 Lethal. Lethal is an attribute. Its reminder text reads "Any combat damage from a lethal unit will kill a player." See rule 802.1.
802.24a If a column with Lethal deals any combat damage to a player, however little, that player is killed (see rule 104). See rule 104.1.
 Example: Gublin (1/4) attacks unblocked and deals 1 combat damage to the defending player, who is killed.
802.24b Lethal applies only to combat damage dealt to a player. It does not change noncombat damage, or damage dealt to units.
 Example: A Lethal unit blocked by a 2/2 kills it as any unit would; Lethal does nothing to the blocker.
802.24c If a Lethal column's combat damage to a player is replaced by an effect that still deals it to that player (Blightsea Polyp, which deals it as rot), the damage was still dealt, so the player is still killed. If it is all dealt to a unit instead (Oorblak), the player was dealt nothing and is not killed; Piercing excess that gets past and is dealt to the player kills. See rules 608.8a, 112.12.
 Example: Blightsea Polyp turns a Lethal column's combat damage into 1 rot. The player is still killed.
 Example: A Lethal column's combat damage is all redirected into Oorblak. The player is not killed.
 Example: Piercing Lethal damage beyond Oorblak's lethal damage gets past and reaches the player, who is killed.
 Example: Oorblak and Blightsea Polyp together: the redirect takes it all, so the Polyp sees nothing and no one is killed.
title: CR 802.24–802.24c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.24: Lethal is an attribute. Its reminder text reads "Any combat damage from a lethal unit will kill a player.")
802.24d [Removed: no source states how Lethal meets prevention of damage to a player, and no card in the pool prevents damage to a player; the owner ruling of 2026-08-23 on prevented damage is about damage to units. See D-U20-22.]
title: CR 802.24d

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
802.25 Pure. Pure is an attribute. Its reminder text reads "Pure cards and cards they are interacting with ignore all other attributes." See rule 802.1.
802.25a A Pure card ignores its own other attributes too. Its own stat-changing attributes, Tough, Balanced, Inverted and Unaware, do not apply to it at any time, whether or not it is in an interaction. Nor do its other attributes apply when its column strikes a player: an unblocked Pure column has no Swift, Sluggish, Powerful, Thieving, Lethal or Blessed. See rule 802.12.
 Example: An Alluring column that is itself Pure ignores its own Alluring and never triggers.
 Example: A Pure unit that is also Feeble can block.
 Example: A Pure Rampart Guardian (0/4, Tough) that is in no interaction reads 0/4.
 Example: A Pure Child of Aether (2/0, Balanced) ignores its own Balanced, reads 2/0 and dies in the state check.
 Example: A Pure Bubb ignores its own Unaware, so the counters on it count.
 Example: An unblocked Pure column strikes in the normal sub-step and does not double or draw.
802.25b In combat, an interaction is one attacking half-column and the blocking half-column paired with it. An unblocked attacking half-column is an interaction too, with an empty blocking half, when it strikes the player. If either half contains a Pure card, the attributes of both are ignored for that exchange. See rule 608.4.
 Example: In an unblocked column with a Pure unit, a column-mate's attributes are off too.
802.25c In a combat exchange involving a Pure card, neither side has any of its other attributes: no Piercing, Deadly, Powerful, Poisonous, Resonant, Blessed, Afflicting, Thieving, Lethal, Electric or Reaping, and a Vulnerable unit in it is not dealt double. Neither side has Swift or Sluggish, so both strike in the normal sub-step (see rule 608.2d). This holds for an unblocked column striking the player too (rule 802.25b). See rules 608.2d, 608.6e.
 Example: Just a Unit switches off a Deadly attacker's Deadly.
 Example: A printed Swift column blocked by a Pure unit strikes in the normal sub-step.
 Example: Without Pure, Swift, Sluggish, Powerful, Thieving, Lethal and Blessed each change an unblocked strike on the player; with a Pure unit in the column, none of them does.
title: CR 802.25–802.25c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.25: Pure is an attribute. Its reminder text reads "Pure cards and cards they are interacting with ignore all other attributes.")
802.25d When blocks are declared, a Pure card in either the attacking column or the units blocking it switches off Flying, Evasive and the lone Sneaky attacker's protection for that column, and a Pure unit's own Feeble does not stop it blocking. See rules 802.2, 802.12, 802.13, 802.14.
 Example: Just a Unit can block a Flying column, and only it can among the defender's units.
 Example: Just a Unit blocks an Evasive column alone.
title: CR 802.25d

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.25: Pure is an attribute. Its reminder text reads "Pure cards and cards they are interacting with ignore all other attributes.")
802.25e Pure does not change a unit's printed stats: a Pure 2/3 is destroyed by 3 damage. But Tough, Balanced and Inverted are attributes, so in an interaction involving a Pure card they do not apply (rule 802.1n). See rules 802.6, 802.7, 802.8.
 Example: A Tough 0/4 blocks a column containing Just a Unit (Pure). Tough does not apply in that exchange, so the blocker has 4 defense, not 8.
802.25f Unaware is an attribute, so in combat it does not apply in an exchange involving a Pure card: the units in that exchange are read at their current stats, not their printed ones (rule 802.1n). See rule 802.9.
 Example: Bubb (Unaware) blocks a Pure 3/3 that has four +1/+1 counters. Unaware does not apply in that exchange, so the counters count: the 7/7 kills Bubb and survives.
title: CR 802.25e–802.25f

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.25: Pure is an attribute. Its reminder text reads "Pure cards and cards they are interacting with ignore all other attributes.")
802.25g Outside combat, an interaction is one effect and one recipient of its damage. Pure applies to each such pairing separately.
802.25h A Pure source deals plain damage to every recipient: its own Powerful, Deadly, Piercing, Electric, Poisonous, Resonant, Blessed and Unaware do not apply, against units or players.
802.25i A Pure recipient is dealt plain damage by any source: the source's attributes do not apply to it, and neither do its own other attributes, Vulnerable, Unaware, Tough, Balanced and Inverted included.
 Example: A Vulnerable unit that is itself Pure is dealt 2 by a 2-damage effect, not 4.
 Example: A plain source deals 5 to a Pure Rampart Guardian (0/4, Tough). Its own Tough does not apply, and it dies.
 Example: A Deadly column's combat damage is redirected into a Pure Oorblak. Deadly does not apply to it, so 2 damage does not kill it.
802.25j A recipient that is not Pure, damaged by the same effect as a Pure recipient, is dealt damage with all attributes applying.
 Example: A Powerful source deals 1 to Just a Unit and 1 to Bubb in one resolution: 1 to the first and 2 to the second.
802.25k During a battle, a unit in a column with a Pure unit has Pure for noncombat damage too, as a source and as a recipient (see rule 802.1). See rule 802.1.
 Example: A unit stands in a column with Just a Unit. A Powerful spell deals 1 damage to it: it is dealt 1, not 2.
802.25m Pure does not change what can be targeted. See rule 110.
 Example: Arc Lightning, which says "any target", can target Just a Unit like any other unit.
title: CR 802.25g–802.25m

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
802.26 Modular. Modular is an attribute. Its reminder text reads "You can apply mods to a modular card from your hand and/or bin as it is played. You still pay their costs." See rule 720.
802.26a As a Modular card is played, its controller may apply mods to it from their hand and from their bin, paying each mod's cost. The mods go onto the stack with the card (see rule 702.3b). See rule 702.3b.
title: CR 802.26–802.26a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.26: Modular is an attribute. Its reminder text reads "You can apply mods to a modular card from your hand and/or bin as it is played. You still pay their costs.")
802.26b Any card in the player's hand or bin whose cost they can pay may be applied to a Modular card, including a card that will do nothing as a mod there. No other condition restricts what may be applied.
title: CR 802.26b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.26: Modular is an attribute. Its reminder text reads "You can apply mods to a modular card from your hand and/or bin as it is played. You still pay their costs.")
802.26c Applying a mod to a Modular card is not playing that mod (see rule 701.2). See rule 701.2.
802.26d A graft mod applied to a Modular spell adds its graft effect to the spell as an extra part, and the spell and its grafted effects resolve as one. See rule 722.
title: CR 802.26c–802.26d

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.26: Modular is an attribute. Its reminder text reads "You can apply mods to a modular card from your hand and/or bin as it is played. You still pay their costs.")
802.26e A mod whose type line grants attributes as an augment gives those attributes to the Modular spell's effect. See rule 721.
 Example: A Powerful mod applied to Spellbind carrying Twin Flame turns its 2 damage into 4.
802.26f An augment mod's text-box ability does nothing on a Modular spell: a spell cannot gain static or triggered abilities that way.
title: CR 802.26e–802.26f

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.26: Modular is an attribute. Its reminder text reads "You can apply mods to a modular card from your hand and/or bin as it is played. You still pay their costs.")
802.26g A Modular card with a mod applied is modded, so it is Unstable: when it leaves the stack, whether it resolved, failed to resolve or was negated, it and its mods are erased instead of going to a bin. An unmodded Modular card goes to the bin as usual. See rules 803, 405.
 Example: A graft card in the bin is applied to Spellbind, resolves with it, and is erased, so it cannot be applied this way again.
title: CR 802.26g

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 802. Attributes
(continues 802.26: Modular is an attribute. Its reminder text reads "You can apply mods to a modular card from your hand and/or bin as it is played. You still pay their costs.")
802.26h Modular is not shared with the other units of a column. See rule 802.1.
 Example: A unit given Modular keeps it in a column, and its column-mate does not get it.
title: CR 802.26h

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 803. Other Keyword Abilities
803.1 Some keywords are not combat attributes. Burst and Unstable are printed in purple text and are called non-combat attributes: they describe a card, and generally have nothing to do with combat. The other keywords in this section (Haste, Battle, [once], Ambush and Prophecy) are timing marks, limits and ways to play a card. See rules 802, 720, 204.5.
 Example: A modded Chitin Shredder attacks in a column with a vanilla unit: the vanilla unit shares its Powerful, but it does not become Unstable.
803.1a Non-combat attributes are not shared in formation. A unit with Burst or Unstable does not give it to the other units in its column. See rules 712.8e, 802.1.
 Example: A modded unit is Unstable; a unit in the same column is not, and when it dies it goes to the bin.
title: CR 803.1–803.1a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 803. Other Keyword Abilities
803.2 Haste is a timing keyword. A card with Haste can be played during the haste step as well as during deployment. See rules 207.3, 504.
 Example: Tidal Menace, a {Haste} 7/2, can be played in the haste step.
803.2a Printed text that names the "mana step" means the haste step. See rule 504.1.
 Example: Dispatch Courier says "play a unit during the mana step as if it had [Haste]": its controller may play a unit in the haste step.
803.2b An effect can let a card without Haste be played in the haste step "as if it had [Haste]", as Dispatch Courier does. This changes only when the card may be played. See rules 504.7, 803.3a.
 Example: With Dispatch Courier in play, its controller can play a unit without Haste in the haste step, once each turn.
title: CR 803.2–803.2b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 803. Other Keyword Abilities
803.3 Battle is a timing keyword. A card with Battle can be played only while its player is in battle with another player. It cannot be played during deployment. See rules 207.4, 505.
803.3a Gaining Haste does not let a Battle card be played outside battle. A Battle unit or Battle spell unit that an effect lets be played "as if it had [Haste]" still cannot be played in the haste step. See rules 207.4a, 504.2a.
 Example: Dispatch Courier's grant does not let a {Battle} unit be played in the haste step.
 Example: Nor does Dispatch Courier let a {Battle} spell unit be played in the haste step.
803.3b A [Battle] icon printed in front of one ability or play mode, rather than as the card's timing, governs that line only. An activated ability marked [Battle] can be activated only during battle; an Ambush marked [Battle] can be played during battle even if the card itself has no Battle timing (803.6b). See rules 207.8, 203.5.
 Example: Grox's [Battle] ability cannot be activated outside battle.
title: CR 803.3–803.3b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 803. Other Keyword Abilities
803.4 [once] is a keyword that limits an ability: an ability marked [once] can be activated or triggered only once per turn, tracked for each card. Its rules are in 109.9. See rule 109.9.
 Example: Unstable Apparition's [once] trigger fires once in a turn and again the next turn.
title: CR 803.4

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 803. Other Keyword Abilities
803.5 Burst is a non-combat attribute printed on spell tokens. When a player casts a spell token with Burst, they cast every spell token of the same name that they control in that region at the same time. It is all or nothing. See rules 304.11g, 702.7b.
 Example: Casting one Fireball in the battle region casts every Fireball its controller has there.
title: CR 803.5

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 803. Other Keyword Abilities
(continues 803.5: Burst is a non-combat attribute printed on spell tokens. When a player casts a spell token with Burst, they cast every spell token of the same name that they control in that region at the same time. It is all or nothing.)
803.5a Spell tokens with different names are separate Burst groups. A player with a Poison and a Fireball may cast one, let it resolve, and then cast the other. See rule 304.11g.
 Example: Casting a Fireball casts the other Fireballs and leaves a Poison alone.
title: CR 803.5a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 803. Other Keyword Abilities
(continues 803.5: Burst is a non-combat attribute printed on spell tokens. When a player casts a spell token with Burst, they cast every spell token of the same name that they control in that region at the same time. It is all or nothing.)
803.5b Spell tokens cast together by Burst are still individual spells. They are played at the same time. See rule 304.11g.
 Example: Two Fireballs cast together go on the stack as two items, each with its own target.
title: CR 803.5b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 803. Other Keyword Abilities
(continues 803.5: Burst is a non-combat attribute printed on spell tokens. When a player casts a spell token with Burst, they cast every spell token of the same name that they control in that region at the same time. It is all or nothing.)
803.5c Each spell token in a Burst group chooses its own targets. The tokens do not have to share a target. See rule 110.
803.5d A Burst group goes on the stack all at once. Its caster chooses the order one token at a time, in the order the tokens will resolve, and aims each as it is chosen; the token chosen first resolves first. The other players receive priority only when the whole group is on the stack. A lone token is not ordered. See rule 703.4b.
 Example: The Fireball picked first ends on top of the stack.
title: CR 803.5c–803.5d

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 803. Other Keyword Abilities
803.6 Ambush is a keyword that lets a unit card be played during battle with the effect "Recall target ally, put me into their position in play." See rule 203.1.
 Example: Mirage Walker's Ambush recalls an ally and takes its formation slot.
803.6a An Ambush is paid for with the cost printed beside the keyword, not the card's own cost: that mana is spent and its affinity pips are required. See rules 203.2, 203.3.
 Example: Lurking Slimebeast's Ambush [3b] costs 3 mana and needs one water pip.
 Example: With four fire mana and no water pip, Lurking Slimebeast cannot be played as an Ambush [3b]; with one water and three fire it can, and exactly 3 mana is spent.
803.6b An Ambush can be played only during battle. The [Battle] icon in front of the keyword lets the card be played as an Ambush during battle even if the card itself has no Battle timing. See rules 203.5a, 803.3b.
 Example: Good Whale, a deploy-timing unit, is played as an Ambush in battle into the attacking column.
 Example: During deployment, Lurking Slimebeast can be played normally, but not as an Ambush.
803.6c The target of an Ambush must be an ally of the Ambush's controller in the battle region. An opponent's unit is never a legal target, even through an effect that redirects targets. See rule 110.
 Example: An Ambush can target the attacking ally, but not an enemy unit in the battle region, nor an ally that stayed home.
 Example: An opposing Enigmatic Warder tries to redirect an Ambush onto itself: the Ambush still recalls its own ally, and the Warder stays in play.
803.6d An Ambush is a targeted effect on the stack. Players can respond to it before it resolves. See rule 703.
 Example: The ally can be removed in response, and then the Ambush fizzles.
803.6e When an Ambush resolves, the target ally is recalled and the ambushing unit is put directly into the ally's position in play: into its formation slot if it was in formation, attacking or blocking, and otherwise into the battle region outside formation. See rules 801.7, 801.7a.
 Example: Orblish Horroth ambushing a blocker takes the blocker's formation slot.
 Example: Mirrorback Ambusher recalls an ally and takes its position.
title: CR 803.6–803.6e

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 803. Other Keyword Abilities
(continues 803.6: Ambush is a keyword that lets a unit card be played during battle with the effect "Recall target ally, put me into their position in play.")
803.6f If, as the Ambush resolves, its target is gone or is no longer an ally of the Ambush's controller, the Ambush fizzles: nothing is recalled, and the ambushing card is put into the bin. Its controller loses both units. See rules 704.6e, 405.2b.
 Example: An Ambush whose ally changed sides before it resolved recalls nothing.
803.6g Ambushing a unit that is the target of another effect saves it. The other effect does not change targets to the ambushing unit; it fails to resolve (fizzles). See rule 704.
 Example: A Fireball is aimed at a unit, and that unit's controller answers with an Ambush on it. The unit returns to its hand; the Fireball fizzles, and the ambusher takes no damage.
803.6h An Ambush on the stack is not a spell effect: the card played as an Ambush is a unit, not a spell. An effect that targets, negates or recalls spell effects cannot affect it, but one that names an effect, or a nonspell effect, can. A negated Ambush puts its ambushing card into the bin. See rules 700.1a, 704.4a.
 Example: Nothyr ("negate up to one target nonspell effect") can target an Ambush on the stack and negate it; the ambushing card goes to the bin.
 Example: Void Mandible negates an Ambush on the stack: the ambusher never takes the slot and its target is not recalled.
 Example: Dreadwave Devourer, which negates a target spell effect, cannot target an Ambush on the stack, and the Ambush resolves.
 Example: Cosmic Reversal ("Recall all other spell effects and spell units") recalls a spell on the stack and leaves an Ambush beside it, which then resolves.
title: CR 803.6f–803.6h

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 803. Other Keyword Abilities
(continues 803.6: Ambush is a keyword that lets a unit card be played during battle with the effect "Recall target ally, put me into their position in play.")
803.6i A card in the cache under a live permission can be played as an Ambush, as it could from the hand. Under a fulfilled prophecy it is free; under a glimpse its controller pays the Ambush mana but ignores the affinity. See rules 702.2d, 403.3c.
title: CR 803.6i

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 803. Other Keyword Abilities
(continues 803.6: Ambush is a keyword that lets a unit card be played during battle with the effect "Recall target ally, put me into their position in play.")
803.6j An effect that plays a card for free, such as Tides of the Cosmos, may play an Ambush card as an Ambush. The Ambush cost is not paid, and a limit on the card's cost reads its main cost, not its Ambush cost. See rule 701.2c.
 Example: Tides of the Cosmos plays Mirrorback Ambusher as an Ambush: the ally leaves play and the ambusher stands in its place.
 Example: With 3 of the Tides budget left, Lurking Slimebeast (main cost 4, Ambush 3) cannot be chosen, but Mirage Walker (main cost 3, Ambush 4) can, and playing it as an Ambush spends no mana.
title: CR 803.6j

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 803. Other Keyword Abilities
803.7 Prophecy is a keyword printed on a card's banner as a cost and a condition. A card with a Prophecy banner may be prophesied: its controller pays the banner's cost, and the card moves to the cache with its prophecy attached. See rules 203.4, 801.14, 403.
title: CR 803.7

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 803. Other Keyword Abilities
(continues 803.7: Prophecy is a keyword printed on a card's banner as a cost and a condition. A card with a Prophecy banner may be prophesied: its controller pays the banner's cost, and the card moves to the cache with its prophecy…)
803.7a An effect can give a card a prophecy as it caches the card. The prophecy works as a printed one does once the card is in the cache. See rule 403.
 Example: Grob caches a unit with 'One Battle Passes' attached, and the prophecy is fulfilled once a battle has passed.
title: CR 803.7a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 803. Other Keyword Abilities
(continues 803.7: Prophecy is a keyword printed on a card's banner as a cost and a condition. A card with a Prophecy banner may be prophesied: its controller pays the banner's cost, and the card moves to the cache with its prophecy…)
803.7b A card may be prophesied only during deployment. A card whose prophecy condition ends in a [Haste] icon may also be prophesied during the haste step. See rule 504.9.
title: CR 803.7b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 803. Other Keyword Abilities
(continues 803.7: Prophecy is a keyword printed on a card's banner as a cost and a condition. A card with a Prophecy banner may be prophesied: its controller pays the banner's cost, and the card moves to the cache with its prophecy…)
803.7c A card is prophesied from its controller's hand. It may be prophesied from the bin only if the card says so, and from the cache only while a glimpse permission on it is live; a card prophesied in the cache stays where it is. See rules 403.8, 801.9h.
title: CR 803.7c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 803. Other Keyword Abilities
(continues 803.7: Prophecy is a keyword printed on a card's banner as a cost and a condition. A card with a Prophecy banner may be prophesied: its controller pays the banner's cost, and the card moves to the cache with its prophecy…)
803.7d Prophesying costs the banner's cost: its mana is spent and its affinity pips are required. See rules 203.2, 111.12.
803.7e A prophecy's condition counts forward from the moment the card is prophesied. "Two Turns Pass" means two turns after the card was prophesied, not two turns of the game.
803.7f In a 1v1 game, both battles of a turn count toward "One Battle Passes". See rule 505.
 Example: A card prophesied with "One Battle Passes" in deployment, after that turn's two battle rounds, is fulfilled once the first battle round of the next turn is over.
803.7g Once a prophecy's condition has been met, the prophecy stays fulfilled, even if the state that met it goes away.
 Example: A card prophesied on "your life is 5 or less" stays playable after its controller gains life back.
803.7h Once the prophecy is fulfilled, the card may be played from the cache for free, ignoring affinity, as if it were in its controller's hand. See rules 403.3c, 111.13.
803.7i A fulfilled prophecy changes what the card costs, not when it may be played. The card is played at its own printed timing, and a [Haste] icon in the banner does not move the release. See rule 504.9a.
803.7j An X spell released by a fulfilled prophecy is cast with X = 0. A variable bracketed cost on it is a cost, not its X, and is still paid. See rule 702.6c.
803.7k A card whose prophecy is fulfilled may also be grafted or augmented from the cache, for free and ignoring affinity. Until the prophecy is fulfilled, the card cannot be played, grafted or augmented from the cache at all. See rules 403.3a, 403.3c, 720.
803.7m A condition that counts units dying, such as Vengeance's "13 Units Die", counts only the deaths its controller witnessed: deaths in a region where that player was present. A player is present in their own region, and in an enemy region once they have attacked into it, until regroup. See rules 601, 604.3a.
 Example: A player attacks into the opponent's region with a unit, so both players are present there. Two of the opponent's units die in that region: each player counts two deaths toward "Units Die".
title: CR 803.7d–803.7m

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 803. Other Keyword Abilities
(continues 803.7: Prophecy is a keyword printed on a card's banner as a cost and a condition. A card with a Prophecy banner may be prophesied: its controller pays the banner's cost, and the card moves to the cache with its prophecy…)
803.7n An effect that plays a card for free, such as Tides of the Cosmos, may play a card with a Prophecy banner as a Prophecy: the card is cached with its prophecy attached, and the banner cost is not paid. See rule 701.2c.
title: CR 803.7n

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 803. Other Keyword Abilities
803.8 Unstable is a non-combat attribute. If an Unstable card would enter a bin from an active zone (play or the stack), it is erased instead. See rules 405.5, 407, 803.8a.
 Example: Aberrant Statweaver, printed {Unstable}, dies into the erased pile, not the bin.
title: CR 803.8

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 803. Other Keyword Abilities
(continues 803.8: Unstable is a non-combat attribute. If an Unstable card would enter a bin from an active zone (play or the stack), it is erased instead.)
803.8a Unstable applies only to a card leaving an active zone. The active zones are play and the stack. An Unstable card that goes to a bin from a hand, the deck, a bin or the cache is put into the bin normally, and is trashed. See rules 400.2a, 405.5.
title: CR 803.8a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 803. Other Keyword Abilities
(continues 803.8: Unstable is a non-combat attribute. If an Unstable card would enter a bin from an active zone (play or the stack), it is erased instead.)
803.8b A card may print Unstable on its type line. Oorblak and Aberrant Statweaver do. See rule 204.
 Example: Oorblak, unmodded, is erased when it dies.
803.8c An effect may give a card Unstable. It is often given to cards played from the bin, so that they cannot be used more than once: Abyssal Evocation and Spell Excavation give the spells they let you play from the bin Unstable until regroup. See rule 405.9a.
 Example: A spell played from the bin under Abyssal Evocation is erased after it resolves, never re-binned.
 Example: A spell played under Spell Excavation is erased rather than re-binned.
title: CR 803.8b–803.8c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 803. Other Keyword Abilities
(continues 803.8: Unstable is a non-combat attribute. If an Unstable card would enter a bin from an active zone (play or the stack), it is erased instead.)
803.8d Unstable given "until regroup" lasts until regroup, even after the permission that came with it has ended. A spell unit played under such a grant passes it to the unit it puts into play. See rule 506.
 Example: A bin-played spell unit body is still Unstable in the second battle round, after the permission to play spells from the bin has ended, and stops being Unstable at regroup.
title: CR 803.8d

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 803. Other Keyword Abilities
