(continues 803.8: Unstable is a non-combat attribute. If an Unstable card would enter a bin from an active zone (play or the stack), it is erased instead.)
803.8e A card is Unstable for as long as it is modded. When a modded card dies or is erased, it and all of its mods are erased. See rules 410.4b, 720.
 Example: A modded host exchanged out of play by Hooba-Mon is erased with its mods, which reach the erased pile.
title: CR 803.8e

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 803. Other Keyword Abilities
(continues 803.8: Unstable is a non-combat attribute. If an Unstable card would enter a bin from an active zone (play or the stack), it is erased instead.)
803.8f A spell is modded, and so Unstable, when a Virus is applied to it on the stack or a mod is applied to it through {Modular}. When it leaves the stack it is erased with its mods. See rules 704.2c, 723, 802.26.
title: CR 803.8f

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 803. Other Keyword Abilities
(continues 803.8: Unstable is a non-combat attribute. If an Unstable card would enter a bin from an active zone (play or the stack), it is erased instead.)
803.8g A copy of a modded unit is not Unstable when it is made, because it has no mods of its own. A mod attached to it afterwards makes it Unstable in the usual way. See rule 710.2a.
 Example: A Borrower of Forms that copied a modded unit is not Unstable and dies to the bin.
title: CR 803.8g

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 803. Other Keyword Abilities
(continues 803.8: Unstable is a non-combat attribute. If an Unstable card would enter a bin from an active zone (play or the stack), it is erased instead.)
803.8h Moving a mod moves its Unstable with it. The unit the mod leaves stops being Unstable when its last mod is gone, unless something else makes it Unstable; the unit it moves to becomes Unstable. See rule 720.
803.8i Unstable replaces where the card goes, not its death. An Unstable unit that is destroyed still dies: its death triggers and other abilities that watch for a unit dying see it. See rules 713.8, 801.2h.
 Example: A modded unit is destroyed. A whenever-another-unit-dies ability triggers, then the unit is erased, not binned.
title: CR 803.8h–803.8i

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 803. Other Keyword Abilities
(continues 803.8: Unstable is a non-combat attribute. If an Unstable card would enter a bin from an active zone (play or the stack), it is erased instead.)
803.8j Unstable does not stop a unit from being recalled. A recalled Unstable unit goes to the hand as a card; if it was modded, its mods are put into the bin. See rule 801.7b.
title: CR 803.8j

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 8. Keywords › 803. Other Keyword Abilities
(continues 803.8: Unstable is a non-combat attribute. If an Unstable card would enter a bin from an active zone (play or the stack), it is erased instead.)
803.8k An Unstable card that leaves the stack for a bin, because it resolved, fizzled or was negated, is erased instead. See rules 704.2c, 406.4.
 Example: Aberrant Statweaver negated off the stack is erased.
 Example: A printed-Unstable virus whose host dies fizzles to the erased pile.
803.8m An effect that itself says to put a card into a bin overrides Unstable. Pull Under ("Delete target unit. If you do, put it and all of its mods into your bin.") leaves a modded unit and its mods in that bin. See rule 101.
title: CR 803.8k–803.8m

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 9. Multiplayer and Formats › 900. General
900.1 There are four game modes: live draft, constructed, cube draft and team draft. See rules 100, 901, 902.
900.1a The 2023 Rulebook calls cube draft "pre-draft": players draft a complete deck of at least 30 cards before the game begins, then play constructed games with it. See rule 902.
title: CR 900.1–900.1a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 9. Multiplayer and Formats › 900. General
900.2 A game is played in one of these player setups: 1v1, free-for-all (FFA), teams, or archenemy. See rule 100.
900.2a A 1v1 game is played between two players. It is the recommended setup for a first game. See rules 903, 904.
900.2b Free-for-all is described in 903. Team games and archenemy are described in 904. See rules 903, 904.
title: CR 900.2–900.2b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 9. Multiplayer and Formats › 900. General
900.3 A 1v1 game counts as a team game: each player is their own team. Free-for-all is not a team game. See rule 904.
 Example: With The Silent in play, two spells you have played this battle make your next spell cost [4] more, while your opponent still pays the printed cost: in 1v1 your team is you alone.
title: CR 900.3

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 9. Multiplayer and Formats › 900. General
900.4 Where the players sit sets which regions neighbour each other. See rules 601, 904.3.
900.4a In 1v1 the players sit across from each other. Each has one neighbouring region. See rule 601.
900.4b In a game of more than two players the players sit in a circle, so each player has a player to their left and a player to their right. Each player has two neighbouring regions. See rule 601.
title: CR 900.4–900.4b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 9. Multiplayer and Formats › 900. General
900.5 Battle normally resolves one region at a time, in the order of 601. Once players are comfortable with the game, they may resolve at the same time any regions that have no player in common. See rules 601, 505.
 Example: With an attack and a counterattack, the battle in the defending region runs to its end before the counterattack battle begins in the other region.
title: CR 900.5

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 9. Multiplayer and Formats › 900. General
900.6 The client plays 1v1 live draft and 1v1 constructed only. It has no free-for-all, team, archenemy, cube-draft or team-draft games, and no intent cards. Rules 903, 904 and 905, and the parts of 902 about cube draft and team draft, describe the printed game, which the client does not enforce. See rule 100.
title: CR 900.6

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 9. Multiplayer and Formats › 901. Constructed
901.1 In constructed, each player brings their own deck, built before the game, and plays from it. See rules 103, 401.
title: CR 901.1

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 9. Multiplayer and Formats › 901. Constructed
901.2 A constructed deck has at least 30 cards. No source sets a maximum.
 Example: A 29-card deck is not a legal constructed deck.
title: CR 901.2

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 9. Multiplayer and Formats › 901. Constructed
901.3 A constructed deck may hold at most 2 copies of any one card. See rule 901.8.
 Example: A third copy of a card makes the deck illegal.
title: CR 901.3

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 9. Multiplayer and Formats › 901. Constructed
901.4 Constructed has no shared deck and no packs. See rules 103, 401, 409.
title: CR 901.4

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 9. Multiplayer and Formats › 901. Constructed
901.5 In constructed, the draw step and the draft step are taken together as one draw phase: each player draws 4 cards from their own deck, then puts 2 cards from their hand on the bottom of their deck. See rules 503, 408.
 Example: Turn 1 of a constructed game: each player has their 4-card opening hand, draws 4, and must then put 2 back.
901.5a The player chooses the 2 cards and puts them on the bottom in any order. Because every card put on the bottom of a deck goes into the recycle pile, which is shuffled before it is drawn from again, the order has no effect on play. See rule 408.
title: CR 901.5–901.5a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 9. Multiplayer and Formats › 901. Constructed
(continues 901.5: In constructed, the draw step and the draft step are taken together as one draw phase: each player draws 4 cards from their own deck, then puts 2 cards from their hand on the bottom of their deck.)
901.5b For state checks the draw of 4 and the put-back of 2 are one step: a player's units are not checked for death while that player still has 2 cards to put back, so they are judged on the hand that remains. See rules 503, 713.
 Example: Dreadspawn Horror with 1 card in hand: drawing 4 does not kill it, and after the put-back it is a 4/2.
 Example: With 3 cards in hand, Dreadspawn Horror's controller draws 4 and puts 2 back, keeping 5 cards: the Horror then dies.
title: CR 901.5b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 9. Multiplayer and Formats › 901. Constructed
901.6 A player in a constructed game may make a resource of any element, whether or not their deck holds a card of that element. See rules 106, 502.
title: CR 901.6

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 9. Multiplayer and Formats › 901. Constructed
901.7 Card text that refers to a constructed format applies in a constructed game. See rule 503.
 Example: Worldbender in constructed: the player skips the draw-4-put-2-back, the hand gains 3 cards, and the player loses 3 life.
 Example: Worldbender in a live draft: the hand gains 3 cards and life is untouched.
901.7a The matches of a cube draft are constructed games, so such text applies in them too. See rule 902.
title: CR 901.7–901.7a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 9. Multiplayer and Formats › 901. Constructed
(continues 901.7: Card text that refers to a constructed format applies in a constructed game.)
901.7b The client has a testing mode called "shared", which is not a format. Card text that asks whether the game is constructed treats a shared game as constructed. See rule 900.
 Example: Worldbender in shared takes the constructed branch: three cards and 3 life.
title: CR 901.7b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 9. Multiplayer and Formats › 901. Constructed
901.8 Single Card Duel is a variant of constructed that the client offers. Each player picks a single card before the game, and their deck is 30 copies of that card. See rule 901.3.
901.8a A Single Card Duel deck is the one exception to the limit of 2 copies of a card. See rule 901.3.
901.8b A Single Card Duel has no draw phase. Each turn, each player simply draws 2 cards; nothing is put back. The opening hand is still 4 cards. See rule 503.
 Example: Each player starts turn 1 with 6 cards (4 + 2) and nothing to put back, and draws exactly 2 more on turn 2.
901.8c If neither player's card can make a unit, the game is not played. It is a draw: each player is told the other's card, and both choose again. A card can make a unit if it is a unit or spell-unit card, or if it creates a unit token. See rule 104.
 Example: A unit card and Self-Assembly (which creates a Robot unit token) can make a unit; a spell that creates no unit cannot.
title: CR 901.8–901.8c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 9. Multiplayer and Formats › 902. Draft and Cube
902.1 In live draft, the players share one deck, built from the chosen elements, and draft cards from it during the game. See rules 103, 401, 409.
902.1a Live draft is the standard Algomancy format, and 1v1 live draft is the format suggested for learning the game.
title: CR 902.1–902.1a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 9. Multiplayer and Formats › 902. Draft and Cube
902.2 A live draft uses 3 elements for 2–3 players and 4 elements for 4–6 players. For 6 or more players, a cube draft with all 5 elements is recommended instead of a live draft. See rules 105, 103.
902.2a In casual games, players take turns choosing the elements, or assign them randomly. The printed rules defer the competitive procedure to Algomancy.io.
title: CR 902.2–902.2a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 9. Multiplayer and Formats › 902. Draft and Cube
902.3 In live draft each player begins with 16 cards to draft from: a 6-card hand (the 4-card starting hand plus the first turn's 2 draws) and a 10-card pack. See rules 103, 503.
title: CR 902.3

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 9. Multiplayer and Formats › 902. Draft and Cube
902.4 The draft step is described in 503, and the pack, its refresh every N+1 turns and an eliminated player's pack in 409. See rules 503, 409.
 Example: Turns 2 and 3 draw 2 and reopen the draft step; the packs refresh on turn 4.
title: CR 902.4

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 9. Multiplayer and Formats › 902. Draft and Cube
902.5 The client lets a live draft be created with custom rules. Custom rules change the deal and nothing else: they never change how a card works.
902.5a Pack size may be set from 3 to 15 cards (standard 10). Every pack is dealt and refreshed at that size, and the draft step leaves exactly that many cards in the pack. See rules 409, 503.
 Example: With packs of 5, each pack is dealt with 5 cards, the draft step leaves 5 in it, and the turn-4 refresh deals 5.
902.5b The number of elements may be set from 2 to 7 (standard 3). The pool is every deck card whose elements all lie within the chosen set. Two elements default to fire and wood. See rule 105.
902.5c The opening hand may be set from 1 to 15 cards (standard 6), the draws per turn after turn 1 from 0 to 5 (standard 2), and the starting life from 1 to 99 (standard 30). See rules 103, 503.
902.5d With "simple cards only", the pool holds only cards with the silver (Simple) complexity symbol. See rule 209.
902.5e Cards may be banned by name, and an advanced card filter may be set: only cards that match it are in the pool. A banned or filtered-out card is nowhere in the game.
902.5f Custom rules do not change the pack refresh: it still comes every N+1 turns. See rule 409.
 Example: With packs of 5 the turn-4 refresh still comes, and deals 5.
902.5g A custom pool must hold at least 2 × hand + 4 × pack + 6 × draws cards (64 for the standard game). Custom rules below that floor are refused before the game is created. When the elements are to be chosen later, every set of that size must pass.
 Example: The standard game needs 64 cards, the beginner deal 44.
902.5h Custom rules are not printed rules. Packs of other than 10 cards are not in the printed rules, and the client's Beginner preset (two elements, simple cards only, packs of 5) is the client's own softening of the Quick Start.
title: CR 902.5–902.5h

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 9. Multiplayer and Formats › 902. Draft and Cube
902.6 Cube draft is a format for large groups (6 to 10 or more players). The players draft decks before the game, then use them to play constructed matches, often in a 1v1 tournament bracket. See rule 901.
902.6a The cube is all of the game cards, hybrids included, shuffled together: 320 cards from one box. For more than 8 players, two complete sets are used (640 cards).
902.6b To draft, deal each player a pack of 10 cards. Then repeat these steps 15 times, until each player has a 30-card deck: (1) each player draws 2 cards from the cube; (2) players may combine their hands with their packs; (3) each player chooses 10 cards from their combined hand and pack and passes them, as a new pack, clockwise to their neighbour.
902.6c Players then play constructed matches with the 30-card decks they drafted. See rules 901, 901.7.
title: CR 902.6–902.6c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 9. Multiplayer and Formats › 902. Draft and Cube
902.7 A traditional cube draft may be used instead. Each player is dealt three packs of 13 to 15 cards: 15 cards for 6 players, 13 for 8 players.
902.7a Each player looks at their pack, takes one card from it and passes the rest to their neighbour, until the pack is empty. This is done three times, once per pack, passing left, then right, then left.
902.7b From the cards they drafted, each player builds a 30-card deck for the constructed matches that follow. See rule 901.
title: CR 902.7–902.7b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 9. Multiplayer and Formats › 902. Draft and Cube
902.8 In team draft, each team brings a constructed deck of 30 cards for each player on the team, with at most 2 copies of each card. The team live drafts from that deck during the game. See rules 904, 901.3.
902.8a In team draft, a player who has finished drafting passes their pack to the nearest teammate, not clockwise to the nearest player. See rule 503.
902.8b In team draft, packs are never refreshed. See rule 409.
902.8c All the other rules of live draft apply in team draft. See rules 503, 409.
902.8d The 2023 Rulebook sizes the team-draft deck differently: the team builds a deck of 100 cards, with at most 2 copies of each card. See rule 901.3.
title: CR 902.8–902.8d

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 9. Multiplayer and Formats › 903. Free-for-All
903.1 In a free-for-all (FFA) game, every player plays for themselves. All players fight to be the last one standing. See rule 104.
903.1a A free-for-all game is for 2 to 9 players, or more if more copies of the game are available.
title: CR 903.1–903.1a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 9. Multiplayer and Formats › 903. Free-for-All
903.2 Free-for-all has no attack and counterattack: there is one battle round, and no counterattacks. See rules 505, 610.
title: CR 903.2

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 9. Multiplayer and Formats › 903. Free-for-All
903.3 In free-for-all, all players declare their attacks at the same time, using intent cards (see 905). See rules 905, 604.
title: CR 903.3

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 9. Multiplayer and Formats › 903. Free-for-All
903.4 After the attacks are declared, battle in each attacked region follows these steps in order: (1) the attacker sets their units into formation; (2) a priority window; (3) the defender sets their blocking formation; (4) a priority window; (5) the combat damage step, in which all units in formation deal combat damage at the same time; (6) the after combat step, the last priority window in that region before regroup. See rules 602, 605, 607, 608, 609.
title: CR 903.4

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 9. Multiplayer and Formats › 903. Free-for-All
903.5 When two players attack the same player, all three players take part in that battle together, in one region. See rule 601.
903.5a The defending player defends against both attacking formations. See rule 606.
903.5b All three players can interact with each other and with each other's units in that region. See rule 601.
title: CR 903.5–903.5b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 9. Multiplayer and Formats › 903. Free-for-All
903.6 In a region with more than two players, priority passes around the players in a circle, clockwise, instead of back and forth. The initiative player receives priority first if they are present in the region; otherwise the player nearest to the initiative player, clockwise, does. See rule 703.
903.6a The stack works the same way with three players in a region as it does in 1v1. See rules 703, 704.
title: CR 903.6–903.6a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 9. Multiplayer and Formats › 903. Free-for-All
903.7 Apart from the battle phase, which is only partly simultaneous, every phase of a free-for-all game may be taken by all players at the same time: players may make resources in the planning phase, and deploy units in the deployment phase, all at once. See rules 501, 507.
903.7a Players who are learning, or playing competitively, may instead take their phases one player at a time, in clockwise order from the initiative player.
title: CR 903.7–903.7a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 9. Multiplayer and Formats › 904. Teams
904.1 In a team game, two teams play against each other, 2v2 or 3v3. 3v3 is the standard team structure. See rule 900.3.
title: CR 904.1

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 9. Multiplayer and Formats › 904. Teams
904.2 A team game may be played with split teams, where each player has their own region, or with joint players, where a team shares a single region. A joint-player game is in effect a 1v1 game with more players. See rule 601.
title: CR 904.2

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 9. Multiplayer and Formats › 904. Teams
904.3 In a team game, each player sits between two opponents. See rules 900.4, 601.
title: CR 904.3

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 9. Multiplayer and Formats › 904. Teams
904.4 In a team game, a team wins when it has eliminated the entire opposing team. See rule 104.
title: CR 904.4

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 9. Multiplayer and Formats › 904. Teams
904.5 Teammates act together in every situation and every phase of the game.
title: CR 904.5

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 9. Multiplayer and Formats › 904. Teams
904.6 The team of the player who holds the initiative token has the initiative: it is the initiative team (IT), and the other team is the non-initiative team (NIT). The initiative team makes all its plays first; the non-initiative team acts after it. See rules 500, 508.
904.6a The teams trade the initiative every turn. See rule 508.
title: CR 904.6–904.6a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 9. Multiplayer and Formats › 904. Teams
904.7 In the deployment phase, the initiative team deploys first, its players in any order they wish, and then passes to the non-initiative team, whose players do the same. See rule 507.
title: CR 904.7

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 9. Multiplayer and Formats › 904. Teams
904.8 Teammates share priority. They take actions in whatever order they choose among themselves, and a team receives and passes priority as one. See rule 703.
title: CR 904.8

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 9. Multiplayer and Formats › 904. Teams
904.9 A team game's battle has the same attack-and-counterattack structure as 1v1. The difference is that attacks and blocks take place across several regions, with a separate priority window in each region. See rules 505, 610.
title: CR 904.9

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 9. Multiplayer and Formats › 904. Teams
904.10 In a team game the battle runs in this order (the Manual gives it for 2v2): (1) the initiative team declares all its attacks at once, into several regions; (2) a priority window in each non-initiative region, in order clockwise from the initiative player; (3) the non-initiative team declares all its blocks and counterattacks at once, into several regions; (4) battle is finished in each non-initiative region in turn, in order clockwise from the initiative player; (5) battle is finished in each initiative region in turn, in order clockwise from the initiative player. See rules 505, 609, 610.
904.10a Finishing battle in a region means its remaining steps: a priority window, the combat damage step, and the after combat priority window. See rules 607, 608, 609.
title: CR 904.10–904.10a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 9. Multiplayer and Formats › 904. Teams
904.11 Card text that refers to a player's team refers, in 1v1, to that player alone, since in 1v1 each player is their own team. See rule 900.3.
 Example: The Silent in 1v1: once its controller has played 2 spells this battle, their next spell costs [4] more, while the opponent, who has played none, pays the printed cost.
title: CR 904.11

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 9. Multiplayer and Formats › 904. Teams
904.12 Archenemy is a player setup, typically 2v1, in which the single player gets to take 1 or 2 turns before the other two players begin the game. See rule 900.2.
904.12a The 2023 Rulebook describes the 2v1 game differently: the single player has bonus cards and resources, and faces two weaker opponents.
title: CR 904.12–904.12a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 9. Multiplayer and Formats › 905. Intent Cards
905.1 Intent cards are how players declare attacks in free-for-all: all players declare at the same time, each placing intent cards that show what their cards intend to do. See rules 903.3, 604.
title: CR 905.1

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 9. Multiplayer and Formats › 905. Intent Cards
905.2 Attacks are declared with intent cards in these steps: (1) each player places an intent card face down in front of each of their units and other cards, such as spell tokens, showing that card's intended action; (2) when all players have finished, all the intent cards are turned face up; (3) the chosen attacks take place at once. See rule 604.
title: CR 905.2

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 9. Multiplayer and Formats › 905. Intent Cards
905.3 A player may group several of their units behind one intent card.
title: CR 905.3

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · 9. Multiplayer and Formats › 905. Intent Cards
905.4 A player may place several copies of the same intent card in front of different units.
title: CR 905.4

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · Annex D — Digital Play Conventions › D1. General and Precedence
D1.1 The pacing and concurrency conventions in this annex are not rules changes: none of them changes what is legal. See rules D3, D3.3, D3.4b.
 [Verification of D1.1 was only partial.]
D1.1a A warning or a confirmation never removes a legal option. Where a choice looks like a misclick, the client may ask the player; it does not refuse the choice. See rule D2.8.
title: CR D1.1–D1.1a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · Annex D — Digital Play Conventions › D1. General and Precedence
D1.2 The client never makes a choice that belongs to a player. A real choice is always put to the player who makes it.
D1.2a An option the rules would refuse is not offered. The client shows only legal options; it does not show an option and then refuse it. See rule D1.3.
D1.2b The game takes an action for a player only where the battle leaves them nothing to decide: an attacker with no unit able to attack has the empty attack declared for them; a lone counterattacker has its one-unit formation declared, its sent spell tokens riding (see rule D1.2c); and a defender with no unit in the battle region, or facing an attack with no attacking unit left and unable to send a counterattacker, has the empty block declared for them. These forced actions are logged like any other. A player holding full control is not forced: the window is left to them. See rules 610, D1.2c, D1.2f, D1.2e, D2.7.
 Example: In round 2 the lone counterattacker is destroyed before blocks: the initiative player's empty block is declared for them, though they have a unit in the region.
D1.2c In round 2, a counterattack pool that holds exactly one unit able to attack declares the one-unit formation by itself, with every spell token sent with it riding along: the unit and its tokens must attack, and one unit has only one shape. See rule 610.
 Example: A player who sent one unit to counterattack, and no spell token, is not asked to form it: the one-unit formation is declared for them.
 Example: A unit sent with a spell token is formed for the player with the token riding, and a formation that drops the token is refused.
D1.2d When all of one player's simultaneously queued triggers are identical (the same card, the same ability and the same composed parts), the player is not asked to order them. They go on in the order they fired. Triggers from different cards or abilities, or composites whose parts differ, are still ordered by the player. See rule 706.
 Example: Three allies spawn at once beside Flourishing Flora: its three identical triggers go on the stack without the player being asked to order them.
title: CR D1.2–D1.2d

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · Annex D — Digital Play Conventions › D1. General and Precedence
(continues D1.2: The client never makes a choice that belongs to a player. A real choice is always put to the player who makes it.)
D1.2e A non-target choice that an ability makes as it begins to resolve (such as the ally a Wraith's start-of-deployment trigger chooses) is recorded without asking when there is only one candidate. With two or more candidates the player is asked. See rules 507, 706.
 Example: A lone Wraith aims at its only ally without asking; with a second ally the player is asked.
D1.2f A target is asked for even when exactly one candidate is legal. A forced target is still a click. See rule 110.
 Example: Divine Foresight ("target opponent") cast in battle still asks its caster to choose the target, though the opponent is the only choice.
D1.2g Where a choice has a usual answer, the client may offer it as the first option, but it never picks it. The elective combat-damage split leads with "default — share front-to-back", and no automatic action answers that question. See rule 608.
D1.2h The caster always chooses the order of a Burst group, one token at a time; the client offers no automatic order. A lone token is not asked to be ordered. See rule 803.
D1.2i When a player chooses the order of replacement effects (see rule 708.4a), each choice is the unit whose effect it is: the player answers by clicking that unit on the board, the choices are not also buttons in the prompt bar, and the prompt says what is being chosen. A question raised by combat damage or by rot is asked before any of that damage or rot is dealt. The other player sees that a question is open, but not the question; while the rot question is open at the start of deployment, the other player cannot deploy.
 Example: Two Oorblaks: the prompt asks which Oorblak takes the damage first, and clicking the second Oorblak chooses it.
 Example: The attacker sees that the defender is being asked, but not the question.
 Example: Two Skittering Blights at the start of deployment: the rot question is answered on the board, and the other player can deploy only once it is answered.
 Example: A Poisonous blocker and two Counter Thieves: the question comes before any of the combat damage is dealt.
title: CR D1.2e–D1.2i

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · Annex D — Digital Play Conventions › D1. General and Precedence
D1.3 The client holds no opinion of its own about legality. Wherever the client decides something the engine also decides, the client's answer is derived from the engine's, in one place.
 Example: In the block step the client marks a card exactly when the engine would refuse the whole plan, read off the engine's own validator; every placement of three defenders is checked against the engine.
D1.3a A highlighted card, a clickable unit, a drop target or a one-click shortcut claims that the engine will take the action. The client draws one only where the engine would accept it, with one exception: the block step (see rule D1.3b).
 Example: A unit that cannot be sent to counterattack is not highlighted, and clicking it does nothing.
D1.3b In the block step a unit may be placed in a column where the engine would refuse the block. While it is there the card wears a red (!) mark, and the block bar names the engine's reason; the mark comes off when the unit is moved out. A card is marked only when the engine would refuse the plan. See rules 802.12, 606.2e.
 Example: Bripp, a Feeble unit, is clicked into a block column: it wears the (!) before Confirm, and loses it when it is moved back out.
 Example: An unmet Alluring duty marks the lured unit, wherever it stands.
title: CR D1.3–D1.3b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · Annex D — Digital Play Conventions › D1. General and Precedence
D1.4 A hidden simultaneous segment is a part of the turn in which both players act at once and neither sees what the other does until both are done. The resource step, the haste step and deployment are hidden simultaneous segments. See rules 501, 504, 507, D6.
D1.4a The hiding is done by the server's view of the game, the same way hands are hidden. The rules engine itself hides nothing.
D1.4b A segment ends at a barrier, when every player is done. At the barrier each player is shown what the other did, in the recap. See rules D5, D6.
D1.4c Battle is not a hidden segment. Nothing that happens in battle is held back from either player.
title: CR D1.4–D1.4c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · Annex D — Digital Play Conventions › D1. General and Precedence
D1.5 Where the printed rules have the initiative player take the resource step and the haste step first, and the initiative team deploy first (rules 501.4 and rule 507.3), this client runs those steps for both players at once, each hidden from the other (rule D1.4). The non-initiative player neither waits for the initiative player nor sees what they did before acting. This is a house rule of the client. See rules 501, 507, D1.4.
 Example: The non-initiative player is offered plays at once in deployment, and can finish deploying while the initiative player is still acting.
title: CR D1.5

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · Annex D — Digital Play Conventions › D1. General and Precedence
D1.6 In a draft, a player who has made their pick may begin the resource step, activating and recycling, while the other player is still drafting. The printed turn ends each step for every player together (rule 501.4a); this client does not hold the faster player back, because the resource step is hidden and the other player cannot see the head start. See rules 501.4a, D1.4.
 Example: A player who has committed their draft pick may activate a resource while the opponent is still drafting.
title: CR D1.6

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · Annex D — Digital Play Conventions › D2. Priority and Auto-Pass
D2.1 While a decision is open for a player (a question the game is waiting on them to answer), that player must answer it, or concede, before taking any other action. See rule 104.4a.
D2.1a In battle, a decision open for one player stops the other player too: nobody may act until it is answered. See rule 703.
D2.1b Inside a hidden simultaneous segment, a decision open for one player does not stop the other player, who keeps every action they had, except as described in the next sub-rule. See rule D1.4.
 Example: While one player answers their Wraith triggers at the start of deployment, the other player goes on deploying.
D2.1c Exception: when answering the open decision would rewind the game to before the other player acted (a resolution that stopped halfway), the other player is stopped as in battle. Online, an action they send meanwhile waits and is applied when the decision closes; they are told it is waiting, not that it is illegal.
D2.1d Only one decision can be open at a time. An action that would change what the other player's open decision reads when it is answered is refused, and the game stays as it was before the action.
D2.1e Conceding is never blocked by an open decision, whichever player it belongs to. See rule 104.4a.
D2.1f Each player's screen shows only that player's own open question: the other player's question and its options are never sent to it. The player being asked has only the question.
title: CR D2.1–D2.1f

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · Annex D — Digital Play Conventions › D2. Priority and Auto-Pass
D2.2 When a player holds priority, the client offers up to three ways to pass: Pass, Pass through stack and Pass all. Pass through stack and Pass all are standing passes: promises the client keeps on the player's behalf in later windows. See rule 703.
D2.2a Pass passes priority once. It sets up nothing for later windows.
D2.2b Pass through stack passes for the player until the stack items that were there when it was clicked have resolved, and then ends. It hands priority back sooner if a stack item outside that set appears, or if the player is offered an option they did not have when they clicked.
 Example: A player clicks Pass through stack; the opponent answers with a new spell, so priority comes back to the player.
D2.2c Pass through stack is offered only while there is a stack to pass through.
D2.2d Pass all passes for the player until the phase it was clicked in ends. A new stack item or a new option does not hand priority back.
 Example: The opponent casting a spell does not stop Pass all.
D2.2e Both standing passes still stop before the one pass that would end the battle phase while the player holds spell tokens they could cast, so that that pass is the player's own click. See rules D2.6, 506.
 Example: A player clicks Pass all while holding a castable Fireball token: it passes through the battle but hands back the last pass, the one that would end the battle phase.
D2.2f What counts as new for a standing pass is measured against the moment it was clicked. An option the player already had then is not new when it comes back later.
 Example: An activated ability the player could use when they clicked Pass all becomes unusable for a window and then usable again: the pass does not stop for it.
D2.2g A standing pass is set up only by a click and can be cancelled at any time: one stop control drops whichever is running. The client shows which promise is running and how it ends.
title: CR D2.2–D2.2g

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · Annex D — Digital Play Conventions › D2. Priority and Auto-Pass
D2.3 A player may turn on auto-pass. With it on, the client passes priority for the player only in a window where passing is the only thing they could do. Auto-pass never passes through an open decision.
 Example: With a castable card in hand the window is put to the player even with auto-pass on.
title: CR D2.3

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · Annex D — Digital Play Conventions › D2. Priority and Auto-Pass
D2.4 An answer the client sends without a click (an automatic pass, or the automatic haste-step ready) is sent once for each time it is owed. It is latched by being unanswered, not by counting game updates, so updates that arrive while it is outstanding do not send it again. Engine differs, see F-U23-2.
 [The online client currently plays D2.4 differently; a fix is filed.]
D2.4a If the server refuses an action the client sent on its own, the refusal is not shown as the player's error. It goes to the log and to a plain notice that says the client sent it.
title: CR D2.4–D2.4a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · Annex D — Digital Play Conventions › D2. Priority and Auto-Pass
D2.5 When the haste step opens and the only legal action a player has in it is to finish the step, the client finishes it for them at once, unless they have turned on bluff haste. See rules 504.5, 504.5a.
D2.5a If the player has any legal play in the haste step, the client never finishes the step for them.
 Example: A playable haste card in hand keeps the player in the step, bluff haste on or off.
D2.5b Bluff haste is a preference, off by default and remembered by the browser. With it on, the client never finishes the haste step for the player; they stay in the step until they finish it themselves, whether or not they hold anything to play. See rule 504.5a.
D2.5c The server never finishes the haste step for a player. The automatic ready, when there is one, comes from the player's own client. See rule 504.5a.
D2.5d While the haste step is open, neither player is shown whether the other has finished it. Each player sees their own readiness, and the end of the step is shown to both.
D2.5e The game's action counter is still sent to both players and rises on every action, in every hidden segment, so a modified client can tell that its opponent acted and when. The shipped client shows nothing from it. See rule D1.4.
title: CR D2.5–D2.5e

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · Annex D — Digital Play Conventions › D2. Priority and Auto-Pass
D2.6 When passing would end the battle phase while the player still holds spell tokens they could cast, the client asks before sending the pass, because moving to regroup erases them. It asks on that pass only, not in the battle's other windows. See rule 506.
D2.6a When the battle phase ends with no pass to ask on (an attack declined with no window left, or a whole battle declined), the loss is announced instead: as regroup starts, each player who loses unused spell tokens is told which. Nothing is announced when nothing is lost.
 Example: A battle both players decline opens no priority window, and the token loss is still announced.
D2.6b A battle ended by a card while it resolves (Temporal Rift) cannot be warned about before the pass, since that cannot be known when the pass is made. The announcement covers it, as it covers every way a battle ends.
 Example: Under Temporal Rift, a pass does not look like it will end the battle, so the client does not ask; when the Rift ends the battle, the lost spell tokens are still announced as regroup starts.
title: CR D2.6–D2.6b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · Annex D — Digital Play Conventions › D2. Priority and Auto-Pass
D2.7 Full control is held, not set. While a player holds the Control key, the client gives them every stop: auto-pass, standing passes, auto-yields and the automatic haste-step ready all stand down. In battle, an action taken while holding it also keeps priority (rule D2.9). When they let go, everything returns to how it was.
 Example: Holding the Control key as a player acts asks to keep priority; letting go stops asking.
D2.7a Full control changes nothing in deployment. No player holds priority there (rule 703.7), so holding the Control key asks for nothing, and each deployment stack still resolves on its own. See rule 507.
 Example: In deployment there is no Hold priority toggle, and holding the Control key adds no ask.
D2.7b The client's own automatic actions stop at once when Control is pressed. The server's automatic actions stop only once the message reaches it, and an automatic action already sent is not recalled, so full control should be held before acting, not after.
D2.7c Leaving the window (switching away, hiding the page) releases full control, as if the key had been let go.
 Example: Alt-tabbing away is letting go.
D2.7d Pressing another key while Control is down (Ctrl+Z, or a browser shortcut) makes a chord, not full control: it drops the hold until Control is released. See rule D4.
 Example: Ctrl+Z is undo, not full control.
D2.7e Full control is not remembered between sessions. The client shows whether it is being held.
title: CR D2.7–D2.7e

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · Annex D — Digital Play Conventions › D2. Priority and Auto-Pass
D2.8 When a spell has one target slot that must be an ally and another that may be any unit, and the player picks an ally for the second slot, the client asks whether they meant to target their own unit. It also asks when a single "up to one target unit" slot, other than a "you may" one, can reach only the player's own units: each of them asks, and when an enemy is in reach nothing asks. It never refuses: yes resolves exactly as chosen, and no returns to the same target pick with nothing sent. The option to pick nothing is still offered, and asks nothing. See rules D7, D1.1a.
 Example: A player casts Fight and picks two of their own units: the client asks once before the cast goes out.
 Example: Minor Kraken attacks beside Curio Drifter with no enemy in reach: picking Curio Drifter to recall asks first.
 Example: With an enemy unit in reach, the same pick asks nothing.
D2.8a The cards that ask are found from their target slots, not listed by name. Of the two-slot shape, today they are Fight and Squish; Organic Exchange, which targets two units with no ally slot, does not ask. The up-to-one shape is found the same way, from a slot that takes at most one unit and may take none, and is not a "you may" slot.
title: CR D2.8–D2.8a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · Annex D — Digital Play Conventions › D2. Priority and Auto-Pass
D2.9 This client does not keep priority for a player who acts unless they ask: in battle, once their action is on the stack, priority goes to the opponent. A player asks to keep it by acting while holding the Control key (rule D2.7) or with the Hold priority toggle beside Pass turned on; then they keep priority and may act again (rule 703.2a). A pass never asks. A player who did not keep priority can still respond to their own spell once priority comes back to them with it on the stack. See rules 703, D2.7.
 Example: With the toggle off and no Control key held, a play goes out as it always did, and priority passes to the opponent.
 Example: The Hold priority toggle sits beside Pass; a tap turns it on.
 Example: Holding the Control key asks too; letting go stops asking.
 Example: A pass never carries the ask.
 Example: The defender casts a spell, the attacker passes, and the defender casts a second spell on top of the first.
title: CR D2.9

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · Annex D — Digital Play Conventions › D3. Clocks
D3.1 A game may be played with a chess clock, in which each player has a bank of time. The home screen offers three settings: no clock, 45 minutes and 60 minutes.
D3.1a Unless the player chooses otherwise, the bank is 45 minutes for a constructed game and 60 minutes for a live draft.
D3.1b A game with no clock shows no clocks.
D3.1c Choosing a clock setting does not make a game a custom game.
D3.1d A player's clock is shown as critical when it is down to a tenth of the game's bank or to one minute, whichever is less.
 Example: On a ninety-second bank the warning comes at nine seconds; on a ten-hour bank five minutes left is not yet critical, because the threshold stops at one minute.
 Example: On the 45- and 60-minute banks the clock turns critical at one minute.
title: CR D3.1–D3.1d

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · Annex D — Digital Play Conventions › D3. Clocks
D3.2 A player's clock runs only while the game is waiting on that player, and only while both players are connected. Neither clock runs while a proposed fix waits for its answer (see rule D4.5e).
 Example: A player proposes a fix: both clocks stop, and they run again once the proposal lapses.
D3.2a In a step both players take at once, both clocks run; a player's clock stops when that player finishes the step. See rule D1.4.
D3.2b A player's clock does not run in a priority window that their standing pass is answering, and the other player, who has nothing to do there, is not billed either. A real choice is billed even while a standing pass is set. If the client's pass has not arrived within a short backstop, the server passes for the player, and that pass is logged like any other. While a proposed fix waits for its answer, the server does not pass for a standing pass. See rule D2.2.
D3.2c A player watching a recap is off the clock until the playback ends or the server's hold on it lapses. Acting ends the hold. See rule D5.
title: CR D3.2–D3.2c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · Annex D — Digital Play Conventions › D3. Clocks
D3.3 A player whose clock runs out loses the game, and the log says they ran out of time. This happens even if neither player acts. See rule 104.
title: CR D3.3

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · Annex D — Digital Play Conventions › D3. Clocks
D3.4 A game is closed when nobody has moved in it for an hour, if fewer than five actions have been taken, or for twelve hours otherwise, and nobody (no player and no watcher) has been connected to it for the five-minute reconnect grace. An open tab keeps an idle game open.
D3.4a A connected player or a watcher keeps an idle game open, and an empty game is given a grace period for a player to reconnect.
D3.4b A game closed for being idle has no winner, is not rated, and is recorded as unfinished.
title: CR D3.4–D3.4b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · Annex D — Digital Play Conventions › D4. Undo
D4.1 Inside a hidden simultaneous segment, a player may undo their own actions, one at a time, back toward the start of the step, within the limits of the rules below. See rule D1.4.
D4.1a The opponent acting in the same step does not stop a player's undo.
 Example: A player undoes a unit they spawned in deployment after the opponent cached a card off the shared deck.
D4.1b An undo cannot go back past what the step itself did as it began, such as a payment or an ability that happens at the start of the step. A player's own undo, in any step, never takes back an agreed edit (see rule D4.5), and takes back an action from before one only if the edit would mean exactly the same afterwards. It never goes back past the point an agreed rewind returned the game to: only another agreed rewind can.
 Example: An undo stops at what the step did as it began: the answer to a start-of-deployment trigger cannot be taken back.
 Example: After an agreed rewind of one action in planning, the player cannot undo, alone, the action before it.
 Example: After an agreed fix in planning names a card by its place in the hand, the player cannot undo the earlier recycle that would put a different card there, while the other player may still undo a move the fix does not depend on.
D4.1c One player cannot undo actions taken in battle, except the steps of a cast that has not yet gone on the stack (see rule D4.2); both players together may take them back with an agreed rewind (see rule D4.5d). For that reason, in battle, an activated ability whose cost spends life, debt or the unit itself, with no choice to make before that cost is paid, asks for confirmation. While it asks, only a second click on the same unit, the Yes button or Enter confirms; No and Escape cancel; every other input does nothing. An ability whose cost asks which card to discard or which other unit to sacrifice does not ask for confirmation: choosing what to pay is the question. In deployment such an ability activates on the click, and undo is the safety net. See rule D7.
 Example: Cadaverous Cultivator ("[Battle] Discard a card: …") raises no confirmation: the click activates it, and the game asks which card to discard.
 Example: While the confirmation is up, clicking a card in hand plays nothing.
title: CR D4.1–D4.1c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · Annex D — Digital Play Conventions › D4. Undo
D4.2 A cast that has not yet gone on the stack, while its X, costs or targets are still being chosen, may be cancelled, in battle as well. A Burst group is cancelled whole, with Start over. See rules 702, 803.
D4.2a While the order of a Burst group is being chosen, its caster may also take back one step at a time with Undo last pick: the last token picked, or the last aim chosen. The earlier picks stand. Undo last pick is offered once a token has been picked, and only the caster can take a step back. See rule 803.
 Example: The caster picks which Fireball resolves first, then takes the pick back: the question "which resolves first?" returns with nothing picked, and nothing is on the stack.
 Example: After picking and aiming the first Fireball, one step back returns to aiming it; the pick stands.
 Example: The opponent's undo cannot reach into the burst.
title: CR D4.2–D4.2a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · Annex D — Digital Play Conventions › D4. Undo
D4.3 An action that showed a player hidden cards cannot be undone, and neither can anything that player did before it.
 Example: A Glimpse in deployment cannot be undone.
D4.3a Actions the player took after that one can still be undone, back to just after it.
 Example: A unit played after the glimpse can be undone, back to just after the glimpse, and not past it.
D4.3b The refusal reads "you've seen those cards — that can't be taken back".
D4.3c Only the player who saw the cards is locked. The opponent looking at a shared deck does not lock a player's undo, since inside a hidden step it shows that player nothing.
 Example: The opponent glimpsing from the shared deck does not lock the player's undo.
D4.3d An undo is refused if it would change cards the opponent has already been shown.
D4.3e Whether an action showed a player hidden cards is measured, not listed: an action counts if what it shows the player depends on the order of hidden cards. A glimpse, a draw, a reveal or a look at a hand counts. Playing a card from hand, recycling, or putting a card on the bottom of a deck does not. In a Single Card Duel nothing locks, since every card in the deck is the same. See rule D8.
 Example: A unit's spawn trigger that glimpses 1 in the haste step locks undo too.
D4.3f The lock survives a server restart and an undo.
D4.3g The lock binds one player's own undo. An agreed rewind (see rule D4.5d) may take the game back past an action that showed a player hidden cards: the other player's agreement waives the lock.
title: CR D4.3–D4.3g

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · Annex D — Digital Play Conventions › D4. Undo
D4.4 In Learn to Play, undo works in every phase, under the same lock: a turn's draw, a glimpse or a look at the Bot's hand ends the undo of whatever came before it. Starting a turn again after a loss is a fresh attempt, not an undo. See rule D8.
title: CR D4.4

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · Annex D — Digital Play Conventions › D4. Undo
D4.5 In a game between two players, either player may propose a fix, and the fix happens only if the other player agrees. A fix is an edit or a rewind. Test mode, a scenario, and a game that has not started or is over take no fixes. A fix sent as an ordinary action is refused: only an agreed proposal makes one. See rule D4.
D4.5a An edit is one of: setting a player's life total, to a whole number from 1 to 999; a player drawing from 1 to 10 cards off the top of their deck; moving one of the proposer's own cards from their hand, bin or cache to their hand, bin or cache, or to the top or bottom of their deck; or taking a unit off the board to its controller's hand, bin or the bottom of their deck. A token taken off the board is simply gone.
 Example: A fix cannot set a life total to 0, nor move a card that is no longer where the proposer saw it.
D4.5b An edit is quiet: nothing triggers on it. A unit it takes off the board neither dies nor despawns, a card it puts into a bin is not trashed, a card it takes out of a bin does not count as leaving the bin, and the cards it draws are not a draw for anything that listens for one. See rule 405.4.
 Example: Afflicting Anima does not hear a card that a fix puts into the bin.
 Example: Rotling does not hear a card that a fix takes out of the bin.
D4.5c An agreed edit may be made in any step, the hidden planning, haste and deploy steps included, except while a decision is open for either player; it is shown to both players at once. A rewind may be proposed at any time. See rule D1.4.
 Example: An edit is accepted inside the hidden planning step and inside the hidden deploy step.
 Example: An edit is refused while either player is being asked something.
 Example: A fix made in the hidden planning step reaches both players at once, and the other player's frozen view of the board shows it.
title: CR D4.5–D4.5c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · Annex D — Digital Play Conventions › D4. Undo
(continues D4.5: In a game between two players, either player may propose a fix, and the fix happens only if the other player agrees. A fix is an edit or a rewind. Test mode, a scenario, and a game that has not started or is over take…)
D4.5d A rewind takes the game back to one of: just before the proposing player's own last action, even when more than five actions came after it; just before any of the last five actions, counting only actions a player took (an action the game took for a player is neither counted nor a place to stop); the start of the current step; or the start of the step before, which is the last earlier step in which a player took an action, and whose actions the game took for a player at its start are not taken back. Each option names, in the proposing player's words, what it takes back. Inside a hidden step, a point within the step is offered only if it takes back none of the other player's hidden actions there (their public ones, such as finishing planning or deployment, may be taken back); the start of the step may take back the other player's hidden actions too. The actions taken back are removed from the game, as if they had not been taken. See rule D1.2b.
 Example: On turn 1 the step before the current one began with an action the game took for a player. "The start of the step before" lands after it, before the current step, and is still named "the start of".
D4.5e A proposal states the fix and the proposer's reason, which is required. It lapses after 60 seconds, or as soon as any action lands, and the proposer may withdraw it. Only the other player can accept it; after a decline the proposer must wait 15 seconds before proposing again. The proposer's reason is filed as a bug report. Fixes made one after another, with no game action between them, are one run and file one report, with every fix's reason in order; the run is filed when it ends, for instance when the next game action lands, and a server restart before then does not lose it. See rule D3.2.
D4.5f A game with a fix in it counts like any other game: its result, rating, league result, achievements and card statistics. It is only tagged as fixed where the game is listed.
title: CR D4.5d–D4.5f

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · Annex D — Digital Play Conventions › D5. Recap and Playback
D5.1 When the haste step or deployment ends, each player is shown what the other did there as a playback (the recap): one frame per move, in the order the moves were made. See rule D1.4b.
D5.1a The recap changes nothing in the game. A game played with recap frames is the same game, action for action, as one without them.
D5.1b A frame of the opponent's move shows that move on their side, their hand still face down, and the player's own side as the player left it.
D5.1c A move with nothing to show is not given a frame, but its log line is kept.
D5.1d The end of turn is played as one frame per trigger, in order.
D5.1e The resource step is not played back: its close arrives whole, in one update. See rule 502.
D5.1f Undoing a move inside the step removes that move's frame and keeps the others. See rule D4.
title: CR D5.1–D5.1f

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · Annex D — Digital Play Conventions › D5. Recap and Playback
D5.2 A Glimpse made in a hidden step is shown to the opponent in the recap, exactly once, in the frame of the action that made it, with its card notice. The player who glimpsed sees their own reveal at once. A Glimpse in battle reaches the opponent at once. See rules D6, 801.
 Example: A player plays Oracle of Foretelling in deployment: the opponent sees its glimpse in the recap frame of that play, and nowhere else.
title: CR D5.2

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · Annex D — Digital Play Conventions › D5. Recap and Playback
D5.3 The deployment recap pauses after the opponent's moves and again after the end of turn; the haste step's recap pauses the same way. Skip jumps to the next pause, never past it. A quiet end of turn does not pause twice.
D5.3a A recap can be watched again. Watching again pauses at the same places, shows the glimpse notices again, and hands back the board.
D5.3b The hand-over to the next turn at the end of a recap pauses longer than a frame. Every recap, live, watched again or in Learn to Play, is paced by the same rule.
title: CR D5.3–D5.3b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · Annex D — Digital Play Conventions › D5. Recap and Playback
D5.4 The client shows play no faster than one step per second. This one tempo paces both the updates the client receives and the steps within a single update.
D5.4a Items that happen at the same time under the rules arrive on screen together, then leave one at a time, in resolution order, one tempo step apart. The next group waits until this one has finished.
D5.4b Only an update the player cannot act on is held back to keep the tempo. A decision for the player, the echo of the player's own action and the end of the game are never held, and an update with legal actions is never held unless auto-pass will answer it. See rule D2.3.
D5.4c When an update the player can act on arrives, everything held before it is released with it, in order, so the player is never asked a question over an old board.
D5.4d The player's own input is never delayed by the tempo.
D5.4e The screen never falls more than a fixed number of tempo steps behind the live game.
title: CR D5.4–D5.4e

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · Annex D — Digital Play Conventions › D5. Recap and Playback
D5.5 Outside a recap playback, while play is being held back, the S key jumps to the live state. Skipping drops pending animations but still delivers the held log lines. No skip control is drawn for this. See rules D5.5c, D5.3.
D5.5a While play is held, whether the opponent is connected, and the clocks, stay current; nothing else on the board changes until the held updates are released.
D5.5b A disconnect is shown at once, not queued behind held updates, and showing it does not release them.
D5.5c During a recap playback, skipping does not jump to the live state. Skip (the S key, Space, or the Skip button drawn on the play bar) jumps to the next stop, and on a stop it continues the playback. See rules D5.3, D5.5.
title: CR D5.5–D5.5c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · Annex D — Digital Play Conventions › D6. Reveal Timing of Simultaneous Steps
D6.1 The resource step, the haste step and deployment are hidden simultaneous steps. Inside one, both players act at the same time, and neither is shown what the other does until the step ends. The end of the step is the reveal: everything the other player did in the step is shown then. At the end of the haste step and of deployment it is played back in the recap. See rule D6.2.
 Example: During deployment, nothing a player does in their region reaches the other player until deployment ends.
D6.1a Inside a hidden step, the other player's side of the game is shown as it stood when the step opened. The events the other player's actions produce are held and delivered at the end of the step. Whether the other player has finished the step is not frozen: it is shown live, except in the haste step, where the other player's readiness is hidden while the step is open.
 Example: In Learn to Play, a unit the Tutorial Bot casts during deployment is not shown to the learner until deployment closes.
 Example: In a hidden step, the count of actions each player is shown moves for their own actions and not for the other player's.
D6.1b In the haste step and in deployment, the shared deck count and the shared recycle count are shown to both players as they were when the step opened. A player's own play that moves cards into or out of those piles shows on the counts only at the reveal.
 Example: A player glimpses during deployment. The shared deck count does not drop for either player until deployment ends.
D6.1c Nothing is held during the battle phase. What happens in battle is shown to every player as it happens.
 Example: Premonition is cast in battle. Its Glimpse reveal reaches the opponent at once.
D6.1d While the haste step is open, a player is not shown whether the other player has finished it. Each player sees their own readiness. The end of the step is shown to both players.
 Example: One player finishes the haste step while the other is still choosing. The other player is not told that the first has finished.
title: CR D6.1–D6.1d

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · Annex D — Digital Play Conventions › D6. Reveal Timing of Simultaneous Steps
D6.2 A glimpse that happens inside a hidden step is shown to the other player at the reveal, not when it happens. At the end of the haste step or deployment it plays in the recap, at the moment it happened. See rule D6.1.
 Example: Oracle of Foretelling is played during deployment and glimpses 5. The opponent learns the five cards when deployment ends, in the recap.
D6.2a The player who glimpses sees their own revealed cards when they glimpse.
 Example: A player plays Oracle of Foretelling during deployment and sees the revealed cards at once; the opponent sees nothing of them until the step ends.
D6.2b At the reveal the other player is shown the glimpse exactly once, with its card notice, and the finished game log holds it once.
D6.2c Holding a glimpse until the reveal only delays it. The revealed cards are public, and every player sees them. See rule D6.1c.
 Example: Foretell is played in battle. The card it reveals is shown to the opponent.
D6.2d The same holds in Learn to Play: a glimpse by the Tutorial Bot inside a hidden step is shown to the learner in the recap. See rule D8.1.
D6.2e A card that reveals cards from the deck without the Glimpse keyword, such as Tides of the Cosmos or Big Glimpse Card, shows the revealed cards to every player as cards, in the notice a glimpse uses. A player whose own open question already shows those cards is not shown the notice. Inside a hidden step the reveal is held for the reveal at the end of the step, as a glimpse is. See rules D6.2c, 402.2a.
 Example: Tides of the Cosmos resolves for one player: the other player is shown all eight revealed cards.
 Example: Big Glimpse Card: while the opponent splits the seven cards into piles, its caster is shown all seven.
title: CR D6.2–D6.2e

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · Annex D — Digital Play Conventions › D6. Reveal Timing of Simultaneous Steps
D6.3 During the battle phase, when an item has begun to resolve and is waiting on a choice from its controller, every player is shown that the item is resolving and whose it is. The item has left the stack, and no player can respond to it (see 703.6). See rule 703.6.
D6.3a Outside the battle phase the other player is shown nothing of an item resolving. Its controller still sees the question.
 Example: Oracle of Foretelling, played in deployment, asks its controller which card to cache; the other player is shown nothing of it. The same kind of question from Premonition in battle is shown to them.
D6.3b While a resolution waits on a player's answer, every player is shown the board as it is partway through the resolution: whatever the effect has already done is on the table, including what its controller played and paid.
 Example: Insidious Invitation lets the caster play a unit first, then asks the opponent. When the opponent is asked, the caster's unit and spent mana are already on the table.
D6.3c On a board partway through a resolution, the only actions any player may take are answering the open question and conceding. See rule 104.4a.
title: CR D6.3–D6.3c

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · Annex D — Digital Play Conventions › D6. Reveal Timing of Simultaneous Steps
D6.4 Outside a hidden simultaneous step, that a player owes an answer to a question is public, and so is the card it comes from when that card is already in view. What the question is is not: its prompt, its options, its candidate targets and its kind are shown only to the player who must answer. Inside a hidden simultaneous step, not even the fact that the other player owes an answer is shown.
 Example: The attacker's Tempest Wrangler makes them choose an {Alluring} target. The defender's bar reads "Waiting for Rashi (Tempest Wrangler)" and names neither the prompt nor the candidate.
D6.4a The waiting player may be told which card the question comes from, but only when that card is already visible to them. Inside a hidden step, it is not named.
title: CR D6.4–D6.4a

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · Annex D — Digital Play Conventions › D6. Reveal Timing of Simultaneous Steps
D6.5 No message the client receives names a card in a zone hidden from that player. When cards enter another player's hand, the player is told how many entered, not which. See rule 402.2.
 Example: The opponent draws two cards. The player sees the opponent's hand grow by two card backs and is not sent their names.
D6.5a When an effect lets a player look at another player's hand, the cards are shown to the looker only: the client keeps them in the looker's note-taking strip, and no log line names them to anyone else (where a card's log line names them, it goes to the looker alone). The other players' log says only that the hand was looked at, and names no card. This holds when a player looks at their own hand too: the other player's log says that they looked at their own hand, and names nothing. See rule 402.2a.
 Example: Thought Extraction is aimed at a player's own hand. The opponent is not shown the cards in it.
 Example: Thought Extraction is aimed at its caster's own hand. The opponent's log says a hand was looked at, and names no card.
 Example: Aimed at the opponent's hand, the public line names the hand looked at.
 Example: Hand Peeper looks at the opponent's hand: no log line names the cards, and the look still works.
 Example: Hand Peeper used on its player's own hand: the look is logged for everyone, and nothing is kept in the strip.
D6.5b A card that an effect moves out of a hidden hand into another hidden zone, without the effect saying "reveal", is named only to the player who chose it. The other players are told that a card moved, not which.
 Example: Bripp recycles a card from the looked-at hand. The table is told a card was recycled; only Bripp's controller sees its name.
title: CR D6.5–D6.5b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · Annex D — Digital Play Conventions › D6. Reveal Timing of Simultaneous Steps
D6.6 Both players' caches are shown to both players in full: every cached card, and any prophecy attached to it (see 403.2). See rule 403.2.
D6.6a A cached card whose prophecy condition counts toward a number shows its progress on the board, on its owner's cache, to every player. The count shown is the one for the cache's owner.
 Example: The opponent has prophesied Vengeance ("13 Units Die"). The player can see on the opponent's cache how many of the 13 deaths have been counted.
D6.6b A prophecy whose condition is a state rather than a count shows no meter. A fulfilled prophecy shows as fulfilled instead of a meter.
 Example: A cached card whose prophecy reads "Your life is 5 or less" puts no meter on the board.
D6.6c Any player may open either player's erased pile, from the menu of the bare table (see 407.1a). See rules 407.1a, D6.15.
 Example: A player right-clicks the empty table and opens the opponent's erased pile.
D6.6d Either player may open either player's bin. When something on the stack targets a card in a bin, that card is brought to the top of the bin on the board, for both players.
 Example: A Hooba-Mon trigger on the stack targets a card six deep in a bin. That card is drawn on top of the bin for both players.
D6.6e In constructed, the view each player is sent carries the elements of both players' decks. The client reads only the player's own, to order that player's resource menu (D6.14b).
 Example: A fire deck plays a water deck in constructed. Each player is sent that one deck is fire and the other water.
title: CR D6.6–D6.6e

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · Annex D — Digital Play Conventions › D6. Reveal Timing of Simultaneous Steps
D6.7 Things that happen at the same time in the rules are shown at the same time, and things that happen one after another are shown one after another.
 Example: Combat kills several units at once and their death triggers are queued together. All of them appear on the stack strip in one beat.
D6.7a This pacing only explains what happened. It never delays the game: the board under it is already final.
 Example: While the beats of a death sweep are still playing, the units are already gone from the board state.
D6.7b Cards that make the same move in one update, from the same place to the same place, move together. Moves between different places are shown one after another. A move whose start or end the client cannot name, such as a card being erased, is shown on its own.
 Example: Four units die in one update and their four triggers go to the stack together. They all fly to the stack at once.
 Example: A card going from hand to the stack, one going from the stack to the field and one going to the bin are three moves, one after another.
 Example: Two cards erased from the field, with nowhere named to go, are not grouped.
title: CR D6.7–D6.7b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · Annex D — Digital Play Conventions › D6. Reveal Timing of Simultaneous Steps
D6.8 A unit that has become a copy of another card is drawn with the art of the card it copied, and stays marked as a copy. See rule 710.
 Example: Borrower of Forms copies Sporebloom Siren. It is drawn with Sporebloom Siren's art and a copy mark.
D6.8a A copy is marked even when its numbers match the card it copied. The bin shows the physical card, not the copied face.
 Example: Borrower of Forms (2/2) copies a 2/2. It still wears the copy mark.
D6.8b A card that only borrows abilities from another, without taking its name, keeps its own art.
 Example: Ancient One shares the text box of an adjacent ally but keeps its own portrait.
title: CR D6.8–D6.8b

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · Annex D — Digital Play Conventions › D6. Reveal Timing of Simultaneous Steps
D6.9 Where a card's printed text uses a bare X, or names a card, and this copy of the card has a value for it, the text box shows that value in its place. Stat notation (X/X, +X/+X, -X/-X), the [x] cost pip and reminder text are never changed, even when X has a value. A board-read X on the stack is not written into the text box; it is shown as a forecast (see rule D6.9c). See rules D6.9c, D6.9a.
 Example: A Poison created with X = 5 reads "Put 5 -1/-1 counters on target unit".
D6.9a A token's text box shows its actual X in place of X. Stat notation such as X/X, +X/+X and -X/-X is never changed, and neither is reminder text.
 Example: A Robot reads its X off its counters, so its text changes when they change.
D6.9b A card that names a card shows the named card in its text box, and so does a host carrying that text as a mod. With no card named, the printed text stands.
 Example: The Everywhere has named Triskaidekaphage. Its text box reads "Triskaidekaphage loses all abilities."
D6.9c When a card on the stack reads its X from the board at resolution, and the card itself declares how to forecast that X, the stack shows what X would be right now, worded as a forecast. A declared mode narrows the forecast to that mode. If X was paid, the paid X is shown and no forecast is. A board-read X with no declared forecast shows none (see rule D6.9e). See rule D6.9e.
 Example: Retribution Thing is on the stack. It shows the X it would deal now.
 Example: Retribution Thing was cast in the life-lost mode. The stack shows only that mode's forecast.
D6.9d Spell tokens in play are counted by name, with the X of each, because casting one burst token casts every token of that name (see 803). Each spell token shows its X as a large die face. See rule 803.
 Example: A player holds Fireball 1, Fireball 1 and Fireball 3. The strip shows one Fireball row: three of them, two at X = 1 and one at X = 3.
 Example: A Fireball with X = 3 shows a die face with three pips.
D6.9e A card whose X is read from the board at resolution, but which declares no forecast for it, shows no forecast on the stack. See rule D6.9c.
 [Verification of D6.9e was only partial.]
title: CR D6.9–D6.9e

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · Annex D — Digital Play Conventions › D6. Reveal Timing of Simultaneous Steps
(continues D6.9: Where a card's printed text uses a bare X, or names a card, and this copy of the card has a value for it, the text box shows that value in its place. Stat notation (X/X, +X/+X, -X/-X), the [x] cost pip and reminder text…)
D6.9f A prediction made with Prediction Prophet is shown on that card to both players, as a chip on the card and a line in its text box, from when it is made until the start of deployment reads it. A prediction left from an earlier turn is not shown.
 Example: The opponent sees the Prophet's predicted life on the card and in its text box.
 Example: A prediction of 0 is shown like any other.
D6.9g A triggered ability whose amount is its own column's share of combat damage (Vroot: "When my column deals combat damage, each opponent gains that much life.") shows that share on the stack as its X, the same amount it resolves with, not the total every column dealt.
 Example: Vroot (4/4) and a 1/1 attack in two columns and are not blocked: the stack shows X=4, and the opponent gains 4.
 Example: Vroot's text carried by a host: the stack shows the host's column share.
title: CR D6.9f–D6.9g

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · Annex D — Digital Play Conventions › D6. Reveal Timing of Simultaneous Steps
D6.10 A card whose printed text box is empty, but whose type line carries attributes, shows those attributes and their reminders in its text box instead of "no rules text". A card with no text and no attributes still says it has no rules text. See rule 204.
 Example: Whispering Mantid has no ability text and {Sneaky} on its type line. Its text box shows {Sneaky} and its reminder.
 Example: Tidal Menace has no text and no attributes, and still says it has no rules text.
D6.10a A printed bracket that offers two modes is drawn as two boxes, one around each mode, with the "or" outside them. On the stack, the mode that was not chosen is no longer shown. See rule 111.
 Example: Void Memory's "[unit or spell]" is drawn as a unit box and a spell box with "or" between them.
D6.10b When a once-per-turn ability has been used, its note wears the marker printed on that ability: [Switch1] or [once]. A card that spells the limit out in words, with no marker, gets [Once].
 Example: A spent bounded graft ability shows [Switch1], as its card prints.
D6.10c A card that is {Unstable}, whether printed or acquired, shows {Unstable} on its attribute line, with how it became Unstable.
 Example: A modded unit shows {Unstable} on its attribute line, marked as coming from a mod.
D6.10d A card with a prophecy banner shows the banner in its text box, as printed, and carries the Prophecy reminder.
 Example: The Foretold, whose whole printed text box is its banner, shows the banner instead of "no rules text".
D6.10e A card that can transform shows, in its details, what it transforms into, before the transform's cost is paid. A card that has already transformed shows no such row.
 Example: Scholar of the Void's details say it transforms into Beyond, Codex Incarnate, before its hand-discard cost is paid.
D6.10f In the card zoom, a unit whose attributes are off has only its type bar greyed; a unit whose abilities are off has its text box below the type bar greyed; a unit with both off has both greyed.
 Example: A unit Formless has stamped (attributes off) greys its type bar and not its text box.
 Example: A unit The Everywhere names (abilities off) greys below the type bar and leaves the bar.
 Example: A unit Monke switches off in battle (both off) greys the bar and the box.
title: CR D6.10–D6.10f

text:
Comprehensive Rules (unofficial) · Annex D — Digital Play Conventions › D6. Reveal Timing of Simultaneous Steps
D6.11 The reminder shown for a keyword is the game's own words wherever the game has them, in this order of preference: a reminder printed on a card in the pool; the Manual's sentence under a heading that names the term; a dated quote of a designer-posted card; and only then this client's own sentence.
 Example: {Piercing} reads "Excess damage from piercing sources is dealt to the recipient's controller." — the sentence Protective Adaptations prints.
 Example: The card-library sentence for {Rot} is used only because neither a card nor the Manual states one.
D6.11a No reminder, label or rules text shown to a player cites this client's ruling numbers.
D6.11b Where the game's reminder is shorter than the rule this client enforces, the client's fuller statement is kept and shown under the game's reminder in the card browser. Shortening what a player reads never deletes a rule.
 Example: {Piercing} shows the printed sentence, and the card browser also keeps the client's fuller rule beneath it.
